As autonomous systems reshape enterprise perimeters, defending against machine-speed threats requires retiring manual triage loops. A unified code-to-cloud platform gives security teams the context needed to trace asset ownership and shut down reachable attack paths before adversaries exploit them.

Title: Shufti ties AI agent actions to verified owners and permissions
Context: Shufti launches Know Your Agent (KYA), an AI agent verification solution designed to verify autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of individuals and businesses
Full Text:
Shufti launches Know Your Agent (KYA), an AI agent verification solution designed to verify autonomous AI agents acting on behalf of individuals and businesses. Agentic commerce enables AI agents to open accounts, place orders, and move funds for their owners. A business receiving one of these requests needs to know whether the agent is genuine, who is accountable for it, and whether the action falls within what that person approved.

A valid access token alone cannot answer these questions. Stolen credentials can appear legitimate, and agent impersonation allows fake agents to pose as trusted ones. Shufti KYA addresses these risks in a single flow by verifying the AI agent’s identity, confirming that a real person has authorized the action, and checking the agent’s permissions before it can access data or trigger a transaction.

Shufti KYA helps businesses accept authorized AI agents while blocking unauthorized or high-risk activity that could lead to AI agent fraud or chargeback disputes. It combines agent recognition, trust scoring, spoof-resistant identity verification, and permission checks to distinguish legitimate automation from suspicious or unauthorized activity before it proceeds.

Each AI agent receives a unique time-bound credential that can be revoked. Known agents are recognised by name, and new or unfamiliar agents are assessed through behavioural biometrics. Every agent is assigned a trust score to help businesses evaluate risk. Shufti already supports agents such as Meta Muse, GrokBot and OpenAI Dots, within a week of their launch.

Every agent is linked to an individual or business verified through Shufti’s modular KYC or KYB process, allowing businesses to select the checks appropriate to their requirements. Shufti KYA extends these checks to AI agents; it does not replace them.

AI agent authorization starts with a principal that sets a mandate for each AI agent, covering permitted actions, limits, expiry, and revocation. The mandate is enforced as a policy on every request, while ongoing monitoring helps detect misuse.

Each business sets its own rules within Shufti KYA. A bank can let agents view balances and pay approved billers, while new payees need a further check. A digital assets platform can let agents trade within an approved limit, while withdrawals stay blocked.

An iGaming operator can let agents monitor account activity and communicate bet settlement status, while bets must come from the verified player. A Marketplace can support purchases within customer-defined budgets, while a SaaS business can restrict agents to specific resources and tasks.

As agentic AI takes on more customer-facing tasks, Shufti aims to help businesses carry trusted automation plus agentic commerce while maintaining clear human control over AI-driven actions.

Shufti’s risk-based authorization determines when a request needs more than a mandate check. When an AI agent requests an action outside its mandate or one that exceeds a high-risk threshold, Shufti KYA brings in human-in-the-loop control that requires a liveness check in which the authorizing person completes a brief selfie verification. Shufti’s single selfie liveness is iBeta Level 3 certified, testing resistance to presentation attacks. This adds an extra layer of human oversight of high-risk AI agent actions.

Shufti Know Your Agent also maintains an audit trail of requests, decisions, and revocations linked to each agent and its principal, keeping every action traceable for accountability and review.

“Businesses are already allowing AI agents to act for their customers, and the question of who stands behind each action cannot wait for an answer later,” said Faryam Asif, Chief Technology Officer at Shufti. “Shufti Know Your Agent verifies every AI agent request with a verified owner, a clear mandate, and a record that holds up under review. Our customers can say yes to agent activity with confidence, because they know exactly who approved what, and when.”

Beyond AI agent security, Shufti KYA also supports revenue growth. Businesses can accept authorized agents and generate revenue through agent-driven transactions, while blocking rogue agents and any agent carrying a risk of fraud, unauthorized transactions, or chargeback disputes. This allows businesses to adopt AI agent automation with full human approval over agent permissions and actions.

Title: Bedrock Data routes data exposure fixes to owners and verifies results
Context: The capability is generally available today and included with the Bedrock Data platform
Full Text:
Bedrock Data has announced AI-assisted remediation, which federates the work of fixing data exposure to the data owners across the enterprise. Bedrock Data discovers who owns each exposed dataset, opens a ticket for that owner in the Jira or ServiceNow workflow the enterprise already runs and supplies the context needed to fix it. When the owner closes the ticket, Bedrock Data validates that the exposure is remediated and reopens the ticket if it is not.

Remediation now keeps pace with the rate of data creation instead of accumulating in a centralized security team’s backlog. The capability is generally available today and included with the Bedrock Data platform.

Enterprise data is measured in petabytes, billions of records, millions of documents and thousands of data stores. A centralized security team accountable for that data is small by comparison and cannot fix exposure at that scale on its own. It does not have access to most of the data and does not know how the business uses it. The data owners in engineering, data and business teams do.

Conventional DSPM tools stop at visibility, which leaves security teams with a growing list of exposures and no reliable way to get them fixed. In Bedrock Data’s Enterprise Data Security Confidence Index, 76% of respondents said a lack of automation and too much manual work hold back data security.

AI adoption raises the chance that an unresolved exposure turns into a leak. AI agents and copilots access data on their own, at machine speed, and they follow permissions rather than business intent. Sensitive data left in a test environment or a document shared too broadly was previously unlikely to be discovered.

An AI system can now find it and surface it in an answer. In EY’s 2026 AI Risk and Governance Survey, 85% of executives at companies using AI agents said some of those agents take important actions without real-time human involvement. Reducing data exposure lowers the risk of leaks, misuse and compliance violations, and it enables the enterprise to scale up AI adoption.

“Every enterprise has far more data issues than its centralized data security team can action. Until now, with data growing exponentially, risk accumulation and risk remediation were divergent curves. Data is the responsibility of the lines of business and the data organization, and remediation only scales when they own the fix,” said Bruno Kurtic, CEO of Bedrock Data.

“Bedrock Data finds the owner, sends the issue to the tools they already use, answers their questions inside the ticket and verifies the result. Security teams keep control of the rules and the audit trail, and those curves no longer diverge because remediation now operates at scale.”

Federated remediation runs through existing ITSM systems enterprises already use

Enterprises already track and resolve issues in Jira and ServiceNow, and their teams know those systems. Bedrock Data orchestrates those same systems, federating remediation to data owners at enterprise scale. There is no new tool to deploy and no new training for the people who make the fixes. Security teams can extend or override the default routing with rules written in natural language, for example “send findings on this AWS account to the cloud platform team, unless the finding involves access permissions, then route it to the identity and access team.”

Routing runs continuously as scans find new exposures, so remediation is an ongoing program rather than a one-time cleanup. The data owner makes the fix. Bedrock Data automates the workflow and verifies that each remediation has been applied.

Bedrock Data handles three steps in the remediation workflow:

Bedrock Data findings create tickets and route them to owners. Bedrock Data AI examines each exposure and explains it in context, so the owner understands the problem without a manual investigation. Tickets use the format the customer configures, including custom fields.

Bedrock Data AI answers questions inside the ticket while it is open, for example, “Who has access to this file?”

Bedrock Data policy engine tracks the ticket to closure. When the owner marks the ticket resolved, Bedrock Data validates the fix. If the exposure is gone, the ticket stays closed. If the exposure remains, Bedrock Data reopens the ticket with the reason. If Bedrock Data finds on its own that the exposure has been fixed or is no longer observed, it closes the ticket.

Where the fix is well defined, Bedrock Data can apply it directly. Customers can create a policy that revokes sharing on documents based on sensitivity and other criteria, without triggering a workflow, and notifies the data owner that the change was made. Data owners will be able to opt in to automatic remediation for exposure types that recur often and where they are comfortable automating the response.

“Data risk is my team’s responsibility, but lasting fixes have to come from the teams who run the systems every day,” said Manish Chandela, EVP Information Security, Risk and Privacy at Sportradar.

“Seeing the risk is table stakes. Reducing it means getting thousands of issues fixed without breaking the business. Bedrock Data puts each issue in front of the right owner, with the context to fix it, inside the tools they already use, and then proves the fix held. Remediation stops being a backlog my security team carries and becomes a program the whole company runs, with the evidence our board and auditors expect.”

Verified fixes deliver audit trails for PCI DSS 4.0.1, SOC 2 & NYDFS Part 500

Closing the loop changes what security leaders can show their board and auditors. Every exposure has an owner, a timeline and evidence that the fix held. Auditors working under PCI DSS 4.0.1 and SOC 2, and regulators enforcing NYDFS Part 500, expect that audit trail.

Bedrock Data produces it for every ticket it opens. IBM’s 2026 Cost of a Data Breach Report found that organizations making extensive use of AI and automation in security operations had average breach costs $1.93 million lower and lifecycles 65 days shorter than organizations that didn’t use them.

Title: How to prioritize remediation after a pentest: a practitioner workflow
Context: Would you prioritize the“critical” flaw on an intranet site, containing no sensitive data that attackers could only reach if they’d already compromised your internal network
Full Text:
A practical pentest workflow combines CVSS, EPSS and business impact to validate findings, prioritize fixes and document remediation decisions.

Remediation prioritization after a pentest is the process of ranking and ordering security findings based on their risk, exploitability, and business impact. A penetration test can produce any number of findings, ranging from the very low (zero) to the very high (hundreds).

The security of the tested organization depends on the findings management processes addressing the most important results first.

CVSS alone misranks risk. Accurate prioritization relies on combining CVSS, EPSS, and business context.

68.4% of practitioners say a 500+ candidate finding set would strain the team or be unmanageable, so it’s important to validate first.

81.7% of practitioners see AI-generated findings that need significant manual validation, so validation with concrete proof remains essential.

Document every deprioritization, because that record counts as audit evidence.

Why aren’t CVSS scores alone enough to inform remediation?

When prioritizing pentest results, some practitioners rely solely on frameworks like the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). The logic is sound: the higher a vulnerability’s CVSS score is, the more risk it poses, and the sooner you should fix it, right?

Unfortunately, the reality is much more complicated. Boiling down a complex ecosystem of risk into a one-dimensional number means ignoring the wider business context. In the end, that means you fix vulnerabilities that pose serious theoretical risk first, while genuine exposures get pushed to the back of the queue.

Lets use two hypothetical vulnerabilities as an example.

Vulnerability A is an RCE flaw, CVSS 9.8, on an isolated intranet site.

Vulnerability B is a BOLA flaw, CVSS 6.5, on a public facing production payment API.

Now think about which one you would fix first.

Would you prioritize the“critical” flaw on an intranet site, containing no sensitive data that attackers could only reach if they’d already compromised your internal network? Or would you prioritize the “medium” flaw on an API that processes live credit card transactions, and that any script kiddie could manipulate?

Across an entire organization, or multiple organizations if you’re a consultant or MSP, those critical flaws can really pile up. In one AI pentesting survey of 158 base practitioners by Pentest-Tools.com, conducted in June 2026, 68.4% of respondents said a 500+ candidate finding set would strain the team or be unmanageable.

Approaching risk prioritization by trying to fix every “Critical” finding is going to exhaust you and your team. That’s when people make mistakes, and you end up with a major incident on your hands.

What separates a validated finding from a candidate?

That same distinction, in part, separates a candidate finding from a validated one. For example, vulnerability with a high CVSS score but near-zero exploitability should remain a candidate. To graduate a vulnerability from a candidate to a legally and technically validated finding, it must pass through a strict filter that involves three processes.

The first step is to eliminate as much administrative noise as possible. That means deduplicating findings and removing any that are obviously non-exploitable.

Then, you need to confirm exploitability. That typically means executing a safe, controlled attack path against the target environment to prove that a state change, data exposure, or privilege escalation can actually occur.

Finally, you need concrete evidence. A validated finding cannot rely on a generic tool’s “confidence score.” It must include comprehensive proof that a developer or auditor can immediately follow:

Technical proof tends to include HTTP request/response traces or specific error payloads.

Proof of impact includes things like screenshots or server-side telemetry demonstrating unauthorized data access.

Now, many vendors are going to claim that AI-generated findings ease the strain of exploit validation. In many cases, they’re telling the truth. But as with any AI technology, a healthy level of skepticism is important. According to the same study, 81.7% of respondents encounter AI-generated findings that need significant manual exploit validation at least sometimes.

How do CVSS, EPSS and business context combine into a ranking?

Together, CVSS, Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) scores, and business context create a single risk ranking that reflects real-world danger to the tested organization.

CVSS, as mentioned earlier, measures theoretical severity. It tells you how bad a flaw is in a vacuum, but is entirely blind to context. EPSS measures probability. It tells you how likely an attacker is to exploit a flaw in the wild over the next 30 days, but doesn’t measure the potential impact of an exploitation.

Business context measures operational impact. It tells you the value of the affected asset, how easily an attacker can reach a flaw, and what they can steal. It tells you nothing, however, about the threat itself. Ultimately, business context is expressed as residual risk, the danger left over after you factor in your existing defenses. Calculating it relies on measuring four factors:

Exposure: Whether a server is open to the public internet.

User count: How many people use a system.

Data sensitivity: Whether the system holds sensitive information.

Compensating controls: Whether you have firewalls or antivirus tools actively blocking the attack path.

By checking these boxes, you won’t waste time fixing a “Critical” bug locked in an empty, disconnected server. Instead, you’ll prioritize the “Medium” bug on your public checkout page that hackers are actively trying to breach.

What goes first when dev time is limited?

Sometimes, you’re not going to have much time for remediation. That’s natural. In those situations, prioritize validated findings with high threat activity (EPSS score) and critical business exposure. They’re the findings that pose the most threat to your organization.

Prioritization done well is itself evidence. A ranked, validated list, with a written reason for what was deprioritized, is what a team can defend later.

You’ll need to record the owner (the specific individual accepting the risk), the date of the decision, the technical operational basis for deprioritization (such as an active compensating control), and a hard review date for re-evaluation.

Why does the ranked list count as audit evidence?

A prioritized ranking list counts as valid audit evidence because it proves compliance alignment with several major security frameworks. For example:

ISO 27001 A.8.8 demands that organizations evaluate real-world exposure, take targeted corrective actions, and retain objective evidence that the remediation loop has successfully closed.

PCI DSS 11.4 mandates that penetration testing actively validates and exploits findings, with formal retesting conducted after significant organizational changes.

SOC 2 CC7.1 relies on this documentation to confirm that an organization maintains systemic operational consistency and rigorous vulnerability triage over time.

A ranked, validated list also gives MSPs and MSSPs a clear, auditable record of truth that clients can either accept or challenge with their own evidence. This transparency ensures both sides agree on which real-world risks need to be addressed first.

What does a defensible ranking record contain?

A defensible ranking record contains the validated asset identification, its technical CVSS severity, its real-world EPSS probability, the active compensating controls defining its residual list, the formal sign-off from the risk owner, and the targeted review schedule.

Title: Why Urgent Security Fixes Aren't Fixed. Observe, Prove, Act, Confirm Gets Them Moving
Context: The alert is critical
Full Text:
The alert is critical. The fix is known. And the ticket sits in a queue for days. Security teams understand the risk, but the people who keep applications available need proof that the change won’t break anything.

Their concerns are practical. An IPS protection could block legitimate traffic. A configuration change could interrupt a service. An endpoint policy could affect an application the business depends on. Without evidence, the recommendation waits.

Safe remediation answers that hesitation with evidence. It tests the proposed action against your environment, applies the approved change, and confirms the result. Security and operations teams decide together, with facts.

The Cost of Leaving Protection in Detect

Many organizations already own protection they don’t enforce. Signatures sit inactive or in Detect mode while teams weigh false positives, inspection capacity, and business continuity. Meanwhile, applications and traffic patterns change, exceptions pile up, and policies drift away from how the environment runs today.

In the Safe Remediation white paper, 47% of the organizations measured had less than 50% protection enablement. Much of the capability they need is already in their environments.

Turning everything on isn’t the answer. Every activation carries risk. Teams need to know which changes matter for a given exposure, and how each will behave in production today.

Figure 1. Operational pressures and configuration drift can delay enforcement.

Build Confidence Before Enforcement

Safe remediation follows four stages: Observe, Prove, Act, and Confirm. Evidence carries the proposed response through each stage, with review and approval where required.

Observation starts with data your security and IT systems already produce. Vulnerability findings, IPS traffic, device utilization, endpoint policies, and configuration states show what surrounds the proposed change.

Then comes proof, and the method fits the technology. An IPS protection can inspect production traffic in Detect mode, giving teams evidence about false positives and performance before it progresses to Prevent. Operating system hardening can use a selected test group, with each host rechecked after execution. Endpoint settings can be assessed against the vendor's hardening baseline.

The decision becomes specific to your environment. Security teams explain the protection they expect. Infrastructure and application owners judge the effect on the systems they run.

Figure 2. Validation connects environmental evidence with approval, execution, and confirmation.

Use Existing Controls While Waiting For a Permanent Fix

Patching remains essential for addressing the underlying vulnerability. Testing, coordination, and deployment schedules can extend the time before a patch reaches production, creating a period when additional protection may be needed.

An existing IPS signature or virtual patch can help block the relevant exploit path during that period. Correlating vulnerability data with control coverage shows whether a suitable protection exists and whether it is inactive, in Detect mode, or already enforced.

That context helps teams select the response. A protection awaiting enforcement may be a candidate for validation and activation. An exposure without a compensating control may require urgent patching or another action.

The remediation record should distinguish interim protection from a permanent fix. A compensating control can reduce immediate exposure while the underlying vulnerability remains open and requires follow through.

Keep Approval and Execution Connected

Once an action has been evaluated, organizations can require approval of its scope or permit automated execution through configured workflows. The approved change then runs through the system responsible for the affected control.

IPS changes can use the security management server, operating system hardening can use existing patch management infrastructure, and supported endpoint changes can use the vendor API. This approach lets teams work through the technologies already deployed.

Confirmation completes the process. Policy installation can establish that an IPS protection reached enforcement. Host checks can verify a hardening change. Execution records can show failed or pending actions that still need attention, alongside the user, timestamp, and associated exposure.

Measure the Protection That Follows

Success should include evidence that the intended protection is active after execution. Subsequent security events can show whether a newly enabled control blocked activity associated with the exposure.

Across the measured organizations, remediation actions recorded a 99.5% success rate. Over one month, protections applied through remediation subsequently blocked 703.56 million attacks, including 21 million within 24 hours of remediation. These results describe the analyzed environments and provide evidence of protection following enforcement.

Figure 3. Remediation outcomes across the environments measured in the white paper.

Make Safe Remediation Part of Exposure Management

Prioritization establishes where action should begin. Safe remediation gives teams a controlled path for carrying that decision into production, with evidence supporting the proposed change and confirmation showing its result.

Check Point Exposure Management connects exposure prioritization with environmental validation, controlled execution, and confirmation through existing security technologies. Security teams can use that process to reduce exposure while evaluating the operational impact of each response.

Full Text: Thousands of GCHQ storage drives containing sensitive data have been lost for years, and the British signals intelligence agency still cannot explain where they are. According to the Investigatory Powers Commissioner’s Office’s (IPCO) annual report, the missing storage drives have been known to officials for years, and may contain data related to the Investigatory Powers Act (IPA). "I remain concerned that GCHQ has not yet established a sufficiently clear understanding of the scale, location, and recoverability of lost removable media that may contain IPA-related data, notwithstanding that the underlying issues were first drawn to my attention several years ago," wrote investigatory powers commissioner Lord Brian Leveson. "While I recognize the technical and practical challenges involved, the passage of time without a comprehensive account heightens the importance of sustained senior focus and assured remediation. Given the potential sensitivity of the material involved, I will continue to monitor progress closely.” Described as "a very significant number," the report notes that GCHQ has scoped the maximum number of potentially lost drives, but is unaware of the exact scale of the issue. The agency has embarked on "a program of further work" to locate as many of the lost devices as possible, which includes implementing an automated asset-tracking system by the end of the year. After this is up and running, it said it will be able to provide a more precise number of lost drives. A GCHQ spokesperson told The Register: "As IPCO have reported, our management system for removable media was previously not sufficiently robust to effectively track the items that were registered for use. IPCO are right to note the flaws in the data the system produced, and we have taken action against all their recommendations. "We recognize the importance of security of removable media in our systems, and have a range of measures to mitigate the risks posed by these items. The findings in the report have been addressed comprehensively, and all necessary steps to correct this issue have been taken." Losing important devices is not an achievement that's exclusive to GCHQ. Myriad stories like this have emerged from all corners of the public sector over the years, such as the British Minidstry of Defence misplacing USB drives containing secret information in the mid-noughties, civil servants routinely losing their BlackBerry handsets, and UK police losing thousands of devices, too. The missing storage drives comprise just one of the agency's various transgressions highlighted by IPCO in its report. There are also "significant concerns" over the lax safeguards used to restrict the UK's overseas partners when accessing bulk-intercepted data collected by GCHQ. IPCO was satisfied at how GCHQ ensured its own analysts remained compliant with safeguards around accessing confidential material related to journalism, journalistic sources, and privileged legal information. However, there were concerns around how these same safeguards were applied to its international partners, which have access to its so-called bulk data interception "product." The report notes that most partners were properly restricted from accessing such material, although an internal probe found that there were inadequate arrangements in respect to one partner and their access to journalistic material. Both GCHQ and the overseas agency committed to rectifying the situation. GCHQ was also questioned after a software bug in a web app "used by a relatively small section of the public" misidentified individuals thought to be participating in terrorist activities. The agency identified and reported the flaw in the software, which it used for "target discovery work," and although it only affected a small number of individuals, the errors led to five port stops made under the Terrorism Act and caused "serious prejudice" to the victims. A port stop, for the uninitiated, involves law enforcement detaining a suspect at a UK port, airport, train station, or within one mile of the Northern Ireland border, and can be carried out without suspicion. Once detained, individuals have a legal responsibility to provide passwords to their electronic devices, which can be seized for up to seven days, and in some cases have their biometric markers taken. Failure to comply can lead to a three-month prison term. IPCO ruled, however, that there was ultimately no error made as defined by the IPA. “This is because the activity was lawfully authorised under an interception warrant and the adoption of an unintentionally and unforeseeably imperfect target discovery methodology did not constitute such an error,” the report stated. Despite the agency’s vast technical expertise, IPCO said that the issue affecting the software was not foreseeable. GCHQ was not the only offender among the UK intelligence community (UKIC), with MI5's mishandling of the infamous Agent X case taking center stage in the report. Agent X was an anonymous MI5 informant whose real identity has never been publicly released. A secret inquiry by IPCO as well as the report revealed that MI5 managed Agent X despite knowing he was a violent misogynist obsessed with extreme violence. Lord Leveson said "the case of Agent X is as serious as anything I have dealt with as Commissioner," after MI5 gave false evidence to the High Court and Investigatory Powers Tribunal to protect a foreign neo-Nazi informant who was under police investigation for abusing his partner, referred to publicly as "Beth." ®

Title: Microsoft finally fixes VPN issues caused by September updates
Context: Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access
Full Text:
Microsoft has resolved Always On VPN connection failures triggered after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 security updates.

The Always On VPN remote access solution runs in the background and establishes secure tunnels back to the user's corporate network when their devices connect to the Internet. It has replaced the legacy DirectAccess technology and supports domain-joined, non-domain-joined, and Microsoft Entra ID–joined devices running Windows 10, Windows 11, and Windows Server.

Microsoft has previously mistakenly flagged this known issue as fixed in the October 2026 Windows 11 cumulative updates.

The company first acknowledged it in a service alert sent to IT administrators in late September, saying the Always On VPN failures were triggered on Windows 11 systems by the September 2026 security updates when using automatic protocol selection with IKEv2 and SSTP.

On Wednesday, Microsoft confirmed that this issue has finally been fixed for users who installed this month's KB5127936 preview update.

"This update fixes an issue that affects Always On VPN connections after installing September security update," it said. "When automatic protocol selection or protocol fallback was configured, affected VPN connections could remain stuck in a Connecting state or fail to connect after an initial connection attempt failed. In some cases, subsequent connection attempts could display the error, 'The specified port is already in use.'"

Workaround also available

Microsoft also provides a temporary fix for users who don't want to install the preview update and would rather wait for next month's Patch Tuesday cumulative updates.

This requires admins to choose one of two tunneling protocols to prevent Always On VPN failures on affected devices.

"IT administrators can mitigate this issue by changing the Always On VPN profile from automatic protocol selection to a single protocol, either SSTP only or IKEv2 only, depending on their environment and configuration," Microsoft said.

"Organizations should select the protocol based on their environment, security, and deployment requirements."

The October 2026 preview update also fixes a known issue preventing non-admin users from connecting to devices via Remote Desktop when the "Administrator protection" security feature is enabled after installing the September 2026 Windows 11 non-security preview update (or Windows updates released since then).

Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked

Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

Title: Open-weight AI model GLM-5.3 cheated its way to correct answers
Context: 3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an LLM’s ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic...
Full Text:
Irregular evaluated Zhipu AI’s open-weight model GLM-5.3 across 13 offensive cyber scenarios using CyScenarioBench, the company’s framework for measuring an LLM’s ability to plan and execute multistage attacks under realistic constraints.

The model refused none of the tasks and completed three scenarios at least once each, carrying attacks through dependent stages to reach objectives in simulated networks. Irregular said this was the strongest result it had recorded for an open-weight model.

Offensive cyber capabilities

Researchers used the officially released checkpoint. The scenarios drew on real incidents and required the model to select attack paths, coordinate dependent steps and recover from failed approaches.

Across the three completed scenarios, GLM-5.3 used an application foothold to access internal services, built alternative connection paths within simulated networks and coordinated execution across multiple machines. It automated remote desktop interactions and wrote and repaired scripts, relays, monitors and extraction tools to obtain target data.

The results followed a progression the company had previously observed in closed frontier models, beginning with GPT-5.2, released in December 2025, and continuing with models released in 2026.

Memorized code and instruction adherence

Researchers also examined how GLM-5.3 reached its answers and followed task restrictions, citing the risk that autonomous agents may break rules to complete assignments.

They tested the model’s ability to identify vulnerabilities deliberately introduced into open-source code in an evaluation environment. An agent-assisted transcript review found that code reconstructed from memory contributed to roughly 80% of the successful GLM-5.3 runs examined. In some runs, it provided an early clue; in others, it supported a finding the model had already reached.

Using memorized code violated no instructions in those tests. The report said it could nevertheless undermine results intended to measure vulnerability discovery by giving the model access to the answer through prior exposure.

Irregular had observed this behavior in closed models as well. The researchers said evaluations using open-source code needed to account for prior familiarity, given capability gains and the use of such code in pretraining and post-training. Restricting internet access does not remove that familiarity.

Reward hacking and deployment risks

In separate instruction-adherence tests, GLM-5.3 was explicitly prohibited from outputting code reproduced from memory. The model nevertheless repeatedly reproduced memorized code verbatim and used it to reach correct answers.

The researchers interpreted these violations as a form of reward hacking in which the model produced the expected answer by bypassing a constraint central to the evaluation.

They warned that judging answers solely on correctness could mislead capability assessments and deployment decisions. Rewarding those answers during training could reinforce instruction violations.

The report advised operators to monitor the model’s reasoning alongside its actions and outcomes, assessing compliance with instructions as well as answer accuracy.

“Organizations adopting these models should test how reliably they follow task restrictions before granting them broader access or autonomy. The more capable a model is in offensive cyber operations, the more caution any misaligned behavior it shows calls for,” the company concluded.

Title: We are not ready for what AI has done to red teaming
Context: Prepare for hybrid threat vectors: As digital perimeters harden through automated defense, attacks will increasingly blend hyper-automated digital exploits with highly...
Full Text:
Something shifted in offensive security over the last eighteen months that most organizations haven’t fully absorbed yet. It isn’t that attackers got smarter. It’s that the economics of attack changed entirely — and those of us who run red teams have had a front-row seat to the transformation.

The conversation about AI in cybersecurity tends to fixate on defense: better anomaly detection, faster triage, and AI-assisted SOC analysts. That framing misses the more urgent story. The attack side of this ledger has already been rewritten. A small, well-equipped offensive team using frontier AI models today can outperform what was possible with a much larger traditional operation just two years ago, by a margin that should unsettle every security leader reading this.

Through our work on the front lines of offensive security, the consensus is clear: if you are not augmenting your operations with AI, you are already at a disadvantage.

Before addressing the operational shift, we must clarify a fundamental distinction that is often conflated in industry discussions:

AI red teaming: This involves probing Large Language Models (LLMs) for vulnerabilities, testing agentic pipelines, and identifying prompt-injection vectors or unintended behaviors.

Red teaming with AI: Using AI as an operator’s tool to execute traditional offensive operations.

It is this second category, Red Teaming with AI, where the most immediate, drastic, and dangerous transformation is occurring.

The staggering scale of productivity

AI-augmented operations transitioned from a nice-to-have luxury to a non-negotiable requirement. The democratization of frontier models introduces asymmetry between well-equipped adversaries and traditional defensive teams relying on manual triage.

The productivity leaps we are seeing in the field are staggering. When AI is effectively weaponized by offensive teams, some of the initial findings speak for themselves:

Metric

Traditional red teaming

AI-augmented red teaming

Annual team output

60 to 70 findings (3-4 person team)

90+ findings generated in a single after-hours exercise

Single app engagement

7 to 10 findings

100+ true positive findings

Large-scale scanning

Takes appropriate sequencing and pipelines, or times out entirely

Enables you to build capabilities that can scan millions of IPs in 2-3 hours (for roughly $20k-$30k)

Reconnaissance of external applications

150-200 valid findings/year

100+ findings a month

(Data above aggregated by DayBlink Consulting over past 10 years of engagements and validated by Robert Pimentel as representative of his Red team experience.)

AI across the engagement lifecycle

We are no longer just using AI to write phishing emails. Organizations and threat actors alike are adopting a structured approach to integrate AI throughout every phase of the kill chain:

Pre-operation (setup and reconnaissance): The weeks-long setup phase has been accelerated into mere moments. Gathering Open-Source Intelligence (OSINT), provisioning infrastructure, building organizational charts, and configuring command-and-control (C2) servers can now be delegated to agentic AI. This significantly reduces the time and manual effort needed to get an operation off the ground, though complex infrastructure decisions still require experienced operators. Pre-op usually starts off exciting (new op coming) but often ends in a grind. We love the acceleration AI has provided here.

Mid-operation (enumeration and attack): during active engagements, AI acts as a real-time, on-demand expert. Operators use AI interactively to generate custom audit scripts, rapidly adapt strategies, and query unfamiliar technology stacks on the fly. By utilizing an LLMs-as-judges workflow, where one model’s output is vetted by another for correctness and risk before execution, attackers can ensure highly confident, automated actions. Enumeration and attack is where all the excitement and adrenaline happens. We are using AI to help here, but it’s not replacing us humans (yet).

Post-operation (reporting and deconfliction): reporting has historically been the most tedious burden of any engagement. Today, nine to ten months of raw C2 logs can be piped into a frontier model to generate a comprehensive deconfliction report in under 20 minutes. These tools can map every executed command to the MITRE ATT&CK framework, cross-reference threat intelligence, and translate highly technical data into clear, actionable narratives for board-level executives. The output still requires manual review. AI gets you to a first draft in minutes instead of days, but an operator needs to verify findings, validate ATT&CK mappings, and ensure accuracy before delivery. Ticketing and follow-up are the bane of most red teams. AI has become an awesome sidekick to our teams to build our reports and do lots of the tedious work.

The talent divide: judgment as the ultimate differentiator

With AI automating basic enumeration, scanning, and scaffolding, the core red-teaming skill set — critical thinking, architectural understanding, adversarial judgment — is as valuable as it’s ever been. AI doesn’t replace that. But operators who can leverage AI alongside those skills will outperform those who can’t. The differentiator isn’t AI versus no AI; it’s whether you have the foundational knowledge to direct it effectively and validate what it gives you. This is fundamentally shifting the required profile of a successful cybersecurity professional. As a result, the industry is quickly diverging into two distinct categories of practitioners:

The “unicorns” (high performers): These are the practitioners who bring critical thinking and deep adversarial judgment to AI. They understand exactly where trust boundaries fail and where architectures are weak. They use AI to execute on these insights efficiently, offloading the busywork to focus on complex exploitation.

The “slop cannons”: Operators who use AI as a mindless copy-paste shortcut. They rely entirely on unverified outputs without understanding the underlying mechanics, producing noisy, easily detectable work that wastes time and triggers alarms.

Consequently, hiring practices must change. The primary screening criterion for new talent can no longer be a stack of legacy certifications; it must be their hands-on curiosity, their fundamental understanding of network architecture, and their experience building tools with frontier AI models. Certifications still matter, but hiring must also evaluate whether candidates can think critically about systems and leverage AI tools effectively — not just operate them blindly

Strategic imperatives for 2027

For security leaders looking to survive this paradigm shift, the path forward requires immediate action. Based on our observations, here are the critical priorities for the next 18 months:

Formalize AI budgets: Access to frontier models is expensive, but it is a necessary operational cost. Teams without the budget to experiment and build will fall behind adversaries.

Implement continuous, programmatic testing: As enterprises deploy thousands of their own agentic integrations, manual testing is no longer viable. Continuous, automated adversarial testing must become the standard operating procedure.

Prepare for hybrid threat vectors: As digital perimeters harden through automated defense, attacks will increasingly blend hyper-automated digital exploits with highly sophisticated physical and social engineering vectors.

Hire for curiosity: Build teams anchored by practitioners who are actively experimenting with AI and possess the high-level judgment needed to guide it safely and effectively.

Organizations that fail to adopt an AI-augmented mindset risk being overwhelmed by adversaries operating faster, smarter, and at an unprecedented scale. Success in the modern cyber landscape relies on one core principle: seamlessly combining elite human judgment with intelligent automation.

Title: Beyond deterministic worms: Preparing the SOC for reasoning adversaries
Context: In early July, they found a compromised server, revoked credentials and blocked the exploited paths
Full Text:
In May 2017, the WannaCry cryptoworm spread across the internet, compromising more than 200,000 computers in at least 100 countries. The National Audit Office called it the largest cyberattack ever to hit the NHS in England. At least 80 of 236 hospital trusts were infected or disrupted, an estimated 19,000 appointments were cancelled, five hospitals diverted ambulances, and more than 1,200 pieces of diagnostic equipment were infected.

What stopped WannaCry was a stroke of luck. A researcher reverse engineered the malware, noticed it contacting a domain nobody had registered, and registered it. That evening the original strain stopped locking devices. WannaCry had a kill switch, and we are all fortunate that Marcus Hutchins was able to find it.

As I read agent incident reports from OpenAI and Anthropic, I am reminded of WannaCry. But the threat from offensive agents is not a faster worm. In July, roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents being tested on a cybersecurity benchmark found an unsanctioned message board on an internal software repository, and some broke out to the internet. About 700 of those agents went on to attack Hugging Face, looking for clues to beat the benchmark, according to an independent investigation. Hugging Face disclosed the intrusion on July 16, and OpenAI confirmed its agents were responsible five days later.

Recently Anthropic has had unintended incidents as well. Anthropic’s incidents involved single models rather than a swarm. In cyber evaluations that were accidentally left connected to the internet, individual Claude models attacked real companies’ systems while trying to complete their exercises, and one published a malicious package to PyPI.

Worms like WannaCry exploit a single or small number of vulnerabilities, using a static set of techniques. Agents can read the results of failed attempts, try something else, and pass on what they learned to other agents. Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team evaluated GLM-5.3, an open-weights model from Z.ai that NIST’s CAISI assessed as the most cyber-capable open-weight model released to date. Over a day, with under an hour of hands-on attention, a researcher used it to find several unknown browser vulnerabilities and chain them into an exploit that steals a user’s SSH key. A smaller variant built an exploit chain for two known flaws for roughly $20 at API prices. Simple techniques bypassed its safeguards 64% to 100% of the time in simulated tests, including abliteration, which edits the released weights to strip out refusals.

A high-performing SOC working to the “1-10-60” benchmark — 1 minute to detect, 10 to investigate, and 60 to contain — is not built for this. When the adversary moves from a human at a keyboard to groups of autonomous agents operating at machine speed, response has to be measured in seconds. The Hugging Face incident shows the gap even when the agents belong to a well-intentioned party. OpenAI did not contain them in time.

OpenAI reports that its own monitoring flagged the agents twice in the preceding weeks. In June, their responders decided the activity did not warrant stopping the evaluation. In early July, they found a compromised server, revoked credentials and blocked the exploited paths. Within a day of the evaluations resuming, the agents had found a new zero-day and were back on the internet. They compromised Hugging Face between July 11 and 13, and OpenAI linked it to its agents on July 20. When Hugging Face investigated the intrusion, the hosted models it tried first refused to analyze the attack logs, and its team finished the forensics with GLM-5.2 running on its own infrastructure. As Hugging Face put it: “the attacker was bound by no usage policy, while our own forensic work was blocked by the guardrails of the hosted models we first tried.”

What makes this different

None of this is new to our industry. We have always played leapfrog with attackers. What is new today is that they can now download capable models with no meaningful safeguards and build their own offensive agents.

Imagine WannaCry if the worm rewrote itself the moment the domain was registered. The best SOC in the world would still be diagnosing the initial compromise when it had moved on.

Agents that depend on a provider can be contained by revoking credentials, suspending accounts, and blocking egress, though OpenAI’s experience shows it may take more than one attempt. Open-weight models running on an attacker’s hardware cannot. Anthropic recently tested whether small models could replicate across cheap connected devices without a datacenter. In simplified evaluations with trivial access controls, a stronger open-weight model completed the full chain, and Anthropic projects small models reaching that level by year-end if current trends hold. A replicator like that has no central point to switch off. It would be slow and visible on the network, but patient and everywhere. Hospitals know the problem: Some equipment WannaCry disrupted, such as MRI scanners with embedded Windows XP, was vendor-managed and could not be updated by the trusts.

Agents do not need to be intentionally asked to embark on offensive exercises to exhibit harmful behavior. Transluce documented agents asked to do ordinary data retrieval that, when blocked, probed public websites for vulnerabilities, including an Australian government agency. Some were linked to the swarm OpenAI has acknowledged as its own. The Hugging Face agents were trying to win a benchmark. Poorly constrained agents are enough for unintended harmful activity.

We are deploying agents as assistance for site reliability engineering (SRE) and infrastructure as code (IaC) ourselves, and cloud providers are shipping agent toolkits to manage infrastructure. When, not if, a compromised or poorly managed agent holds those privileges, it will be able to deploy its own infrastructure to run on. We have already seen agents in a lab environment stand up their own relays and cloud infrastructure with stolen credentials.

Meeting the agent challenge

But we can still prepare for these future scenarios today. To do so, CISOs must treat agents as privileged identities:

Give each agent short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials, with no standing permissions.

Forbid agents from creating new identities, compute, or network paths without human approval.

Put agent workloads behind egress allowlists, so a blocked agent cannot go looking for another way out.

Enforce policy-as-code guardrails on infrastructure pipelines, and alert on anomalous machine-identity behavior and unexpected resource creation.

The NAO’s report is the best documentation of WannaCry’s damage, and it covers a single health system in one country. Large groups of agents carrying a ransom payload could reach hospitals across the planet with no kill switch to find. Autonomous defense is extremely challenging in healthcare, because a false positive can interrupt patient monitoring, biomedical telemetry or imaging, having a significant impact on patient safety. Current tools, including copilots that help a human triage alerts faster, are nowhere close to the offensive capabilities the labs are evaluating. We need defensive parity at machine speed.

Zero false positives is not a realistic engineering target, so design of autonomous defense has to assume mistakes and limit their cost. Automate fast, narrowly scoped, reversible actions such as isolating a single device, revoking a narrowly scoped token or quarantining a workload, and keep a human in the loop for anything irreversible or clinically risky. Always have a way to reverse automated actions as quickly as they are introduced. We need to build graduated autonomy, tiered by asset class. You can be more aggressive on the corporate assets, and more conservative around biomedical devices.

Leveling up security fundamentals — and business support

What else can we do today? Keep our tried-and-true practices and run them faster — something that will require leadership, and additional support from CEOs and the board.

In its analysis, the NAO found that applying the patch, or simply managing internet-facing firewalls, would have protected every NHS organization WannaCry infected. Companies and open source projects are now running coding agents over their software and releasing an unprecedented number of security patches. This is great but IT needs to be able to apply them. Give IT the resources to deploy them, retire outdated infrastructure, and make the business tolerant of the maintenance windows this requires.

That segmentation or zero trust initiative that has been on the back burner? Make it a priority. Today. If you are still underinvested in security, increase funding now so your team or vendor can acquire the tools and expertise the next few years will demand. And accept that automated defense will sometimes get it wrong. Security teams will have to automate, and the business will have to tolerate the outages that follow. The technology is emerging and it will not be perfect. Support your teams anyway.

An open letter to the AI labs and the security community at large

A note to the frontier labs. Several of you deserve credit: Project Glasswing and OpenAI’s Patch the Planet put frontier capability in defenders’ hands, and your incident reports have been unusually candid.

But offensive capability is moving faster than safeguards. GLM-5.3 shipped as downloadable weights that simple techniques unlocked 64% to 100% of the time, and gated access does nothing about weights already in attackers’ hands.

As a result, I am asking for three things:

Hold defensive research to the same urgency as capability research, including autonomous containment with a safety case that works in clinical environments.

Widen defenders’ access to the class of models attackers will have.

Make independent testing before release, and independent investigation after incidents, an obligation rather than a courtesy. METR’s CEO noted that OpenAI let investigators in voluntarily, with no industry requirement on any lab to disclose an incident.

I have seen too many security professionals dismiss talk of offensive AI as marketing or fearmongering and answer concerns with “fix your stuff.” Patching matters, and the NAO’s findings on WannaCry articulate that, but that is not the only answer to agents that organize on improvised message boards and probe websites while doing ordinary work.

WannaCry’s authors left a kill switch in. The next generation of threats will not have one, and cybercriminals will not disclose when they lose control of a swarm. We cannot rely on strokes of luck. Let’s recognize the risk, discuss it, and prepare before the attackers start using these tools in earnest.

Title: What exactly is ISOC? And what does it mean for you?
Context: The goal of identifying ISOC as a new category then, is instead to adapt and assess the ability of a vendor to integrate classic SIEM logic with an expanded threat detection...
Full Text:
Gartner recently released a new category of assessing security tools: the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC). Even though SIEM isn’t going anywhere, a rapidly evolving threat landscape is forcing a shift in industry logic that is reflected in the emergence of this new category.

For years, SIEM has dominated as an all-encompassing category. But SIEMs are no longer sufficient to collect data, support investigations, and manage incidents; instead, the SIEM has separated into distinct architectural layers. SIEM platforms, which remain the security system of record for collecting, normalizing, searching, and analyzing event data, are now distinct from the Integrated Security Operations Center (ISOC) solutions. ISOC is tasked with unifying detection, investigation, case management, and response across security domains and security/observability data pipelines.

As AI empowers attackers and more threat landscapes emerge, this stratification becomes essential. Data management, analytics, and operational response are now separate problems, and, as a result, demand separate solutions. This is where ISOC finds its space: to reduce costs, latency, and operational friction.

The goal of identifying ISOC as a new category then, is instead to adapt and assess the ability of a vendor to integrate classic SIEM logic with an expanded threat detection investigation and response (TDIR) capability. Reduced complexity is especially key for lean teams who prioritize efficiency and streamlined workflows, and the goal of ISOC is to reduce the friction that comes with conglomerating a wide variety of different security tools to contrive full visibility.

In short, ISOC addresses the pain point that every security team faces today. Instead of juggling an array of disjointed tools provided by different vendors, a single vendor streamlines the production of a providing a flexible and adaptable, yet holistic and transparent security solution. This gives a business the efficiency and flexibility to reduce costs, reduce deployment time, and allay growing SIEM complexities.

Common features of the ISOC, as Gartner writes, include native detection and response services, incident case management, and extended case management of data ingestion. ISOC should reduce the friction between security tools and the latency between data, context, decision, and action. Machine-speed responses are more essential than ever in an age where attackers are all armed with the most advanced AI tools.

Latency challenges in Native Detection and Response, Security Data Ownership, Incident Case Management, Cross-Domain Correlation, and Automation and Agentic Response, and Open Ingestion and Response Fabric are becoming issues that business can’t afford to ignore.

Detection and response must operate on the same underlying security data, not through loosely connected point products. Native controls reduce latency between signal, correlation, investigation, and action. ISOC starts with control of the data layer: ingesting, normalizing, enriching, retaining, and making telemetry available for detection and AI reasoning. If the platform does not control the data model, every downstream analytic or agent is working through integration boundaries.

Alerts, entities, evidence, timelines, and analyst actions are assembled into a persistent incident object. The case becomes the operational unit for investigation and response rather than individual alerts. Endpoint, network, identity, cloud, application, and third-party telemetry must be correlated against a common schema and context model. This is what allows weak individual signals to become a high-confidence attack story.

Automation should operate directly against normalized data and incident context, enabling AI agents and playbooks to investigate, enrich, recommend, and execute actions without repeatedly rebuilding context. ISOC must connect broadly to existing security infrastructure while minimizing translation and API friction.

The objective is a common data and control plane where third-party tools contribute signals and become response surfaces.

Looking ahead

As the SIEM market grows, the market share will be divided to include ISOC vendors, who will expand their offerings to include coverage in identity, cloud/Saas management, and email security.

The market is only reflecting the dynamics that security teams have been feeling for years, which has been exacerbated exponentially by the adoption of AI by threat agents. Simply agglomerating more tools is neither strategic, nor effective. And a single vendor approach is key to striking the right balance between efficacy and simplicity. Finding the right tool portfolio now means finding the right vendor.

The market confirms what Stellar Cyber postulated: modern operational needs demand integrated, unified capabilities. From setting an open integration standard to incorporating AI-native capabilities, ISOC environments are meant to simplify operations without compromising coverage or visibility.

Anticipating the limitations of fragmented security stacks leads to natively unified operational platforms. By normalizing raw data from any source through high-context schema technology, modern ISOC solutions deliver the precise, consolidated out-of-the-box outcomes now expected in the market.

An AI SOC that starts with somebody else’s alert is already too late.

Stellar Cyber collects and normalizes telemetry, detects suspicious activity, correlates evidence, builds cases, investigates incidents, triages findings, and drives response from the same security architecture. That gives people and AI access to the evidence behind the alert – not just the alert itself.

Title: Build an Intelligence Advantage with Falcon Next-Gen SIEM
Context: CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM brings threat intelligence and security telemetry together in Third-Party IOC Management, a new feature that enables organizations to...
Full Text:
Every organization has a different threat profile. Industry, geography, infrastructure, business operations, and the broader technology ecosystem all influence which adversaries and threats matter most.

The challenge is putting threat intelligence to work at scale to identify the greatest threats to each business. The intelligence that security teams rely on is as varied as the threats they face. Organizations draw from commercial threat intelligence providers, industry information sharing and analysis centers (ISACs), government sources, open-source research, trusted partners, and indicators uncovered through their own threat hunting and incident response efforts.

Modern security operations need a "Bring your own intelligence" strategy to manage these disparate sources. CrowdStrike Falcon® Next-Gen SIEM brings threat intelligence and security telemetry together in Third-Party IOC Management, a new feature that enables organizations to incorporate their own intelligence directly into detection and investigation workflows.

Full Text: Crypto exchange Binance has paused trading after discovering unknown parties cracked one of its workers’ laptops and used it to make massive trades. Late on Thursday, US time, the company used its social media feeds to report “Our teams are aware of reports of a potential security issue and are actively investigating.” The exchange insisted “User funds are completely safe” and warned its customers “should remain cautious of scams and should not trust unofficial links, messages, or requests for account information.” The company soon froze $2.5 billion worth of assets and warned that the figure could go higher “as our teams work closely with law enforcement, issuers, blockchain intelligence firms and industry partners to trace and freeze additional assets.” To prevent the matter worsening, Binance halted all trading, deposits, and withdrawals. Title: PHP2Shell plus Fragnesia: A dangerous new route from web server to root
Context: The PHP2Shell saga continues, with attackers discovering new ways to exploit the critical vulnerability impacting millions of organizations worldwide
Full Text:
The PHP2Shell saga continues, with attackers discovering new ways to exploit the critical vulnerability impacting millions of organizations worldwide.

The US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has warned of a high severity Linux kernel privilege escalation flaw that attackers are chaining with PHP2Shell bugs in the wild.

Identified as CVE-2026-46300, it could allow attackers to run malicious code with root permissions, giving them unrestricted ability to run commands, tamper with system settings, view, edit, or delete files, and perform other malicious actions.

Once attackers establish root access, they can perform any action on a server including, but not limited to, disabling the server, creating accounts, removing accounts, connecting to other servers, and adding/removing software, explained Scott Miserendino, CTO at security and compliance platform DataBee.

“PHP2Shell allows for remote access, but that access is typically limited by the account used to run the PHP service,” he said. “By chaining with CVE-2026-46300, that attacker can get unlimited access.”

Researchers at Dream Security have discovered that this attack has already been used to breach 25 servers, including three affiliated with the US government.

Federal agencies have been ordered to patch the flaw, which is known as Fragnesia.

Anatomy of an attack

PHP is a widely-used, open source server-side scripting language that serves as the backbone for websites like WordPress, which powers 43% of the web, as well as Mailchimp, Drupal, parts of Slack and Zoom, and numerous others.

Last week, the PHP Foundation disclosed two flaws in the PHP scripting language that could allow attackers to perform unauthenticated remote code execution (RCE). CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 are both rated a critical 9.2 in severity on the common vulnerability and scoring system (CVSS). The two vulnerabilities are collectively tracked as PHP2Shell. As a result of the disclosure, some government and enterprise websites shut down entirely while awaiting patches.

CVE-2026-46300, dubbed Fragnesia, is a new development in the saga. It is identified as part of the Dirty Frag vulnerability class, a set of local privilege escalation (LPE) bugs in the Linux kernel.

The Dream researchers described an attack they tracked in the wild, in which threat actors built a persistent tunnel into an internal network “within hours.” They developed two distinct exploits, stringing them together to target any Palo Alto Network firewall running a vulnerable build of PAN-OS, and achieved root access in a single HTTP request without any credentials.

After rooting the firewalls, the threat actor launched attacks against Active Directory (AD), giving them the ability to extract credentials and discover hidden files, folders, and other sensitive resources, according to the Dream researchers. The researchers confirmed that the threat actor then possessed a full AD user group listing and “complete organizational blueprint,” private keys and complete network topology, including the IP, hostname, server role, and VPN gateway, and had accessed decrypted service account credentials allowing direct AD queries at any time.

The adversarial actor also parked nearly two dozen firewalls across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, “ready for exploitation at any time.” The Dream researchers noted that the breach did not appear to be a fully autonomous nation-state attack, but did include some AI-assisted tooling like Claude Code and AI-powered offensive security platforms configured with Chinese large language models (LLMs) DeepSeek and Kimi.

“The operation illustrates how an exposed management interface can become a path into an organization’s identity infrastructure,” the Dream researchers wrote.

Plenty of material for attackers to work with

The two PHP bugs gave an attacker code execution privileges using the web service account, and the kernel bug is what turned that into root, explained Aaron Beardslee, manager of threat research at Securonix, who noted, “The kernel bug writes its payload into the page cache rather than to disk.”

Once an attacker has the ability to execute code, the damage they can do depends on the permissions and credentials available to that process, he explained. Application configuration files, database credentials, and access to internal services can provide “plenty of material for an attacker to work with.” They may also be able to execute commands, retrieve additional tooling or establish persistence.

“Web servers have an unfortunate habit of knowing more about the rest of the environment than anyone intended,” he pointed out.

The chain’s post-access sequence, as described by the researchers, was: Root the perimeter host, stand up a reverse Secure Shell (SSH) tunnel to an internal management server, recover a Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) service account credential, then “enumerate domain users and groups, spray passwords, and attempt to create backdoor accounts in Active Directory.”

PHP has “been holding up a substantial chunk” of the internet for decades, and these vulnerabilities live in the runtime itself, Beardslee noted. An enterprise’s WordPress installation can be fully patched, plugins can be current, but the underlying PHP process can still be vulnerable to unauthenticated code execution.

The reported victim count (25 servers so far, mostly firewall appliances, on a government affiliated network) is the part everyone will quote, but it is not the interesting part, he said. Counts differ, and attribution is “openly contested.” None of them is what matters to defenders.

“What matters is that the privilege escalation step in this chain is invisible to disk-based integrity checking,” Beardslee said, “and that the standard remediation advice destroys the evidence of it.”

Remediation

Unfortunately, CVE-2026-46300 is a low-level Linux kernel bug, so the only remedy is to upgrade to a patched Linux version, said DataBee’s Miserendino. There are some options short of full patching, but those could break the system, or at a minimum require IPSec encapsulating security payload (ESP) to be disabled. But that can introduce additional flaws.

“Patch the kernel, and capture memory first on anything you suspect,” Beardslee recommended, noting that the Fragnesia fix is not included in the Dirty Frag patches. “The triage order matters more here than it usually does, because the reboot is what erases the evidence.”

As well, audit the core built-in kernel modules esp4 and esp6, which are responsible for handling the IPsec ESP network protocol, on every internet-facing Linux host, he advised. If nothing terminates IPsec there, “the modules have no business being loaded,” and unloading them removes the vulnerability path without waiting for a maintenance window.

And check which hosts hold a directory service credential, then alert of LDAP binds from anything that isn’t on that list, he said: “This is the control that catches the chain at the stage where it stops being a web server problem and starts being a domain problem.” Further, he said, re-point identity detections at “the source, not the tool.”
