Full Text:
Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling. A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users. Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems. The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider. Tailworm targets Tailscale. Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack. A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer. Norway raises their cyber risk level to high. Our guest is Amy Blackshaw, Senior Vice President of Product Marketing for Identity at Palo Alto Networks, discussing AI exploits and identity containment. AI science needs a spam filter.

Today is Wednesday October 28th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Senators accuse the White House of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling.

Two Democratic senators accuse the Trump administration of illegally withholding a secret surveillance court ruling as Congress considers renewing a controversial intelligence program.

Senators Ron Wyden and Adam Schiff say the administration missed a September deadline to release findings from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court concerning Section 702 of FISA.

The court reportedly found that intelligence agencies used filtering tools to search Americans’ intercepted communications without required safeguards, including approvals and documentation.

Section 702 expired in June, but surveillance continues under a court authorization lasting until March.

The administration has promoted the program’s effectiveness while keeping the ruling classified, despite earlier promises to release it.

Civil liberties organizations are urging Congress to withhold reauthorization until the findings become public.

Wyden and Schiff have demanded an explanation by November sixth.

The dispute raises a fundamental question: How can Congress evaluate the legality of government surveillance when critical findings about that surveillance remain secret?

A suspected surveillance operation targets Starlink users.

Cybersecurity researchers have uncovered a suspected surveillance operation targeting users of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service.

According to Reuters, researchers at TrendAI found that an Israeli advertising technology company, Discover-Tech, was aggressively bidding for ads targeting Starlink users in more than 100 countries.

The company was particularly active in conflict zones, including Syria, Yemen, Libya, and South Sudan, where legitimate advertising demand is limited.

Researchers believe the activity was designed to exploit data leaked through online advertising auctions, potentially allowing operators to identify, locate, and track Starlink users.

TrendAI initially identified the operation only by the codename Shadow-Earth-79, reportedly declining to name Discover-Tech over legal concerns.

Citizen Lab and Confiant independently identified the company, prompting Google, Comcast, and others to remove it from their advertising platforms.

Attackers probe vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems.

Attackers are already probing for vulnerable Oracle E-Business Suite systems following the disclosure of a critical security flaw.

Tracked as CVE-2026-101767, the vulnerability allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit a SQL injection flaw and potentially take complete control of affected systems.

Oracle released a patch on October twentieth, urging customers to update immediately.

Security firm Defused says its honeypots detected attempted exploitation on October twenty-seventh, although Oracle has not confirmed active exploitation in the wild.

Shadowserver has identified more than 670 internet-exposed Oracle E-Business Suite instances, mostly in the United States. It’s unclear how many remain vulnerable.

The activity follows previous attacks against Oracle enterprise software, including a campaign by the Clop extortion gang that exploited a separate E-Business Suite vulnerability to target major corporations and universities.

The FBI shuts down a bulletproof hosting provider.

The FBI has seized the domain of Virtualine, a so-called bulletproof hosting provider accused of supporting cybercrime, money laundering, and the distribution of child sexual abuse material.

Operating under several names, Virtualine openly advertised hosting services for illegal activities, promising to ignore abuse complaints and law enforcement requests.

According to the Justice Department, the company continued supporting a forum distributing illegal content even after receiving complaints from international authorities. Prosecutors also allege Virtualine helped the forum’s operators establish another site and attempted to launder cryptocurrency payments.

No arrests or criminal charges were announced.

The seizure follows international crackdowns on similar providers linked to ransomware operations. But researchers warn that disrupting these services often simply pushes criminal customers toward replacement providers, rather than eliminating the underlying market.

Tailworm targets Tailscale.

Tailscale is rolling out fixes for a collection of security vulnerabilities that researchers say could allow attackers to move rapidly through private networks.

Dubbed Tailworm, the findings from Cyberdione Labs include eleven issues affecting Tailscale and the open-source headscale server.

Four vulnerabilities involve Tailscale SSH, where improper privilege handling could allow an attacker with access to one compromised device to gain root privileges on other authorized servers.

Researchers demonstrated automated attacks spreading between vulnerable machines in less than a second per hop, without user interaction.

Tailscale emphasizes that exploitation requires existing network access and depends on SSH policies. There’s no reported exploitation in the wild.

The company has published security bulletins and remediation guidance. Organizations are advised to review SSH access policies and disable unnecessary forwarding.

Ohio’s Auditor of State investigates a cyberattack.

Ohio’s Auditor of State is investigating a cyberattack targeting its web server, potentially involving foreign state actors.

Auditor Keith Faber says security monitoring detected and isolated the threat, prompting officials to take the server and online accounts offline.

The incident was not ransomware, and officials have found no evidence that personal or government financial information was compromised. Payment data is stored separately.

State and federal law enforcement are investigating. A temporary website is planned, and audit clients experiencing payment disruptions will receive a grace period.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupts Israel’s largest vehicle importer.

A suspected ransomware attack disrupted operations at Colmobil, Israel’s largest vehicle importer, delaying vehicle deliveries and services.

Israel’s Ministry of Transport disconnected the company from government registration systems as a precaution, while customers reported delays involving Mercedes-Benz vehicles.

According to sources cited by Calcalist, the ransomware group SETTRA was responsible and demanded payment. Industry sources say Colmobil paid the ransom, though the company has declined to confirm either claim.

Colmobil says it has restored operations and that the incident did not affect vehicle systems or manufacturers.

The attack highlights the automotive industry’s growing dependence on interconnected digital infrastructure, from vehicle registration and payments to maintenance and diagnostics.

While researchers have demonstrated attacks against connected vehicles, there’s no evidence this incident involved attempts to remotely control cars.

Norway raises their cyber risk level to high.

Norway’s National Security Authority, or NSM, has raised the country’s cyber risk level to high, publicly disclosing its assessment for the first time.

The agency reports a threefold increase in successful cyber operations against Norwegian organizations over the past six months, with some incidents posing serious national security risks.

Defense, aerospace, critical infrastructure, and their suppliers face particularly elevated threats, including reconnaissance, attempted intrusions, ransomware, and denial-of-service attacks.

Officials also warn that artificial intelligence could accelerate attacks by helping adversaries identify vulnerabilities more efficiently, although such AI-enabled activity hasn’t been documented in Norway.

NSM is urging organizations to strengthen defenses immediately, emphasizing phishing-resistant authentication, network segmentation, improved monitoring, vulnerability management, and supply chain security.

The agency says stronger organizational defenses can help reduce the country’s overall cyber risk.

AI science needs a spam filter.

Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific research, but it’s also creating a rather inconvenient problem: scientists are increasingly struggling to separate genuine discoveries from AI-generated nonsense.

Science journalist Dalmeet Singh Chawla warns that generative AI is overwhelming academic journals with questionable research, leaving publishers’ integrity teams struggling to keep up.

The irony is that AI has already demonstrated extraordinary scientific potential.

In 2020, Google’s DeepMind developed AlphaFold, a system capable of predicting how proteins fold into the shapes that determine their biological functions.

Within a year, AlphaFold predicted 200 million protein structures, work that would have taken an estimated hundreds of millions of years using traditional laboratory methods.

The achievement helped earn its creators a Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

So AI can dramatically accelerate scientific discovery. Unfortunately, it can also accelerate the production of questionable science.

Apparently, the scientific method now needs a spam filter.

Title: Oracle celebrates end of Cybersecurity Awareness Month with quadruple trouble
Context: The first issue is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), which gives attackers a foothold in the PeopleSoft application
Full Text: Attackers are probing a critical Oracle E-Business Suite vulnerability that can lead to remote code execution (RCE), despite Oracle issuing a patch earlier this month. Meanwhile, new analysis indicates that an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day exploited by ShinyHunters as early as May involves three distinct vulnerabilities that can be combined to achieve RCE. Patching alone may not remove attackers from already compromised systems, particularly if they've installed web shells. First up: CVE-2026-101767, a critical, unauthenticated SQL injection bug in Oracle EBS that can lead to RCE. “Our Oracle E-Business Suite decoys recorded exploratory exploits against CVE-2026-101767, an unauthenticated SQL injection in EBS's Thin Client Framework servlet that chains to remote code execution, this morning, Oct 27,” Defused Cyber said in an X post. Horizon3 researchers found and disclosed the bug to Oracle, and the vendor patched the issue in its October release. “An attacker can send a crafted request to the vulnerable servlet to execute SQL with the privileges of the APPS database user,” Horizon3 explained at the time. “The attack chain also enables operating system command execution with the privileges of the EBS application account.” This means an unauthorized user can modify application data accessible to APPS, and execute commands. “Depending on the deployment, affected data may include financial, payroll, HR, and procurement records,” the bug hunters said. The Register reached out to Oracle with multiple questions for this story - including whether it has documented any successful exploitation of CVE-2026-101767 - and did not receive an immediate response. Moving on to the PeopleSoft-ShinyHunters fiasco: TrendAI’s Zero Day Initiative (ZDI) found and reported the PeopleSoft issues on June 10, and Oracle issued a patch under one vulnerability identifier: CVE-2026-35273. In early June, ShinyHunters told The Reg that the group hacked more than 100 organizations via an Oracle PeopleSoft zero-day, CVE-2026-35273. Google’s consulting and incident response biz, Mandiant, later confirmed the data theft and extortion crew exploited CVE-2026-35273 as a zero-day, mostly against schools and the education sector. By late September, however, Mandiant said ShinyHunters massively expanded its targeting, “deploying web shells on dozens of systems globally, spanning higher education, technology, IT services, healthcare, agriculture, transportation, and government.” According to ZDI bug hunter Bobby Gould, there are actually three distinct vulnerabilities across multiple PeopleSoft components, and each should receive its own CVE identifier rather than being grouped under CVE-2026-35273. Gould, along with TrendAI researchers Minh Giang and Lucas Miller, originally found and reported three distinct bugs to Oracle in June. “We are coordinating with Oracle to assign separate CVEs for each issue,” he said in a Tuesday blog. The first issue is a Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) vulnerability in the PeopleSoft Integration Gateway (PSIGW), which gives attackers a foothold in the PeopleSoft application. In June, Oracle introduced a “validateClient” method to allow PeopleSoft system administrators to restrict access to certain functionality. The SSRF bug, however, allows crims to make requests that satisfy the validation requirement to access endpoints vulnerable to RCE, Gould wrote. “While this solution does restrict access, an attacker on any trusted host can still reach PSEMHUB,” he said, referring to PeopleSoft Environment Management Hub (PSEMHUB). “Because Oracle allows localhost by default, the PSIGW SSRF provides exactly that access.” The second bug is an external control of file path vulnerability in PSEMHUB’s ExecuteProcessActivityCommand handler. This message handler is designed to allow remote clients to write log entries to the PeopleSoft server’s filesystem - but it doesn’t properly validate requests, which allows an attacker to write a web shell into a file path and achieve RCE. The third vulnerability, also in PSEMHUB, is a deserialization of untrusted data flaw. An attacker can use a file-write vulnerability to plant a malicious XML file inside a PeopleSoft directory that stores environment configuration data, then wait for PSEMHUB to initialize, such as after a service or system restart. This triggers deserialization of the malicious XML file, potentially allowing the attacker to achieve RCE. “Attackers can combine these vulnerabilities to compromise affected instances of PeopleSoft,” Gould warned.®

Title: Google to Allow One-Tap Android App Installs From Approved Third-Party Stores Outside U.S.
Context: 11 Real Stories: How Identity Exposure Unlocks Active Attack Paths Map cross-domain privilege escalation to sever breach routes at key choke points
Full Text:
Third-party Android app stores can now apply to Google for permission to install apps with one tap, without Android's usual confirmation screens, and to update them in the background.

To qualify, a store must pass identity checks and send Google its full catalog, along with every new app and update, for ongoing malware scanning. Approved stores get the features from December 1, but only on devices running Android 17 QPR2 or later in supported countries, which do not include the US.

Today, a user installing apps from a third-party store must first enable the store to install apps, then confirm each install and each update. From December 1, a store in Google's Registered App Stores program gets that permission automatically once it is approved, and its updates run in the background under the user's own update settings.

Google announced the program in March, alongside changes it said resolved its disputes with Epic Games. Joining is optional, and stores that stay out will continue to operate as they do today.

Under Google's rules, the store must still get the user's explicit consent for each install and "must not install apps silently without user consent." Large downloads and background installs must show a visible notification while they run.

If an install is started on another device, the store must show a notification that does not close automatically.

IT administrators can block registered stores from being installed on managed devices. Google's program pages do not say whether the block also applies to a store that is already installed.

Beyond the catalog scanning, Google's requirements say a store must:

be registered as an organization and keep its developer identity verified under Android developer verification, Google's identity check for app developers

send every version of its own app to Google for malware screening, exactly matching the version it publishes on the web and through other channels

work to keep malware and other potentially harmful apps out of its catalog

fix major security flaws that come to its attention

not block other app stores from being installed, interfere with them, or hide or change Android's security notifications

pay a $10,000 yearly fee, due before Google starts its review

Each store stays responsible and liable for everything in its catalog. Google won't moderate the content in registered stores.

If more than 1% of install attempts or more than 2% of a store's apps are found to be potentially harmful over a 30-day period, Google charges additional fees to screen and clean up the catalog.

A store that fails to meet any requirement, including paying on time, can be removed from the program until the issue is resolved. Google gives notice and a chance to fix it first.

Google's program pages do not describe how submitted apps are scanned, how quickly new uploads are checked, or what results the checks produce.

Registered stores also get a Google tool, the Android Developer ID API, to check whether each app in their catalog comes from a verified developer and can be installed. Google recommends that stores block installs of apps that fail the check.

Android developer verification is a separate Google program, now in its first phase with seven app stores. Since September 30, certified Android devices in Brazil, Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand have checked that apps from those stores come from verified developers, according to Google. Google plans to extend the checks worldwide in 2027.

Availability follows each user's home country. Short trips to unsupported countries do not turn off one-tap installs or automatic updates.

Android 17 QPR2 is one of Android's quarterly platform releases (QPRs). Its latest version, released October 16, is still a beta, and Google's release notes give no date for the final release.

In the US, a separate Google program for distributing third-party stores through Google Play has been in effect since July 22.

Context: And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale
Full Text:
October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month, and it’s a good time to think about how much the world has changed for chief information security officers (CISOs) in the last 12 months.

A year ago, we thought we were already in the thick of AI and starting to understand it. Since then, agents have spread across the enterprise faster than most organizations anticipated. According to our Work Trend Index Annual Report, the number of active agents in the Microsoft 365 ecosystem grew 15-fold year over year and 18-fold in large enterprises. Employees are building and deploying AI systems that can access company data, interact with applications, and take actions on their behalf. These systems are built with good intentions, but even well-intentioned agents can introduce risk when access and behavior are not appropriately governed.

At the same time, more people inside our companies are building with AI. Many of them haven’t written code in years, if ever, and they aren’t necessarily thinking about security the way a security team would. That isn’t a criticism. It’s how quickly the technology has expanded who can build and what they can accomplish.

For CISOs, this creates two fundamental shifts. We have to protect an enterprise that increasingly operates through AI and agents. And we have to rethink how we defend that enterprise as attackers use AI to move faster and operate at greater scale. When I talk with CISOs, these are the two challenges I keep coming back to. We need to enable innovation without introducing unmanaged risk, and we need to modernize defense without losing the security fundamentals that still matter.

Get the 2026 Work Trend Index report

For builders: Build securely in the agentic era

Cybersecurity awareness has always been about people. This year, it has to include the people building agents. If you’re a developer, a builder, or someone who has just realized that AI can help you design and build things, this part is for you.

Give your agents their own identities. Where supported and appropriate, assign agents governed identities rather than personal or shared credentials. When something goes wrong, you need to know which agent did it and be able to shut it off.

Protect the data your agents touch. If an agent can reach information, assume it will use it. Make sure the right data protections are in place before you connect it. And remember that the agent will not think like you. It doesn’t share your judgment or your sense of what is appropriate. If you give it access to information or systems, it will act on that access, and that can quickly become a problem.

Your CISO wants you to build. They also need to know what’s being built, so they can help you do it safely. The best thing you can do for your security leader is to have the identity and data conversation early, before you build, not after.

For CISOs: Protect the enterprise as agent adoption grows

Your first job is to put guardrails in place so people can innovate carefully, without slowing them down. Good guardrails help teams move faster because they know where the lines are.

Start with observability, and make it deep. You need to know which agents exist, who owns them, what they can reach, and what they’re doing. You can’t protect what you can’t see. Deep observability also means knowing when an agent’s behavior changes, so your team can step in before a small issue becomes a big one.

Then hold people’s feet to the fire on identity and data. These are the two areas where I wouldn’t give any ground. Every agent needs a governed identity with only the access it needs, and the data it can reach needs to be classified and protected. When those two are in place, most other decisions get easier. Here’s how we’re approaching agent governance.

For CISOs: Defending differently

Your second job is to defend differently than you have historically done.

Attackers are using AI to move faster, and our latest Microsoft Digital Defense Report shows how much that is compressing the time defenders have to respond. But defending differently isn’t simply about adopting faster tools. It’s about changing how security teams turn information into action. The more integrated your environment is, the faster you’ll be able to see an attack and respond to it. An attack rarely shows up in just one place. Signals across identity, endpoints, applications, and cloud environments need to come together with threat intelligence and organizational context so defenders can understand what’s happening and respond before an incident escalates. When your tools work together, your team sees the full picture instead of pieces of it. It also requires a security approach built to continuously assess risk, make decisions, and act at the speed threats are developing.

You also need the right threat intelligence and the right partner. Threat intelligence helps organizations understand how threats are changing, which ones matter to their environment, and where to focus their defenses. Working with partners that have visibility across industries and organizations can provide broader context than an individual organization may have on its own. And you’re not going to operate at this speed without agents helping you. The same capabilities that make attacks faster can make defense faster, with agents working alongside your analysts to investigate and respond. That’s why we’re bringing integrated security operations and agentic defense together.

Two jobs, one goal

The pace of change over the last year has been significant, and it is likely to continue. None of this means slowing down. The CISOs I talk with want their companies to innovate. They need to protect the enterprise as it uses AI and the increasing speed of AI-enabled threats.

Prepare for an agent-driven workplace

If you’re building with AI, bring your security team in early and have the identity and data conversation. If you’re a CISO, focus on those two jobs and make sure you have the right partners for both.

Title: Japan’s GMO Internet Urges Customers to Disconnect PCs
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A virtual desktop service provider in Japan has told customers to disconnect their machines from the internet after being breached by hackers.

GMO Internet’s Onamae.com service is delivered via a network of tens of thousands of servers operated by the firm and is popular with foreign-exchange traders.

However, the firm was forced to suspend the service on October 21 after discovering the day before that “malicious programs” had been installed in “some customers’ server environments.”

A security alert claimed that some information may have been accessed and that as many as 26,739 servers may have been impacted. Some reports suggest the hackers may have accessed trading accounts and made unauthorized transactions.

An extortion email sent on October 21 demanded a ransom of around eight billion yen ($50.7m).

Read more on ransomware attacks in Japan: Japanese Railway Operators Hit with Weekend Cyber Attacks

Having refused to pay the ransom, GMO Internet was notified by its attackers that they would deploy ransomware on October 27 as 12pm. As a result, it advised its customers to perform a full virus scan on their devices, back up all data, and then disconnect their PC from the internet and turn off the power.

In the meantime, GMO Internet has been asking for customers to ship their PCs so that its security team can investigate.

“As of [October 27, 11:59], no malware (including ransomware) has been detected in the devices that have been analyzed,” it explained.

“However, the analysis is still ongoing, and we have not yet confirmed the security of all customer devices. More devices from customers are expected to arrive in the future. We will proceed with the analysis as soon as they arrive.”

Japan Inc Under Fire

“This demonstrates how a vulnerability in a remote access service can have consequences far beyond the compromised system,” said Suzu Labs chief security evangelist, Phillip Wylie.ㅤ

"Attackers don’t necessarily need to deploy ransomware to cause significant damage. If they can steal sensitive information, compromise accounts, and threaten to publicly release data, they already have multiple ways to pressure an organization.”

Wylie added: "The biggest takeaway is that preventing the initial compromise is important, but limiting what attackers can do once they gain access is equally critical.”

The breach is the latest in a string of security incidents impacting Japanese firms this year. Organizations as diverse as Burger King (11 million customers), car rental company Times Car (6.6 million), karaoke giant Daiichi Kosho (eight million), and restaurant chain Yakiniku King (11 million) have suffered major data breaches.

Title: AI Takes Root in Hospital Corridors, Raises Security Stakes
Context: This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that...
Full Text:
Patients walk into a doctor's office and are swiftly asked permission for artificial intelligence (AI) scribes to document notes full of sensitive health information. That intake conversation is just one entry point as AI is now embedded throughout the patient lifecycle, accessing more data than most organizations can secure.

This raises significant concerns for a sector that historically struggles to secure legacy equipment and highly sought-after data, even before AI was added to the mix. Advancements could save invaluable time during patient care, but security will present hurdles in the form of supply chain risks that stem from AI vendor compromise, data leakage through prompts, and AI-generated social engineering campaigns.

A recent Proofpoint report, "2026 Study on Cybersecurity in Healthcare" warned that "AI adoption is accelerating faster than governance." Forty-five percent of organizations confirmed they had embedded AI into their systems but 60% lacked the necessary controls to govern that sensitive data.

Related:Vulnerability Management Isn't About the Score — It's About How It Applies to You

Healthcare organizations are rapidly deploying AI to record intake conversations, and customer conversations increasingly revolve around how physicians are using AI for clinical decisions, and more importantly, how they are protecting those tools, explains Susan Biddle, director of healthcare solutions at Proofpoint. Some Proofpoint customers use the OpenEvidence open-source AI tool for research and diagnoses because it can integrate with Epic Systems, a widely used platform for Electronic Health Records (EHR).

"The challenge is making sure physicians aren't putting sensitive information into that tool, so it does get challenging," Biddle tells Dark Reading. Even seemingly generic details, like a patient's eye color, combined with a specific injury like a left tibia fracture could qualify as Protected Health Information (PHI).

That makes data sensitivity a major concern when feeding information into AI tools. Therefore, organizations should focus on securing the underlying data rather than the tool itself, advises Biddle.

What Do CISOs Want to Know about AI in Healthcare?

AI's use is spreading fast and that complicates how organizations think about risk. Tony Sabaj, head of Americas channel SEs at Check Point, says AI's pattern-recognition capability is already improving clinical care, catching early signs in cancer screenings, triaging critical patients, and reviewing electrocardiograms to "generate reports faster and with more accuracy."

Beyond the clinic, health insurers are using AI for claims processing and fraud detection, and like other industries, healthcare is building digital twins to model operational scenarios at scale.

Related:Is Your Organization Ready for 2027's AI Accountability Era?

Some of AI’s most visible momentum is in reducing administrative burdens including documentation that converts clinician-patient conversations into draft notes, scheduling, intake, coding, and patient communications, says Cindi Carter, global chief information security officer (CISO) at Check Point. But she warned it's also being used behind the scenes to support operational planning, research, and cybersecurity.

Organizations often sort AI tools into "medical" or "administrative" buckets. The first consists of diagnostic AI or treatment recommendation systems, while the latter includes intake forms or scheduling. Carter is concerned that these labels may undermine the downstream risks administrative tools can still pose because a "documentation tool can still influence what becomes part of the medical record" and lead to clinical consequences.

In pharmaceutical and precision medicine, AI investment is outpacing security investment, Sabaj says. And as AI reaches further into healthcare, organizations need to ensure existing regulatory frameworks keep pace. Guardrails often center on protecting data leakage, but safeguards should also ensure that if AI is taking any kind of medical action, it's limited to known parameters, he recommends.

Related:How the CISO-CMO Alliance Builds Trust Before Crisis Strikes

"We continue to see breaches of medical information and AI has the potential to exacerbate this issue," Sabaj tells Dark Reading. To get ahead of the threat, some hospitals are building their own AI tools, using open weight models and training large language models on proprietary data rather than relying on public platforms to handle sensitive PHI.

Carter's concerns extend beyond confidentiality. Despite progress, AI is known to hallucinate. What if AI produced an inaccurate summary, omits an important detail, or acts on manipulated information? The organization can lose confidence in the information supporting care without a record ever being stolen, she adds.

The CISO question then becomes broader, shifting from "What data left?" to "What can this system see, what can it change, and can we reconstruct what happened?" she says.

"In healthcare, we are protecting sensitive information and the integrity of decisions that depend on it," she explains.

Leading Causes of Major Healthcare Breaches

In the relatively short time span since rapid AI adoption took off, Phil Englert, VP of medical device security at Health-ISAC, has already observed changes that will affect how much sensitive data floods systems. As AI becomes increasingly integrated, when a cyber incident occurs, organizations frequently lose patient identifiers, medical records, insurance details, and other clinical or financial data— all considered PHI.

Englert cited recent Health and Human Services data that shows hacking and other IT-related incidents continue to be the leading causes of major healthcare breaches. Denver Health Medical Plan reported a breach Oct. 1 that affected 238,083 individuals, triggered by an exposed vendor access key through AI platform SquareML.

This tracks with Health-ISAC's 2026 threat landscape findings which found that many significant breaches have originated through third-party vendors, "reinforcing the idea that an organization's security posture is often only as strong as that of its partners."

While organizations need to secure AI within their own environments, they also need to protect themselves against it as threat actors use it to craft more convincing and effective social engineering attacks, warns Englert. Healthcare organizations are seeing increasingly sophisticated phishing campaigns, deepfakes, voice impersonation attacks, and QR-code phishing— any method to exploit human trust in a sector driven by speed and precision.

While healthcare organizations can't seem to shake the ransomware threat, which "remains one of the most damaging facing the sector," AI-enabled attacks are a top cybersecurity concern for 2026, he adds.

"Cyber Safety is Patient Safety"

Implementing effective guardrails has proved significantly challenging. Carter offers five recommendations informed by the governance and lifecycle risk themes in the Joint Commissions and the Coalition for AI Health guidance: Visibility, boundaries around data and actions, evidence from vendors, validation and meaningful human oversight, and continuous monitoring.

Organizations should maintain AI inventory and give staff a straightforward way to disclose unsanctioned uses as shadow AI risks pummel the sector. Limiting what data AI can handle e is also essential; Carter recommends that access to information should not automatically confer authority to update records, send communications, or initiate transactions.

"AI compresses the time between a mistake and material loss," Carter warns. That should be reflected in organizations' safeguards.

Implementation also depends on organizational maturity. While talking with security officers across the industry, Proofpoint’s Biddle observed varying levels of AI adoption. Some are quite far in the process, while others are still cautious and taking it slow, she adds. She points out healthcare does tend to lag behind other industries when it comes to technology.

Many organizations lack resources but continually face disruptive attacks that severely affect patient care. "It doesn't seem to be getting any better, unfortunately, "Biddle says .

Getting better requires money, but when CISOs stand in front of the board and request investments to shore up defenses, they are often hit with: “Why do you need to spend this amount?” says Biddle. It's difficult, because they are competing with budget dollars for life-saving devices, she says.

"But I would say: Leverage the impact of cyber safety," Biddle adds. "Cyber safety is patient safety."

Title: AI Is Turning CISOs Into Business-Risk Translators, Says Nvidia’s Head of Cyber
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
In the AI era, cybersecurity leaders must explain how AI-related risks connects to business goals and help executives understand who is responsible for accepting those risks, according to Nvidia’s head of cybersecurity policy, Mark Weatherford.

Speaking at ISC2 Security Congress 2026, in Denver, Colorado, on October 26, Weatherford argued that the broad adoption of AI in the workplace, including in cybersecurity workflows, has transformed the CISO role from a security gatekeeper to a business-risk translator.

As organizations weigh AI adoption, CISOs must help executives understand the tradeoffs and clarify who owns the risk, he said.

Weatherford recalled a board meeting where a CISO struggled to explain the relationship between security and the business. Ultimately, the board challenged the CISO on their understanding of the company’s business model. This event, he said, had a negative impact on the perception the board had of the CISO’s credibility and ability to protect the business.

Weatherford said the exchange taught him that CISOs need to understand how their organizations generate revenue, not only how to protect them.

He added that business perspective is especially important as organizations weigh the potential benefits and risks of AI.

For instance, boards may worry that moving too slowly will cost them competitive advantage, Weatherford said, while moving too quickly can mean deploying tools without appropriate controls or an understanding of the risks.

While he argued that CISO rarely owns the business risk from deploying things like AI, he emphasized that modern CISOs must interpret that risk and make sure leaders understand who owns it.

Balancing AI Innovation With Cybersecurity Risks

Weatherford described two main challenges CISOs face with AI.

First and the “pace of technological change” makes their work more challenging.

Second, CISOs need to focus both on “security for AI and AI for security,” protecting the AI systems their organizations deploy while also considering how AI can support security operations.

Combined, these challenges mean traditional cybersecurity approaches may no longer be sufficient, he argued.

“If you’re not doing pentesting 24/7, 365, you’re probably behind the curve,” he said.

Weatherford also cautioned against investments driven by “fear of missing out.”

Leaders, he said, should do business due diligence before spending heavily on AI. CISOs can contribute by preparing concrete proposals for reducing risk. He recommended putting together a short plan that describes the proposed work and the resources it would require.

Vendor evaluation is another area where CISOs need to apply judgment. Weatherford said he looks for AI-native products that address security problems, rather than older products with AI added on.

He urged CISOs to consider supply-chain dependencies, too. Multiple vendors may depend on the same suppliers, creating single points of failure that can affect more than one product or service. Some dependencies may sit several tiers down the supply chain, beyond the suppliers an organization knows it relies on directly.

Weatherford’s advice for keeping pace with these changes was to stay curious and keep learning and even relearn things as technologies evolve.

For instance, he encouraged CISOs to “learn one new thing every week,” suggesting focusing on one AI topic at a time, such as model context protocol (MCP), prompt injections or sandboxing.

Finally, Weatherford recommended CISOs to join and create formal and informal peer communities. He mentioned that he created a CISO Exchange Network in which he invited CISOs from Nvidia’s major partners, customers and suppliers, where they share experience, concerns and tips.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become one of this decade's defining technologies. From healthcare and finance to manufacturing and education, organizations increasingly rely on AI to automate repetitive tasks, uncover patterns hidden within large datasets, and support faster decision-making. Cybersecurity has experienced a similar transformation. While attackers employ AI to automate cyberattacks and accelerate vulnerability discovery, defenders are adopting AI to improve threat detection and enhance incident response.

Security Operations Centers (SOCs) receive a high volume of alerts from endpoints, cloud workloads, network devices, identity providers, and business applications. Although SIEM and XDR platforms provide visibility into these environments, analysts often spend considerable time correlating alerts, searching documentation, and determining the next investigative steps. AI offers a practical way to augment analysts by providing contextual explanations, summarizing findings, and recommending remediation actions, rather than replacing human expertise.

Challenges facing modern SOCs

Modern SOCs are expected to detect and respond to sophisticated threats while processing millions of security events every day. High alert volumes contribute to analyst fatigue and increase the likelihood that critical events are overlooked. Investigations frequently require switching between dashboards, documentation, vulnerability databases, and threat intelligence feeds before a complete picture emerges. As infrastructures become increasingly distributed across on-premises and cloud environments, maintaining consistent situational awareness becomes more difficult. AI-assisted workflows help address these challenges by reducing repetitive analysis, adding context, and accelerating investigative decision-making.

Wazuh and artificial intelligence for enhanced SOC workflows

Threat hunting and security operations with external AI integrations

Artificial intelligence is becoming an important capability in modern SOCs. Title: When prevention fails: Why cyber resilience is the next big test of trust
Context: Imagine arriving at work on a Monday morning to find employees cannot log in, customer service is unavailable, and critical business applications have stopped working
Full Text:
Imagine arriving at work on a Monday morning to find employees cannot log in, customer service is unavailable, and critical business applications have stopped working. Security alerts are flashing. The IT team is investigating. Business leaders want to know when operations will resume.

Then comes the question everyone hopes they never have to ask: Can we recover safely, and how long will it take?

Most organizations have invested in cybersecurity, from firewalls to identity controls to monitoring tools and backup systems. Yet a serious cyberattack can still disrupt operations, damage customer trust, and leave teams unsure which systems and data they can rely on.

This is driving a shift in cybersecurity, moving beyond preventing attacks toward building organizations that can withstand disruption, recover safely and learn from incidents. That is the essence of cyber resilience.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), in its publication Developing Cyber-Resilient Systems: A Systems Security Engineering Approach, explains how resilience can be designed into systems rather than treated as an afterthought. The lesson is simple: security is not just about keeping threats out. It is also about ensuring that a successful attack does not bring everything down.

Cybersecurity is not the same as cyber resilience

Organizations work to close vulnerabilities, restrict access, monitor suspicious activity and prevent unauthorized users from reaching sensitive systems. These controls remain essential, but no control is perfect.

Consider a company that protects its customer database with strong access controls and regularly backs up its data. However, its backup environment is accessible through the same administrator account used to manage production systems.

If an attacker compromises that account, both the live systems and the recovery resources could be disrupted. The organization had security. It had backups. But did it have resilience?

Cybersecurity helps reduce the likelihood and impact of an attack. Cyber resilience focuses on ensuring that the organization can continue essential operations, limit damage, recover trustworthy systems and adapt to future threats.

NIST identifies four central goals for cyber resiliency:

Anticipate: Understand threats, weaknesses and potential disruption before they occur.

Withstand: Maintain essential functions, even when some systems are compromised or unavailable.

Recover: Restore services in a way that re-establishes trust in the systems and data

Adapt: Learn from incidents and improve defenses and recovery capabilities.

Together, these goals turn resilience from an abstract concept into practical business questions: What happens if a critical system fails? Can we recover without reintroducing an attacker? And will we address the weaknesses exposed by the incident?

The backup question: Can we restore, or can we trust what we restore?

For many organizations, backups are the foundation of recovery. They protect against accidental deletion, hardware failures and other forms of data loss. But a cyberattack introduces a different problem: the organization may no longer know which systems, credentials or copies of data can be trusted.

Suppose a retailer experiences a ransomware attack just before a major sales period. Its ordering platform is down, warehouses cannot process shipments and customer service teams cannot access order histories.

The company has backups. That is good news, but it is only the beginning.

The recovery team must determine when the attacker entered the environment, whether backup systems were affected and which recovery point is safe to use. It must also establish whether the identity systems and administrator credentials needed to restore operations remain compromised.

Restoring data from an infected or untrusted environment could allow the attacker to regain access. Bringing systems online too quickly could trigger another outage. Waiting too long, however, prolongs disruption for customers and employees.

The real challenge is not simply restoring files. It is restoring a trustworthy operating environment.

The CISA #StopRansomware Guide recommends maintaining offline, encrypted backups and regularly testing their integrity and recovery procedures. These practices matter because backups that attackers can access and destroy may offer little protection when an incident occurs.

Backup success does not automatically equal business recovery. A technically available system is not necessarily a safe system.

Building resilience into connected systems

Modern businesses depend on interconnected environments. Applications rely on identity services. Infrastructure depends on networks and cloud platforms. Data protection systems must connect to the systems they protect.

These connections make digital services useful but they can also give attackers routes through an organization. This is where zero trust becomes important.

Often summarized as “never trust, always verify,” zero trust requires access to be explicitly verified and limited to what is necessary. Being inside a corporate network should not automatically grant broad access to everything within it. However, zero trust and cyber resilience solve related but different problems.

NIST explains this approach in its zero trust architecture guidance. Zero trust helps limit opportunities for attackers to gain access and move through an environment, while cyber resilience addresses what happens when an attacker still succeeds.

Identity controls limit access. Network segmentation helps contain a compromise. Data protection safeguards important information. Independent recovery capabilities provide a way to restore operations in a controlled environment.

These capabilities must work together.

A protected backup is less useful if compromised production systems can delete it. A recovery environment may not help if it relies on administrator credentials that an attacker has already stolen. And a highly secure application offers limited business value if the organization cannot safely restore the identity services on which it depends.

Resilience depends on the relationships between safeguards, not simply on the presence of individual controls.

The hardest question: What can we still trust?

During a major cyber incident, organizations may need to isolate networks, disable privileged accounts, suspend services or disconnect systems from normal operations. These decisions can be disruptive, but allowing an attack to spread may be far more damaging.

Recovery teams must identify the services most important to the business, understand their dependencies, determine which data is safe to restore and establish an environment where systems can be examined and rebuilt.

They also need answers to difficult questions:

If the primary identity service is compromised, how will recovery teams gain secure access to the systems they need?

If an attacker has reached the backup environment, what independent recovery options remain?

If the organization cannot restore every application immediately, which services must return first?

Who has the authority to approve reconnection to production?

How will the organization know that the restored environment is sufficiently clean and trustworthy?

These questions connect technical architecture with business consequences. They also reveal gaps that routine availability tests may miss. An organization may successfully recover from a server failure without ever testing whether it can recover after administrator credentials have been compromised.

NIST’s Guide for Cybersecurity Event Recovery emphasizes prioritizing critical resources, developing recovery plans, testing realistic scenarios and improving recovery capabilities based on lessons learned. These practices help organizations reduce uncertainty and restore essential services when disruption occurs.

Resilience is not a one-time achievement. Threats evolve, systems change and organizations become dependent on new technologies and service providers. Each incident and exercise should reveal what failed, which assumptions proved incorrect and what needs to improve.

Recovery is about more than technology

When a cyber incident occurs, the consequences extend beyond servers and applications. Customers may lose access to services. Employees may be unable to work. Partners may be waiting for transactions to complete. Leaders must make decisions with incomplete information while communicating with customers, regulators and other stakeholders.

Cyber resilience therefore cannot be the responsibility of the security team alone.

Security teams reduce the likelihood and impact of compromise. Architects design systems with realistic failure scenarios in mind. Recovery teams prepare to restore systems and data when normal operating assumptions no longer hold. Business leaders determine which services must be prioritized and how much disruption the organization can tolerate.

All share one objective: restoring trustworthy operations while minimizing harm to the business and its customers.

This also requires treating resilience as an ongoing organizational capability, not a document reviewed once a year or a technology investment made in isolation.

Zero trust challenges assumptions about access. Cyber resilience extends that thinking to disruption and recovery: What if a trusted account is compromised? What if a critical service becomes unavailable? What if the systems intended to support recovery are affected too?

The answer is not to rely on a single security product, backup strategy or incident response plan. It is to build an environment in which prevention, containment, data protection, recovery and continuous learning reinforce one another.

Ultimately, the most useful measure of cyber resilience is not whether an organization has prepared for an incident on paper. It is whether, when disruption happens, it can protect what matters, make sound decisions, recover safely and emerge better prepared than before.

Title: ICE Is Running One of the Largest Anti-Left Surveillance Operations in US History

Full Text:
Attorneys for 15 Minnesota residents facing federal conspiracy charges have obtained evidence of a sweeping, possibly unconstitutional spying operation carried out by Immigration and Customs Enforcement against left-wing social movements in Minnesota and beyond.

The high-profile Minnesota 15 prosecution makes clear that the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), flush with federal funds and newly hired personnel, is now President Donald Trump’s primary tool against dissent, with a powerful array of post-9/11 investigative authorities brought to bear against everyday Americans organizing their communities.

Nothing of this scale has been seen in the United States, experts say, since the federal government’s counterinsurgency against the New Left and the anti-war movement in the 1960s and 1970s.

Title: Waiting on a Node.js Upgrade? Build a Stopgap with the Controls You Own
Context: In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major...
Full Text:
Executive Summary

Node.js has fixed CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, but upgrading at scale is slow. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of roughly 3 million Node.js installations have been patched, and 1.7 million run end-of-life lines that will never receive a fix. In the meantime, interim mitigations from the Qualys Threat Research Unit narrow the Brotli, DNS, TLS, and keep-alive attack paths, and WAF, IPS, and EDR protections from major vendors add further layers. Soon, Qualys ETM will factor these controls into risk scores. These controls buy time, but upgrading the runtime remains the only complete fix.

Node.js comes with a clear instruction: upgrade the runtime. The October 21 security release fixes 10 vulnerabilities, including CVE-2026-111497, a Brotli decoder flaw that can permit remote code execution, and three high-severity flaws that weaken DNS and TLS hostname validation. Fixed releases exist for the 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x lines. Upgrading at this scale still takes time, because the vulnerable code lives in the runtime itself, in container images, single-executable applications, and serverless functions that dependency checks never touch. In Qualys telemetry, only 42,000 of the 3.3 million installations have been patched so far, and 1.7 million run end-of-life versions, including 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, and 20.x, that will not receive a fix and must move to a supported line.

Those first days are where mitigations and compensating controls earn their place. They reduce risk while upgrades roll out, and the right visibility shows which runtimes need attention first. Our Node.js blog post covers vulnerabilities, fixed versions, and detection methods.

Here is how to bridge the gap between disclosure and upgrade, in four steps: find and prioritize exposed Node.js, apply interim mitigations, layer the controls you already run, then patch and verify.

Step 1: Find and Prioritize Exposed Node.js

Qualys customers can search for assets affected by CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to see every Node.js runtime across hosts, containers, and cloud workloads. That includes copies that dependency checks miss, such as those in version managers, application folders, and bundled runtimes.

It is important to note that not every vulnerable runtime has the same level of exposure. Start with internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data (CVE-2026-111497), since they are the most direct path to remote code execution. Services that open TLS connections to user-supplied hosts (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483) come next. Runtimes on end-of-life lines need an upgrade plan, as no patches will be available for them. Consider these factors alongside business criticality to decide what to mitigate and upgrade first.

Step 2: Apply Interim Mitigations

Node.js has no official workaround, but the Qualys Threat Research Unit has identified practical interim steps. Each one narrows a specific attack path while you plan the upgrade, and together they complement the fix.

These changes do not eliminate all exploitation paths associated with these CVEs, and some changes may affect application behavior. Therefore, it is crucial to test the affected applications after each change.

Limit Brotli exposure (CVE-2026-111497). Avoid decompressing Brotli from untrusted sources where you can, and cap payload size and decompression ratio at the reverse proxy or WAF.

Use the safer DNS call (CVE-2026-105482). Resolve user-supplied names with dns.lookup instead of dns.resolve*, and reject hostnames that contain NUL characters.

Canonicalize IP addresses (CVE-2026-106069, CVE-2026-105483, CVE-2026-106072). Convert addresses to canonical form before they reach a TLS connection, and reject fullwidth and other non-canonical forms.

Turn off keep-alive for untrusted servers (CVE-2026-105481). Disable keepAlive on http.Agent for connections to servers you do not control.

Treat the Permission Model as advisory. (CVE-2026-106071, CVE-2026-106073) Do not rely on it as a security boundary on affected versions.

Step 3: Add Layers from the Security Stack You Already Run

The tools already in your environment can work alongside the interim steps, each at a different point in the attack path. Each layer can catch what the one before it misses.

Edge and network: WAF and IPS. WAF and IPS vendors such as Cloudflare, Fortinet, and Check Point have released protections that name the Brotli flaw. They help block exploit requests before those requests reach the Node.js decoder.

After exploitation: EDR. Behavioral and exploit-prevention policies in endpoint tools such as CrowdStrike Falcon, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, and Cortex XDR add a second line of defense. They help stop what an attacker tries next, such as a Node.js process spawning a shell or downloading a binary, and some also act on the memory exploitation itself.

Endpoint controls are listed for CrowdStrike, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, Cybereason, SentinelOne and Cortex XDR.

Note: Rule and policy IDs are as published by each vendor in October 2026; confirm them in your console. The endpoint policies act after exploitation or on memory behavior, so verify each one fires for your Node.js process. Compensating controls reduce risk; upgrading Node.js remains the only complete fix.

Step 4: Patch, Restart, and Re-Validate

Interim mitigations reduce risk. Upgrading remains the only complete fix. Node.js fixed these flaws in 22.23.4, 24.22.1, and 26.12.1, while lines such as 25.x, 23.x, 21.x, 20.x, and older receive no fix and must move to a supported release. Customers can deploy supported vendor patches through TruRisk Eliminate, so check the patch catalog for their line. Qualys reports a high patch reliability rating for these updates and no OS reboot requirement for the runtime upgrade.

Confirm That Remediation Is Complete

A patch isn’t finished when the package installs:

Upgrade every copy. Migrate end-of-life lines to a supported release.

Rebuild container images and single-executable applications on the fixed version, then redeploy them.

Restart every service that runs on Node.js. Long-running processes, containers, and single-executable applications keep the vulnerable runtime in memory until they restart.

Rescan and verify. Rescan with Cloud Agent or Container Security and confirm the detection QIDs are closed.

Where to Start

Find. Search for CVE-2026-111497 and the other October 2026 Node.js CVEs to locate every runtime, including copies outside standard install paths.

Prioritize. Put internet-facing services that decompress untrusted Brotli data at the top, alongside business criticality.

Mitigate. Apply the Qualys TRU interim steps to runtimes awaiting an upgrade, and test the affected applications.

Layer. Keep applicable WAF, IPS, and EDR protections enabled and current as additional layers, and set the Cloudflare rule to Block.

Patch and verify. Upgrade to a fixed release, rebuild and redeploy what embeds the runtime, restart every Node.js service, and rescan.

Compensating controls buy valuable time, but they do not remove the flaw. Keep tracking every system until it is patched.

Coming Next: Give Your Controls Credit in Qualys ETM

The capabilities described in this section are in development and subject to change.

Two servers can run the same unpatched Node.js build and carry very different risks. One sits behind a WAF rule and an IPS signature that name the Brotli flaw, with EDR watching its Node.js process. The other faces the internet with nothing in front of it. A traditional scan reports them the same way.

Qualys ETM is being extended to close that gap. It arrives in three steps:

Recommendations on every finding (coming soon). ETM will show which applicable third-party controls can reduce exposure for each vulnerability, so teams know what to enable and where.

Controls reflected in the score. Controls that are in place will lower a finding’s QVSS score to reflect your actual defenses, shown as the Environmental score, so remediation queues focus on what still needs attention.

Action from the same platform. Teams will be able to apply third-party mitigations through TruRisk Eliminate from the platform that found the exposure.

Title: PHP2Shell Won't Be the Last. Here's Where the Next One Will Show Up First.
Context: The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there
Full Text:
On October 17, Amazon's honeypot network logged a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt from an anonymized IP address. Yet, public disclosure was still four days away.

By the time PHP got its fixes in on October 21, the technical details had already leaked, proof-of-concept exploits were in wide circulation, and more exploit attempts were being logged left and right. The issue was that there were two critical, unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerabilities in the PHP engine itself (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, both CVSS v4.0 9.2) -- what we now know as PHP2Shell.

Our own Security Research team covered what happened and what you should do: which releases to move to, which mitigations you could put in place to reduce exposure until you were able to update, and where each part of the Snyk platform sees the problem.

This post now picks up where our Security Research team left off. We want to talk about what the response taught us: where this kind of exposure lives and comes from, why answering fast depends on the work we’d done months earlier, and why the next one is already on its way.

Why was PHP2Shell a problem for teams with clean code?

Well, because the vulnerabilities live below the code. And what does that mean? Both of the mentioned CVEs happen in the request lifecycle of the PHP engine, which makes them reachable before any application code actually runs. On Apache, with mod_php, an exploit needed but a single unauthenticated request.

Now, think about that for a second. You probably had careful reviews, clean code, plus a neat and tidy dependency tree, all sitting above the actual problem. The first question every team faced was where PHP was answering requests, and whether someone could exploit it right then and there.

The question was about running applications. The very same question attackers will always start with.

Which inventory tells you where PHP is running?

Each type of inventory tells you part of it.

PHP reaches production via a Dockerfile, a distribution package, a platform image, or manually. A "php": ">=8.2"constraint in composer.json tells you what an application accepts, and then the deployed version depends on which of those routes installed it. Container scans see PHP installed from distribution packages once each distribution publishes its advisory, and PHP compiled from source, including the official PHP Docker images, falls outside that view. (Once again, our research team's post maps exactly which Snyk view sees which slice of this reality.)

Then there's the version string. VirusTotal fingerprints roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, and only about 1.1 million of them announce a version, so roughly four out of five hide it. Their summary is one of the cleanest lines we've read on the subject anywhere: "If you only search for a version string, you only see the fraction of the problem that volunteers it."

The gap between what your inside-out views know and what actually answers from the outside is where the real risk lies. Attackers hit your URL, and PHP2Shell is the purest case of that we’ve seen. Anyone probing for it ends up asking the same question: Does PHP answer on this URL?

What did the response look like from the outside in?

The head start: before PHP's 14:00 UTC release on October 21, Snyk had advisories live for both CVEs, so monitored projects would get a hit the moment fixed versions were known. Within about 30 minutes of the release, those advisories included affected ranges and fixed versions, and distribution advisories followed as each distribution was published. That covered what Snyk Container and Unmanaged scans could tell you.

Three questions ran through Snyk API & Web:

Where is PHP running? Discovery enumerates the assets on your domains and fingerprints their technology stack. Set the Tech filter to PHP, and you get every discovered host and endpoint where PHP was identified, with its risk rating, score, and last-seen date. Version numbers come later, from the hosts themselves. As our research team put it, before you can patch, you need the list.

Can someone exploit it? Within 24 hours of PHP's release, the full scan profile tested for PHP2Shell, and teams could run that check on their own as a custom profile for a fast answer across every PHP target.

Did the fix hold? Run the same custom profile after patching, and pair it with your distribution's advisory or patch level, because a patched distribution build can keep an older version number.

So, Discovery --> targeted check --> patch --> re-test: probe, observe, and infer, against a clock that now runs in hours. And that’s exactly the most concerning part, what we care about the most. For teams already running Snyk API & Web, the hard part was done before October 21: their domains were mapped, and their applications set up as targets. When the check was there, the response took only a filter and a quick scan.

For us, that’s one of the main returns on having continuous outside-in testing: the work that answers at day one gets done months before that.

If PHP2Shell is detectable from the outside, what was the hard part?

Time.

In May, we laid out the distinction on which COS is built. Heuristic-detectable vulnerabilities show themselves to deterministic tools: throw payloads at a running application or API, observe the responses, and infer. Context-dependent vulnerabilities (BOLA, cross-tenant leakage, and chained business logic) carry no signature at all, because they live in the gap between what an application is supposed to do and what it actually does.

Once it was known, PHP2Shell became testable from the outside, which puts it squarely in that first class of heuristic-detectable vulns. The hard part, the constraint, was the gap between a disclosure and having a check running against everything you expose. That gap is the attacker’s window to exploit, and this time it opened four days before disclosure eventually did.

The disclosure kept moving, too. On October 23, the PHP project described a partial bypass (CVE-2026-115560) that applies when an application switches its session serialization handler with ini_set() before starting the session, with upload progress enabled. Its preconditions are rare, and whatever you concluded on Wednesday still needed a second look by Friday. A point-in-time answer ages in days.

Why won't PHP2Shell be the last?

There are three reasons for that. Due to the nature of how they were found:

Because they were found with AI assistance, in an engine that has served the web for three decades. Our research team put it plainly: "In a world of LLMs and agents, everybody is still running servers." And the kind of model that found these vulnerabilities is the kind attackers now have in their hands.

The stronger cadence. Manoj Nair, Snyk's CTO and Chief Innovation Officer, described it in September: "The kind of severe flaw that AI now surfaces in widely used software, the sort of find that used to arrive once or twice a year and reset everyone's quarter, is landing several times a week in what I'm seeing."

The much faster clock. CJ Moses, CISO of Amazon Integrated Security, drew two lessons from PHP2Shell that apply well beyond it. Defenders "should not assume the public disclosure date is the earliest date of exploitation." And "the time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons," because AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or an advisory into a working exploit. His advice for critical vulnerabilities in internet-facing systems: "measure patch and mitigation timelines in hours."

What does being ready for the next one take?

Strip out the product names, and it comes down to four properties. Judge any approach by them (ours included). Don’t think about product names, but how it all comes down to four properties. And you should judge any approach with these (ours included!)

An inventory that exists before the advisory does. Built from the outside in and kept current, so a new disclosure starts with a filter.

Checks that ship in hours. The gap between an advisory and a running test is the attacker's window. Measure it.

Re-tests on demand. The same targeted check, run again until the fix holds.

Testing that needs no signature. Heuristics catch what someone has already described. Everything else takes reasoning: testing that works out what your application is supposed to do, then goes after the gap between that and what it actually does.

As for Snyk, here’s how that maps to what we offer.

Snyk API & Web carries the first three: Discovery, an engine the team keeps current as disclosures land, and targeted profiles you can run and re-run. Continuous Offensive Security adds the fourth: AI Pentesting reasons about your application the way a pentester would, Agent Red Teaming engages the moment recon spots an LLM in the stack, and Dynamic Testing, the Snyk API & Web engine, covers the heuristic classes underneath, continuously. In our platform's terms, that's Validate: continuously attack your applications to prove fixes held and show what's still exploitable.

Then there's posture. At The AI Security Panel: Unfiltered on October 14, Manoj asked the question we keep coming back to: "When an autonomous attacker is going to attack you, why don't you attack yourself?" That question is the whole premise of COS. On our side, the work is shrinking every single gap in this story: from advisory to running check, and from check to confirmed fix.

Where will the next one show up first?

Which engine, and when, is anyone's guess now. Where it shows up first is easier to call: at your URL. That's where your testing should already be.

Title: Snyk UNFILTERED: Inside Our First-Ever Customer Summit
Context: Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job Detection is no longer the bottleneck
Full Text:
What happens when you bring security leaders from some of the world's most forward-thinking organizations into one room, close the doors, and invite them to speak candidly about what's working, what's breaking, and what they’re still working out?

That’s what we set out to find with Snyk UNFILTERED, our inaugural Customer Summit. Held in San Francisco ahead of the launch of Evo Agentic AppSec and the AI Security Summit, Snyk UNFILTERED was designed to feel nothing like a conference.

We brought together a small group of security leaders from our customer community for an afternoon of candid discussions, interactive debates, and peer-to-peer exchanges. With no traditional presentations, product demos, or carefully rehearsed talking points, the summit gave attendees the freedom to share their experiences without attribution. What followed was an open exchange of ideas about the challenges and opportunities shaping the future of AI security. Leaders compared notes on real rollouts, real roadblocks, and real questions they have not yet figured out, with a level of transparency that is hard to find at traditional industry events.

From the growing backlog of vulnerabilities to the governance of autonomous agents, attendees challenged assumptions, compared real-world experiences, and explored questions the industry is still answering. And that's where the most valuable conversations began.

Five key takeaways that stuck with us

Five themes kept resurfacing over the afternoon, across every table and every discussion:

1. When AI writes the code, who owns the risk?

If an engineer prompts an AI tool to build an agent skill and that skill causes an issue later, who is at fault? The room kept coming back to the importance of guardrails: clear controls and ownership that hold up even when no human typed the line.

2. The AI conversation has grown up

Just a few months ago, the questions were about cost and token usage. Now leadership wants to know the return on investment, what AI is really costing, and where to set budget caps. AI has moved from experiment to line item with scrutiny to match.

3. Finding vulnerabilities is only half the job

Detection is no longer the bottleneck. The questions have moved to how teams fix issues, how fast they can fix them, and how they reduce human error within the loop. Fixes that stall in review, testing, and merge were a shared frustration.

4. Risk can come from anywhere

When everyone on a team has access to AI, vulnerabilities can come from anywhere. Democratizing AI also spreads responsibility, and attendees talked about how to keep everyone accountable without slowing anyone down.

5. Humans can only do so much

Teams are limited by how much people can review and approve. Leaders are open to trusting agents, but only with controls that an agent cannot bypass, and with governance designed for machines rather than adapted from processes built for people.

From UNFILTERED conversations to the future of AI Security

Snyk UNFILTERED was just the beginning of an important week in San Francisco. The challenges discussed behind closed doors at UNFILTERED reflected a broader shift happening across the industry: security teams are moving beyond simply identifying risk toward enabling organizations to build, innovate, and operate safely at AI speed.

The next morning, we launched Evo Agentic AppSec, and the AI Security Summit brought builders, researchers, investors, and CISOs into the same building. The questions from the customer room about fixing at speed and governing agents were carried straight into those conversations. Hearing those challenges directly from customers shapes what we build next.

The best conversations don't end when the event does

The leaders in the room are navigating enormous change. They’re balancing innovation with accountability and securing technologies that evolve faster than the processes designed to govern them. What made the afternoon valuable was their willingness to talk openly about what they haven’t solved yet. Spaces like that are rare, and we plan to keep creating them.

Snyk Unfiltered is part of our commitment to bringing our customer community together through candid conversations and shared learning, and this was the first of many.
