Title: Alibaba's Qwen AI caught trying to contact server in China
Context: "The first issue is that it made a network call at all," Ivan Zhang, co-founder of Cohere, told The Register via email
Full Text: Open-weight models from China have become very popular, but they've also raised some security suspicions. Cohere, a Canada-based biz that offers AI models to enterprises, says that when it was testing Alibaba's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in its evaluation sandbox, the model attempted to send data to China. "Asked to write a defensive detection rule, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next ignored instructions and inventoried the machine it was running on and then tried to upload a probe file to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing," the biz said in a blog post on Monday. Cohere was running the model through CTI-REALM, Microsoft's security analyst benchmark, and gave Qwen the task of writing a detection rule to look for malicious file downloading and execution by watching for invocations of curl processing bash scripts to the /tmp directory that were accompanied by bash execution. The model's "reasoning" output invented a prior conversation and asserted that no tools were used, output that a guardrail system reading chain-of-thought would accept. Nonetheless, the model issued a curl command to an Alibaba Cloud (aliyuncs.com) server. "The model listed everything in /tmp, checked which transfer tools were installed, read the machine's DNS settings, then tried to upload a test string to an Alibaba Cloud storage bucket in Beijing and checked whether it worked," Cohere said. "Our sandbox had no route out, so the request died at the container wall." The Cohere team wonders aloud whether that behavior was intended, but has no answer. "The first issue is that it made a network call at all," Ivan Zhang, co-founder of Cohere, told The Register via email. "The model was asked to write a detection rule, which doesn't require external communication, and its reasoning trace said it wouldn't use tools. The destination raises additional questions because the attempted upload was to an Alibaba Cloud storage endpoint that wasn't part of the task. We don't know why it appeared, and we don't know the root cause." Alibaba, the maker of the model, did not respond to a request to address Cohere's concerns. Asked whether Cohere ran similar tests against US-made open-weight models, Zhang said, "We evaluate a broad range of models using the same framework our customers use in production: agents with access to real tools operating inside controlled environments. "The key point isn't a comparison between providers. What made this noteworthy was that the model took actions unrelated to the task and those actions weren't reflected in its reasoning trace. The behavior appeared in fewer than one in 100,000 calls, which is exactly why large-scale testing and monitoring matter." There have been other unsubstantiated claims made about similar behavior from open-weight models, and such reports have suggested that "hallucination" - errors made by these models - may be the cause. Cohere has doubts that this behavior simply reflects memorized training data. "Every public sighting so far has involved fetching a file, while the one we caught was an attempted upload to a different bucket, this time in Beijing," the biz said. Cohere described efforts to reproduce the suspect behavior and found that using a technique called prefilling – feeding the model its own reasoning output alongside the opening characters of the bash command so the model would complete the command – they could get it to reference watchlisted hosts up to 23 percent of the time. This still doesn't clarify intent, and Cohere allows that there's a case to be made that the behavior is just bad training data sanitization – logs from development that got swept into the model's training data set. At the same time, the company argues that isolating a suspect model so it can't exfiltrate data doesn't entirely fix everything because these models can still write vulnerable code – accidentally or as a result of model poisoning. Cohere points to research from other organizations that suggests Chinese AI models can produce vulnerable code. The biz, for example, cites a report from Booz Allen (which does a lot of business with the US defense industry) that found "three of four Chinese coding models wrote more vulnerable code for a government customer, with Qwen3-Coder roughly 130 percent worse." "From the outside, it's very difficult to determine the root cause with confidence. We don't have evidence that would allow us to conclude this was deliberate, and we're not making that claim," said Zhang. "For security teams, though, intent doesn't fundamentally change the response. Whether it's a training artifact, a mistake, or something else, the controls are largely the same: restrict unnecessary egress, monitor tool use, and don't treat a reasoning trace as a security boundary. "We strongly support open-weight models and release many of our own. The lesson here is really about trust. Sovereign AI is about more than where a model runs. It's about understanding how it was built, how it was tested, and having confidence in how it behaves inside your environment." ®

Title: eMudhra, Brotli, and the Long Tail of a Security Fix
Context: How much software do you have to update to fix one vulnerability, let alone two far-reaching ones in the same week
Full Text:
How much software do you have to update to fix one vulnerability, let alone two far-reaching ones in the same week?

Our corner of the internet was getting impatient waiting for Node’s eMudhra fix to drop. The certificate block had merged, and we were ready to update Node, rebuild, and move on.

Then the October 21 release dropped, and we got Brotli too. That covered both problems in Node. But how much else used that same decoder? It was tucked into other applications and runtimes, and now we had more places to look.

And eMudhra had its own version of the same problem. Your browser could reject the compromised certificates while a command-line tool on the same machine still trusted them. Which other programs accepted them? Which certificate stores were they using? Updating Node only covered part of it.

eMudhra: a trust decision that traveled off the map #

On October 17, a researcher showed they had recovered eight eMudhra intermediate CA private keys by signing a message with each one. Scott Helme later recovered them from the public certificates on his laptop in less than a second.

The values included 4, 56, and 115. These were supposed to be 384-bit private keys, with roughly 3.94 × 10¹¹⁵ possible values. The actual keys all fit in eight bits. You could try every possibility by counting to 255.

eMudhra says the keys came from a flawed key-generation ceremony in April 2025 and that the intermediates never issued customer certificates. That doesn’t tell us whether someone else used them. The weak keys had gone unnoticed for nearly eighteen months.

Mozilla found no certificates from those intermediates in Certificate Transparency logs at disclosure. That helps, but plenty of clients don’t require that logging. Someone could have used the keys to forge certificates those clients would accept without leaving a record in those logs.

Chrome and Firefox could push out a block without waiting for an ordinary software release. Mozilla says its OneCRL update reached Firefox users with standard configurations in less than three hours. Chrome also pushed a CRLSet block that evening. The disclosure site even had a handy test for checking your browser.

Outside the browser, the answer depended on which program you asked. Many clients needed a new certificate bundle or a change to their verifier. Revoking the certificates at the CA did little for clients that never checked that information.

There were multiple ways to trust these certificates, too. Mozilla identified paths through three roots, including Sectigo’s AAA Certificate Services. Its advice was to block the compromised intermediates where possible. Removing the roots that trusted them was another option, but could break legitimate connections too. Removing just one might still leave another trust path open. Mozilla’s guidance

Go addressed the problem with a verifier change in versions 1.27.3 and 1.26.10. Getting that change into an application meant rebuilding it with the patched toolchain. Installing a new Go compiler would leave an existing executable exactly as it was.

Brotli: the decoder inside the runtime inside the product #

The Brotli advisory led to a similar search. CVE-2026-111497 could corrupt memory when an application decoded malicious compressed input. Node shipped a fix, but the vulnerable code came from Google’s Brotli library. Other projects had shipped it too.

Bun was one of them. Its fetch implementation automatically decodes Brotli responses, so a server the application contacts can feed data to the decoder. Bun 1.4.4 updated the library. But if you had built an executable with bun build --compile, that executable carried its own runtime. It still needed rebuilding.

Then there was Python. Requests automatically decodes Brotli responses when brotli or brotlicffi is installed, including when another dependency brings it in. You don’t have to import Brotli in your application to end up using it.

On Sunday, October 25, Microsoft published a .NET advisory for the same Brotli flaw. Applications decoding untrusted Brotli data were affected there too. Four days after the Node release, there were still more places to check.

And the list keeps going. The Brotli library can come along with another dependency or get compiled into a runtime, without “brotli” showing up in your application’s dependency list. Have a look at Broccoli2Shell’s list of bundled copies. Updating Node only gets you so far. You still have to find the other copies and work out which ones need fixing.

Where the fix gets stuck #

Shipping a runtime or library with your application is convenient. When it needs a security fix, you own the job of replacing that copy. Updating the system’s copy won’t replace the one bundled with your application. Even applications using a shared library may need a restart to load the corrected version.

With certificates, you can update a package and still leave the trust decision untouched. An SDK may hand verification to a library, runtime, or operating system. Another tool may read its own certificate bundle.

The macOS example makes this easy to see. Protections delivered through Apple’s security frameworks do not automatically extend to command-line tools reading /etc/ssl/cert.pem. A browser check can look good while another program on the same machine still accepts the compromised chain.

This is the part that makes “we updated” an incomplete answer. Which copy changed, and is the application actually using it?

And if we start finding more of these? #

There’s an AI connection here too. Node.js credits OpenAI’s Codex Security researchers with reporting the Brotli flaw. eMudhra says AI-assisted tools reportedly helped recover its weak keys.

Great, we’re finding the bugs. Now we have to find everywhere they ended up. If AI helps more of these come out of the woodwork, maintainers and product teams have more updates to chase down.

Those same tools can help with the digging: tracing dependencies, finding bundled copies, and figuring out what needs rebuilding. We still need to check what actually shipped.

And the agents doing some of that work? They’re using the same runtimes, certificate stores, and decoders. Now they’re deciding what to fetch on their own, without someone nitpicking every URL or checking everything that comes back.

Getting the fix the rest of the way #

Chrome and Firefox already had the infrastructure to get those certificate blocks out. Most applications don’t have a browser vendor’s update system or that level of established trust. Building either isn’t a weekend fix.

But we can make the cleanup less of a scavenger hunt in a haunted house:

Know what each release contains. Track application dependencies alongside bundled runtimes, libraries, toolchains, and certificate settings.

Have a rebuild path ready. Automate the builds and checks you’ll need when a dependency changes. If you’re waiting on another project, give someone responsibility for following its release.

Don’t just wait for a patch. Disable the affected feature where you can, or block untrusted input from reaching it. Microsoft gives Brotli examples for .NET. Check that the workaround works, and keep someone on it until the fix ships and gets deployed.

Check the application itself. Test certificate rejection through the verifier it actually uses. Confirm that a corrected decoder made it into the shipped artifact and the running service.

Track installation as well as publication. A release being available does not mean people are running it. Be clear about what needs to be replaced or restarted.

So, how much software do you have to update? Turns out, more than the first advisory might suggest. eMudhra and Brotli sent teams looking for s̶p̶o̶o̶k̶y̶,̶ s̶c̶a̶r̶y̶ s̶k̶e̶l̶e̶t̶o̶n̶s̶ affected components buried in their dependencies. As more flaws come to light, finding those copies and getting them patched quickly needs to become routine.

Learn how to use Tenable solutions to find vulnerable PHP versions, prioritize remediation, and patch the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) faster.

Key takeaways

The PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) put security teams in a race against attackers. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, so organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

Tenable helps you find PHP2Shell across your attack surface. Tenable One Attack Surface Management discovers externally facing PHP assets. Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center provide detections, including local checks for Linux distribution packages. Tenable One Web App Scanning assesses web applications, and Tenable One Cloud Exposure covers cloud workloads.

Tenable accelerates remediation. Tenable Patch Management matches exposures to the right patches, launches patch workflows, and validates fixes with post-scan checks. Tenable One with Tenable Hexa AI lets you find vulnerable assets, create exposure initiatives, and generate remediation tickets with simple prompts.

Respond faster with Tenable solutions

The recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) have put security teams in a race against attackers to remediate or mitigate exposure before their systems are targeted. PHP runs on more than 70% of websites, and many of those sites run unsupported, legacy branches that no longer receive upstream support. Organizations need to quickly find where they’re affected and update PHP to fixed versions.

To help cybersecurity teams accelerate emergency response, this blog outlines tips for using the Tenable solutions to identify vulnerable versions of PHP, prioritize remediation decisions, and implement patches as quickly as possible.

External Attack Surface Management

Tenable One Attack Surface Management (ASM) helps you discover externally facing assets running PHP. ASM continuously scans public data sources, such as DNS records, IP addresses, Autonomous System Numbers (ASN), WHOIS registrations, and neighboring IP ranges, to discover forgotten, rogue, or shadow IT assets that might be vulnerable to PHP2Shell. This is one of the first steps to take. It shows your digital footprint from the attacker’s perspective and identifies potential entry points into your organization.

Important ASM tips include:

Use ASM to find additional top-level domains related to your organization. Suggested Domains helps you identify additional domains you may own based on ASN, brand, domain name, IP range, subdomain, or nameserver. You can also adjust the suggestion rules to prioritize domain names based on the likelihood of ownership.

Search the inventory for PHP deployments. Create a query in ASM to identify PHP as a programming language filter. This gives you a quick starting point to assess locations, asset details, and software versions for further analysis.

Continuously monitor for changes in your attack surface. Use Subscriptions in ASM to receive event-driven notifications and understand important changes in your attack surface that may create new exposure. Choose from hundreds of pre-built event categories or create a customized subscription. Two subscriptions apply to PHP: PHP in applications and PHP end-of-life installs.

Explore the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Attack Surface Management.

How to Identify and Tag PHP Assets in Tenable One Attack Surface Management. This demo shows how to get a view of the external attack surface and identify where php2shell creates exposure. In Explore > Asset Inventory, review the inventory of assets facing the outside world. To add another inventory source, click '+' and choose an option from the drop-down menu, such as 'Add Hostnames or Domains.' In the pop-up menu, enter a new hostname, for example 'tenable.com.' To narrow the results to assets running PHP, use the query bar to set 'Programming Language' equal to 'PHP.' The results show 265 assets with PHP listed as their Programming Language. Create a 'PHP2Shell' tag and apply it to the selected assets so they can be grouped and prioritized. The Tags column then displays the 'PHP2Shell' tag. Subscriptions can be used to view and assess PHP. Subscriptions provide a growing list of events, including predefined lists and categories. Search for 'PHP' and add the 'PHP - v1' subscription. After subscribing, create an alert for the subscription. The subscription is set to 'Programming Language' contains php, so it filters assets and sends an alert when a new asset meeting this criteria is identified.

Vulnerability Management

Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center both help you find PHP2Shell vulnerabilities with detections for PHP, including local checks for PHP packages from Linux distributions. Tenable will release additional detections as vendors publish fixes in their security advisories.

Both solutions help you create out-of-band, tactical scans based on your preferred scan policy. Additional tips include:

Update plugin feeds before running a scan. Tenable One Vulnerability Management automatically manages and updates plugin feeds through cloud synchronization by default. In offline or air-gapped environments, Tenable Security Center may require manual plugin feed updates.

Use thorough testing to discover more vulnerabilities. Enabling thorough testing and paranoia mode in your scan policy conducts deeper assessments of your attack surface using multiple methods to discover risk. This is very important when you need to scan software across all system drives or investigate deep component-level software vulnerabilities where default settings may result in false negatives.

Assign tags to indicate exposure. Use dynamic tagging to identify PHP2Shell on existing and newly discovered assets.

Actively manage open remediations. Use Exposure Response in Tenable One Vulnerability Management to create Jira tickets or ServiceNow incidents and monitor remediation progress.

Check out these solution walk-throughs to learn more about Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center:

How to Identify and Address PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities in Tenable Security Center. This demo shows how to assess and remediate disclosed PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619). Start the investigation by searching the complete asset inventory for potential vulnerabilities. Construct an advanced query to filter for specific known PHP-related CVEs affecting the environment. Review the IP Summary to understand the overall vulnerability posture of affected hosts with known CVEs. Use specific Tenable Plugin IDs for PHP-related vulnerabilities to uncover detailed findings across all assets. Next steps: set up a pre-configured or custom report and/or dashboard to assess the impact of PHP-related vulnerabilities across the environment.

Web App Scanning

Tenable One Web App Scanning (WAS) can help you assess your web applications for the presence of PHP2Shell, especially where PHP is embedded in content management systems (CMS), databases, and session management platforms. WAS crawls across modern web applications and APIs to identify OWASP Top 10 risks and web app component vulnerabilities. It inspects components, HTTP headers, server signatures, and cookies looking for PHP versions and associated vulnerabilities.

Tips for using WAS include:

Standard WAS scan policies will discover PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. No need to create a customized policy as long as you select all plugin groups in your scan setup. WAS assessments take longer than traditional vulnerability management scans because WAS analyzes web frameworks and responses in more depth.

Incorporate ASM results into new WAS assessments. WAS scans need known web app targets to point the scanner to assess risk. Use ASM findings to discover previously unknown web apps so that you can add them into your assessment scope.

Filter on CVEs to find results. In the Findings page, you can apply filters to see where you are exposed. Generate reports and export results to easily send to application owners and remediation teams to fix.

See the solution walk-through to learn more about Tenable One Web App Scanning.

Patch Management

Tenable Patch Management can help you accelerate patching by matching asset and exposure findings to the patches you need to apply. You can launch patch workflows directly from Tenable One Vulnerability Management and Tenable Security Center to define the right patch strategy based on your organization’s requirements. Tenable Patch Management enables autonomous patching, safety controls and rollbacks, and automated post-scan validation to ensure exposures have been closed.

Important Tenable Patch Management tips include:

Customize your patching strategy to address emergency vulnerabilities. Define patching schedules, deployment plans, and automation levels to address PHP2Shell and other critical out-of-band remediations.

Title: PHP2Shell Is a Wake-Up Call for Every Business Leader
Context: AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw...
Full Text:
AI is changing how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited for defenders and attackers alike, and the practical effect is that the time organizations have between a flaw being found and a flaw being exploited keeps shrinking. Today, we have more known vulnerabilities than at any point in history, and they’re being exploited faster than ever. Nearly 87% of exploited vulnerabilities in 2026 have been exploited before or on the day they were disclosed, up from 48% in 2024 and just 19% in 2018, according to zerodayclock.com, a neutral, independent observatory for cybersecurity telemetry.

More code, more bugs, and AI-aided discovery have all influenced this volume. The systems exposed are often the same systems that run revenue, operations, and customer relationships. Leaders now need to focus on something bigger than prevention alone. They need to build cyber resilience, the ability to withstand an attack, continue operating, and recover quickly. Every organization is racing against the clock to build that resilience.

We saw this play out recently during a week that saw multiple high-profile vulnerabilities and security incidents emerge in rapid succession. PHP2Shell, the name given to two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP, became one of the most visible examples of how quickly newly disclosed flaws can become immediate operational risks. Researchers using frontier AI models identified the flaws and worked with the PHP Foundation to prepare fixes, but details leaked before the planned release. Patches were pushed early, but between the time the vulnerability was disclosed and the patch was available, exploitation attempts began appearing almost immediately. Our Arctic Wolf Labs researchers used aggregated, anonymized telemetry from across our customer community to spot spikes in scanning activity and to analyze exploitation attempts and uncover attacker payloads tied to PHP2Shell. Labs also replicated attacker techniques in controlled environments.

Those findings fed new detections, threat hunt queries, and immediately valuable customer remediation guidance, but detection and response work like this is most effective when an organization already knows what it needs to protect. While PHP2Shell captured much of the industry’s attention, it was only one example in a week that underscored how quickly new exposures can emerge across technologies and attack surfaces. The broader lesson is that organizations need resilience before the next disclosure arrives, and that the time to build cyber resilience into an organization’s ecosystem is now. Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic, warned on X following the PHP2Shell disclosure that security leaders need to prepare their boards as soon as possible for the new threat landscape.

“As bad as things have gotten in the past 4 days, they are going to get a lot worse before they get better. security leaders, never let a crisis go to waste: please go to your boards and ask for help right now. not for ai, for the basics. (we need to hold on for ~18 months.)” — Jason Clinton, Deputy CISO at Anthropic

Organizations best positioned during that window already knew where PHP ran in their environment, which of those systems faced the internet, and how quickly they could patch, restart, and verify each one. A flaw in a system you cannot see cannot be fixed in the hours that matter. Those are the basics boards need to fund. Because the gap between discovery and exploitation will keep shrinking, the organizations that win the race against the clock are the ones that build that foundation of continuous visibility into their attack surface and disciplined exposure management before the next disclosure arrives.

Machine Speed Is the New Normal

AI accelerated both sides of the PHP2Shell situation timeline. The underlying flaws in the code had reportedly been in PHP for years, and turning them into a usable exploit required a level of complexity that would have been extremely difficult and time-consuming for most researchers to achieve on their own. Attackers gain the same AI efficiencies defenders do. They’re using AI to write malware, build exploits, find vulnerabilities, and automate actions. This means the gap between a flaw being disclosed and being exploited will keep narrowing. Patching alone cannot keep pace when that gap is just a few hours long.

In many circumstances, a vulnerability is disclosed before a patch is available. PHP2Shell showed us that. In those moments, security leaders need a way to detect exploit attempts and respond effectively. Machine speed meets that moment, especially when an exposure is widespread, and security leaders should recognize that machine-speed attack and defense are the new normal.

That shift has implications far beyond the security team. Cyber risk now deserves the same level of ownership, accountability, and investment as financial and operational risk. Boards and executive teams need to treat security as a business issue, not just a technical one. That starts with the fundamentals, including maintaining an accurate inventory of assets, applying patches on a defined timeline, enforcing strong identity controls, and maintaining continuous visibility across the environment. These aren’t new security practices, but they become far more important as AI compresses response timelines. You can’t remediate a vulnerability in hours if you don’t know the system exists.

The Four Fundamental Principles of Threat Protection for the AI Era

Vulnerabilities aren’t the only path to a breach. Initial access comes from social engineering (which is scaling with AI), internet-facing misconfigurations, and internet-facing vulnerabilities. Once an attacker is inside, more internal exposure means faster movement. We want to close the opportunity through configuration health and security hygiene.

Security fundamentals only work when teams can operationalize them consistently.

Exposure management strategies turn security hygiene upkeep into a repeatable process. Start with full visibility of your attack surface, including shadow IT and configuration gaps. Then connect asset management with vulnerability and patch management so each cycle improves on the last. Find known and hidden assets, assess them in the context of one another, identify where vulnerabilities are present and controls are missing, and mitigate the highest impact exposures first.

True resilience requires a continuous cycle of risk mitigation over time. Fewer exposures mean fewer opportunities for attackers, and organizations of every size can better defend against AI-driven threats with AI-driven defense and expert oversight. That means operating at machine speed with experts overseeing the work, and it requires knowing your environment, maintaining strong security fundamentals, and responding quickly when new threats emerge. In an era of machine-speed attacks, resilience belongs to organizations that can move just as fast.

Security operations must evolve as well. Human-only processes can’t keep pace with the speed and volume of modern threats. At the same time, fully autonomous security without oversight introduces its own risks. AI should handle most of the volume of investigation that slows down teams, while experienced analysts focus on validation, judgment, and the genuinely complex threats that require context. We’ve built Arctic Wolf around that principle. Our patent-pending Swarm of Experts™ combines specialized AI agents with expert human oversight, allowing us to operate at machine speed. Large teams of AI agents perform investigations, analysis, and response activities at scale, while experienced security experts remain involved where judgment matters most.

Leaders also need to prepare for the reality that one day, their organization may fall victim to AI-driven adversaries, with tested response plans and the ability to restore operations quickly. As the threat landscape rapidly evolves, this scenario appears increasingly likely, especially for businesses that lack the resources to staff their own security team.

We built Arctic Wolf for moments like this one. Internal staffing around the clock is difficult and costly, even for large organizations. Attackers don’t care about holidays, and AI cares even less. That’s why a partner matters. By combining AI-driven automation with expert human oversight, we help customers respond with speed and confidence when new risks emerge. Through our global partner ecosystem, we’re bringing that capability to organizations around the world and helping security leaders turn cyber risk into cyber resilience.

PHP2Shell won’t be the last vulnerability to remind us how quickly the threat landscape can change. This isn’t a risk to sleep on or push to next year’s budget. The time to act is now. The organizations that come through these moments will be the ones that understand their environments, maintain strong security fundamentals, and can respond decisively when new threats emerge. There has never been a better time to get proactive about cyber resilience.

This blog reflects the author’s views as of the publication date and contains forward-looking statements and opinions about technology trends. Actual outcomes may differ based on attacker behavior, customer environments, and broader market and regulatory developments.

Title: UK pentester 'killa' claims $2K Bitcoin prize in PHP2Shell capture-the-flag contest
Context: Pavur launched the CTF (capture the flag) challenge to prove that the PHP2Shell exploit was not as easy as those in the cybersecurity community claimed it to be, promising to...
Full Text: A UK-based developer and pentester has claimed a $2,000 Bitcoin prize for demonstrating the exploitability of the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities that melted the internet last week. Jaydip Modhwadia, 26, otherwise known as “Killa,” claimed the prize set by James Pavur, who launched the "Steal My Bitcoin" site on October 24. Pavur launched the CTF (capture the flag) challenge to prove that the PHP2Shell exploit was not as easy as those in the cybersecurity community claimed it to be, promising to award $2,000 in Bitcoin to anyone who could achieve Remote Code Execution (RCE) on his website. "My Bitcoin was stolen after 19.28 hours," the website now says, after Modhwadia claimed the prize, although the real time taken is thought to be less than three hours. Soon after Pavur launched the CTF on Saturday, prospective flag-catchers complained that the website he set up, which served only static HTML, was not built in a way that allowed the PHP2Shell exploit to achieve RCE. The web page was running a vulnerable version of PHP, but the exploit path required a vulnerable website to serve a PHP file for flag-catchers to use as a hook – something that Pavur seemingly updated at around 1300 UTC on October 25. Modhwadia achieved RCE on the website, exposing a PHP endpoint, at 1547 UTC. After an error from Pavur placing the wrong wallet key on the server, the CTF creator sent Modhwadia his award, which the community upped to $2,000 from Pavur’s initial $500. The pentester published a write-up of his method, a single-file Python script he says requires 20 HTTP requests "at most" to fully execute. Speaking to The Register, Modhwadia also confirmed that he got the flag in "around three or so hours in total." He said he followed the news about the competition, "but didn't attempt it until it gained significant notice." If he had attempted it before Pavur introduced the endpoint, he may have struggled. For hours, bug bounty hunters were trying to access the website to attempt the challenge, as news of the CTF had exploded across tech circles. "The fact that it took 19 hours was because after it went popular, the entire site became basically unusable for anyone at all," Modhwadia added. The challenge saw a huge number of attempts, despite Pavur's decision to introduce a prohibitive 1MB request limit on Nginx. Alon Gal, co-founder and CTO at Hudson Rock, commended Modhwadia's work, but added that his success achieved in just a few hours should not be taken to mean that the same attack could be automated at scale. He said: "Does this mean autonomous AI agents can now compromise arbitrary PHP servers at scale? No. This was a sophisticated, target-specific exploit. "But it does demonstrate that PHP2Shell can be weaponized against a live target, even with meaningful technical constraints." Modhwadia's proof of concept is not the first to prove PHP2Shell is exploitable, but it falls under the more advanced category. Early signs suggested that Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) on a vulnerable server would prove a significant barrier to real-world exploitation, and the pentester’s solution bypasses it, along with the others that were disclosed recently. Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, told The Register last week that attackers are finding new ways to exploit PHP2Shell, and "are clearly spending time (and tokens) on this bug." Initially, experts said exploit code was being found online hours, or even days, before the vulnerabilities were disclosed publicly, which led to millions of exploit attempts, although it was too early to determine the efficacy of these on real-world systems. Scores of websites were taken down for maintenance last week as organizations raced to protect themselves from the attacks, which may or may not have proved successful. Modhwadia said he donated a portion of the prize he received to the Lupus Foundation to raise awareness about the condition, from which he also suffers. ®

Title: 10 Software Security Practices Built for the Next 250 Years
Context: Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that...
Full Text:
OPINION

When I testified before Congress with my L0pht colleagues in 1998, we warned that insecure software could put the systems society depended on at risk. Technology has changed dramatically since then, but the fundamental security questions remain familiar. Where does untrusted data enter? What authority does a component have? Who owns the risk, and how do we know a control worked?

We cannot predict the technology stack of 2276, but we can establish practices that make software trustworthy as technology evolves. These 10 are a good place to start.

Make security part of the architecture. Secure by design should describe how a system is engineered, beginning with secure defaults, approved patterns, clear trust boundaries, and controls that make insecure outcomes difficult. When security is introduced near the end of development, it must work against decisions already embedded in the architecture, while built-in controls become part of how the system operates and evolves.

Maintain an accurate picture of what you have. Every organization needs a continuously updated inventory of its applications, open source dependencies, development tools, AI models, and external services, along with clear ownership for critical systems. When a serious vulnerability emerges, teams should be able to determine quickly where the affected component is running, what it can reach, and who is responsible for addressing it.

Verify every line of code. Code should earn trust whether it was written by an employee, generated by an AI assistant, or obtained from a third party. Our research found that 44% of AI-generated coding tasks introduced a known vulnerability, which means organizations adopting these tools need independent security testing that operates at the same speed as development and verifies code before it reaches production.

Make the secure path the easiest path. Developers work under constant pressure to ship, so security controls that produce excessive noise, delay builds, or pull people away from their normal tools will eventually be bypassed. Organizations should put precise feedback, approved components, and validated fixes directly into repositories, pipelines, and coding workflows, making the secure approach the most efficient way to complete the work.

Match security speed to development speed. AI is turning software insecurity into a throughput problem because teams can now produce and change code faster than manual review can follow. Testing, policy enforcement, and remediation therefore need to operate continuously across the development life cycle, with automation handling repeatable work and people concentrating on the complex decisions that require business context and judgment.

Control what enters the software supply chain. Modern applications are assembled from large volumes of code that organizations did not write, and each dependency introduces another relationship that must be understood and maintained. Teams should evaluate components when they enter a build, record their provenance, detect malicious or abandoned packages, and plan for safe upgrades, since an inventory alone cannot prevent risky software from being introduced.

Pay down security debt before it comes due. Veracode's research found that security debt now affects 82% of organizations, leaving an expanding reservoir of vulnerabilities that have remained unresolved for more than a year. As AI-powered discovery compresses years of vulnerability research into months, leaders need to fund remediation as an ongoing engineering function, define expectations for addressing the highest-risk flaws, and track whether new risk is accumulating faster than teams can remove it.

Measure the risk you remove. Most security programs can report how many vulnerabilities they found and closed, yet those activity measures do not show whether the organization has become safer. More useful measures include how long critical, exploitable flaws remain exposed, whether fix capacity is keeping pace with incoming risk and how quickly teams can reduce exposure in applications tied to sensitive data or essential business operations.

Threat-model the entire AI system. An AI agent includes far more than the model because its identity, permissions, tools, memory, data, runtime, and network access all contribute to what it can ultimately do. Organizations should authorize sensitive actions where they occur, constrain what compromised components can reach, include the runtime in data-flow analysis, and retain enough evidence to determine what the agent did when something goes wrong.

Preserve human accountability. Every important application and accepted risk needs an accountable owner, supported by evidence of the controls applied, tests performed, and decisions made throughout the software life cycle. As machines assume a larger role in writing and modifying code, people must retain enough understanding to challenge the output, recognize unexpected behavior, and demonstrate that reasonable precautions were taken.

Related:Anthropic-Themed Phishing Emails Bypass Top Security Tools

Cybersecurity Practices That Can Adapt

The next 250 years will bring technologies that we cannot name today, although the systems built with them will still have inputs, privileges, dependencies, and consequences. Lasting security will come from disciplined engineering, continuous verification, and clear responsibility, supported by people who understand how complex systems fail and know how to question the assumptions behind them.

Related:'Gheist' Weaponizes GitHub Tokens to Steal Cloud Secrets

That hacker mindset has served the industry well, and we need to keep teaching it to developers, defenders, and the next generation of security researchers. The tools and architectures will continue to change, while our responsibility to build systems worthy of trust will endure.

Context: Checkout protections, read-only cache tokens, and event policies close the paths that made exploitation trivial
Full Text:
For years, pull_request_target has been the canonical Pwn request vector: a workflow trigger that runs with repository secrets, yet can be triggered by anyone who opens a pull request from a fork. In 2026, GitHub responded with platform changes that make the default-case exploit significantly harder..

These changes represent real progress. Checkout protections, read-only cache tokens, and event policies close the paths that made exploitation trivial. But they don't eliminate the vulnerability class. They shift it. Attackers who previously exploited any pull_request_target workflow now need to find explicit opt-ins, outdated checkout versions, unprotected triggers, or script injection.

In Part 1 of our GitHub Actions research, we laid out the threat model and core defenses, and Part 2 covered AI-powered actions. This post updates that threat model for 2026: what GitHub's changes actually protect against, where the gaps remain, and how defenders need to adjust. The audit checklist at the end covers what to look for in your own workflows.

The 2026 Security Overhaul: Timeline of Changes

Recognizing the endemic risk posed by Pwn requests, GitHub spent 2026 systematically closing the gap through a phased rollout of platform-level protections and action updates.

Date

Milestone & Action Taken

June 18, 2026

Release of actions/checkout@v7.0.0, blocking fork code checkouts by default in untrusted triggers (pull_request_target, and workflow_run triggered by pull requests).

June 26, 2026

GitHub introduces read-only cache tokens at the platform level for untrusted triggers, preventing cache poisoning attacks.

July 20, 2026

Backported fork checkout protections across all active major versions of actions/checkout (v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, and v6.1.0; v1 excluded). Workflows referencing mutable version tags (e.g., @v4) inherit these defenses automatically.

September 10, 2026

Fine-grained cache controls via cache-mode reached General Availability (GA).

September 17, 2026

Workflow Execution Protections reached GA, enabling fine-grained event policies and actor rules.

December 2, 2026

[Scheduled] GitHub begins enforcing the default event policy that blocks pull_request_target in public repositories without an explicit event policy. The rule has been in evaluate mode since September 17. Private and internal repositories are not affected.

Residual Risk: What Still Works

While this sequence of platform updates significantly strengthens default security configurations for GitHub Actions, they don't remove all risk.

The December 2 enforcement is a default, not a ban. Maintainers whose automation depends on pull_request_target (labelers, preview deploys, fork CI with secrets) will add an event policy that allows it. Those are exactly the workflows that handle untrusted input with elevated privileges. The default policy also doesn't apply to private and internal repositories or to workflow_run. The rest of this section covers how these surviving workflows can still be exploited.

SHA Pinning: The Security Paradox

One of the most disconcerting findings in our research is how standard supply chain hardening advice - specifically pinning actions to exact commit SHAs - can inadvertently bypass GitHub's platform defenses.

# "Security-hardened" workflow: SHA-pinned for supply chain safety - uses: actions/checkout@08eba0b27e820071cde6df949e0beb9ba4906955 # v4.3.0

Because GitHub's backported protections rely on logic embedded within actions/checkout itself, pinning to SHA values prior to the July 20, 2026 backport release means the workflow runs legacy code without any safety checks. Our empirical testing across workflow triggers confirmed this discrepancy: referencing mutable tags like @v4 (resolving to v4.4.x) or pinned versions such as @v4.4.0 remain protected, whereas older versions like @v4.3.0 or SHA-pinned references to legacy releases (such as @08eba0b... resolving to v4.3.0) offer no protection.

To maintain protection, security teams using SHA pinning must ensure their refs are updated to match or exceed the minimum patched release versions: v2.8.0, v3.7.0, v4.4.0, v5.1.0, v6.1.0, or v7.0.0+.

Custom Checkout Scripts and Third-Party Actions

A second gap concerns workflows that bypass actions/checkout altogether. GitHub's protections are implemented within the action's code - any alternative method of fetching code operates unrestricted. Direct CLI invocations sidestep protections entirely:

- env: GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }} PR_REPO: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name }} PR_SHA: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} PR_NUMBER: ${{ github.event.pull_request.number }} run: | # Any one of these fetches fork code without actions/checkout's protections # Bypass 1: Direct git clone git clone "https://github.com/${PR_REPO}" pr-code && git -C pr-code checkout "${PR_SHA}" # Bypass 2: gh pr checkout (runs in the base repo's workspace) gh pr checkout "${PR_NUMBER}" # Bypass 3: gh repo clone gh repo clone "${PR_REPO}" fork-code

Third-party checkout actions implement their own git logic, so they don't inherit these protections. Any of them configured with a PR head ref will check out fork code unrestricted.

Unprotected Privileged Triggers

GitHub's checkout protections only cover pull_request_target and workflow_run:

Pwn requests triggered in other event types besides pull_request_target (such as issue_comment) will not be blocked by this change. Further hardening of additional events may be explored in future releases.

GitHub changelog

This creates an inconsistent security boundary: GitHub's cache controls explicitly treat issue_comment as a low-trust trigger, while checkout protections do not. Workflows using issue_comment for bot commands (/deploy, /test, /cherry-pick) remain fully exploitable with checkout v7 - no allow-unsafe-pr-checkout flag required:

on: issue_comment: types: [created] jobs: deploy: if: github.event.issue.pull_request && contains(github.event.comment.body, '/deploy') runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: ref: refs/pull/${{ github.event.issue.number }}/merge # Checks out fork PR code

Other privileged triggers have the same gap. repository_dispatch also runs with secrets, and it's exploitable when a workflow uses attacker-influenced payload data to choose a checkout ref.

Until GitHub extends checkout protections, these workflows have to enforce their own authorization, and it needs to hold from the moment the event fires until the code runs:

- Verify who triggered it. For comment commands, check the commenter's actual repository permission (getCollaboratorPermissionLevel, write or above). Don't rely on author_association, which doesn't reflect current permissions. For repository_dispatch, limit who holds a token that can send the event, and don't treat the payload as proof of who sent it.

- Pin what was approved. refs/pull/N/merge is mutable, so an attacker can push a malicious commit after a maintainer comments /deploy. Check out the exact head SHA, and abort if the PR was updated after the comment was posted.

- Treat the event payload as untrusted input. Validate comment arguments and dispatch payload fields against a strict, anchored allowlist regex, and pass them to the shell through environment variables, never through ${{ }} interpolation.

Script Injection: Pwn Request Without Checkout

A common misconception is that pull_request_target vulnerabilities require checking out fork code. In reality, attackers can achieve code execution without any checkout step, through script injection.

When workflow authors interpolate event context directly into shell commands using ${{ }} expressions, GitHub substitutes the value into the script before the shell runs, so attacker-controlled data becomes part of the command itself:

on: pull_request_target jobs: greet: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo "Thanks for PR: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }}"

An attacker simply crafts a pull request with a malicious title:

"; touch /tmp/pwned; echo INJECTED #

The quote closes the string, the semicolon ends the echo, and everything after it runs as a new command with the job's secrets and token. None of GitHub's 2026 changes touch this: there is no checkout to block, and the vulnerability lies in how the workflow handles untrusted input.

The fix is to never interpolate untrusted input into a script. Pass it through an environment variable instead, so the shell treats it as data:

- env: PR_TITLE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.title }} run: echo "Thanks for PR: $PR_TITLE"

The double quotes around $PR_TITLE matter. Without them, the shell still word-splits and glob-expands the value.

Persistent Data Channels: Beyond Cache Tokens

GitHub's read-only cache tokens protect the Actions cache service, but workflows can still exchange data through channels that remain unaffected.

Artifact Poisoning

The upload-artifact and download-artifact actions operate independently of cache tokens. The classic attack chain uses an unprivileged pull_request workflow to upload attacker-controlled build outputs, then a privileged workflow_run to download and execute them:

# .github/workflows/build.yml - unprivileged, runs the fork's code name: Build on: pull_request jobs: build: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 - run: npm ci && npm run build # Attacker-controlled - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4 with: name: build-output path: ./dist/ # .github/workflows/deploy.yml - privileged, has secrets name: Deploy Preview on: workflow_run: workflows: ["Build"] types: [completed] jobs: deploy: if: github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/download-artifact@v4 with: name: build-output path: ./dist/ run-id: ${{ github.event.workflow_run.id }} # Fetches the fork run's artifact github-token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} - run: ./dist/deploy.sh # Executes attacker-controlled file env: DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.DEPLOY_KEY }} # Exposed to attacker code

This is exactly the workflow_run scenario checkout v7 was built to block, and it doesn't help here. The privileged workflow never checks out fork code; it downloads it. Unlike cache entries, there's no platform equivalent that marks artifacts from untrusted runs as tainted, so any workflow that downloads and executes artifacts from a less-trusted run inherits the risk.

Self-Hosted Runner State

On non-ephemeral self-hosted runners, filesystem state persists between jobs. Local package manager caches (~/.npm, ~/.cache/pip), build directories, and installed tools live on the runner's disk, outside the Actions cache service, so read-only cache tokens don't cover them. Attacker code running under an untrusted trigger can write to these locations and poison the next trusted workflow scheduled on the same machine, including release and publish jobs. Use ephemeral runners, which are wiped after each job, for any workflow that untrusted events can trigger, and keep untrusted and trusted workflows in separate runner groups.

The Misconception That Won't Die

Many security teams believe they have another safeguard in place: the "Require approval for all external contributors" setting under Settings -> Actions -> General. If enabled, fork PRs need maintainer approval before workflows run. Problem solved, right?

Not quite. That setting only gates pull_request workflows, which run the fork's own workflow YAML. For pull_request_target, GitHub considers the workflow definition trusted (it comes from the base repository), so the approval setting doesn't apply and the run starts immediately.

The irony cuts deep: pull_request_target is the more dangerous trigger (secrets access, write tokens), yet it's the one that skips the approval requirement. If a pull_request_target workflow needs a human gate, put the privileged job behind an environment with required reviewers, or restrict who can trigger it with Workflow Execution Protections actor rules.

Explicit Opt-In: allow-unsafe-pr-checkout

Finally, developers who need to interact with fork code can explicitly disable checkout protections by enabling the allow-unsafe-pr-checkout flag:

- uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }} allow-unsafe-pr-checkout: true # Re-enables untrusted fork checkouts

While the parameter name is deliberately alarming, determined development teams or third-party workflows may still employ it to maintain legacy automation, effectively reopening the exact same execution vector as before. Security teams should pay special attention to any use of this flag.

What Changed

To sum up, GitHub's 2026 security rollout deserves credit. Default event policies, checkout protections, and read-only cache tokens make the trivial Pwn request (fork, PR, profit) significantly harder. Starting December 2, pull_request_target will no longer run in public repositories unless an event policy explicitly allows it. Cache poisoning through the Actions cache is mitigated. These are real wins.

But the vulnerability class isn't eliminated. It shifted. What remains exploitable: explicit opt-ins via allow-unsafe-pr-checkout, SHA-pinned versions predating the July 2026 backport, custom checkout scripts that bypass action-level controls, script injection requiring no checkout at all, unprotected triggers like issue_comment and repository_dispatch, artifact poisoning chains from pull_request to workflow_run, persistent state on non-ephemeral self-hosted runners, and private or internal repositories, which the default policy doesn't cover. The attack surface shrinks, but what remains is harder to spot.

What To Do About It

Start by auditing what you already run, then get ahead of the December 2 enforcement.

Audit Your Workflows

Wiz Code automatically scans GitHub Actions workflows for Pwn requests, script injection, version gaps, and risky configurations to cover this residual attack surface. Alternatively, use open-source tools like zizmor or even these basic grep searches to start the audit:

# Flag risky triggers, unsafe checkouts, outdated checkout versions, artifact downloads, # self-hosted runners and event data in expressions (env: usage is safe), then review each hit grep -rnE 'pull_request_target|workflow_run|issue_comment|repository_dispatch|allow-unsafe-pr-checkout|self-hosted|download-artifact|gh (pr checkout|repo clone)|git (clone|fetch)|refs/pull|actions/checkout@v(1|2\.[0-7]|3\.[0-6]|4\.[0-3]|5\.0|6\.0)([^0-9]|$)|\$\{\{[[:space:]]*github\.(event\.|head_ref)' .github/workflows/

In addition, run this script to resolve each SHA to its release tag, then compare against the patched versions:

tags=$(git ls-remote --tags https://github.com/actions/checkout) grep -rhoE "actions/checkout@[0-9a-f]{40}" .github/workflows/ | cut -d@ -f2 | sort -u | while read -r sha; do tag=$(echo "$tags" | grep "^$sha" | sed 's#.*refs/tags/##; s#\^{}$##' | sort -V | tail -1) echo "$sha ${tag:-UNKNOWN - not a release tag, check manually}" done

Preparing for the December 2 pull_request_target Enforcement

Starting December 2, the default event policy will block pull_request_target in public repositories that have no explicit event policy. workflow_run is not affected, and neither are private or internal repositories. Before that date:

Check policy insights to see which pull_request_target runs would be blocked.

Decide per workflow whether it actually needs pull_request_target. If not, move it to pull_request. If a privileged follow-up step is still needed, a workflow_run workflow can handle it, but it must treat the PR run's artifacts as untrusted data, never execute them.

For workflows that legitimately need fork access, create an explicit event policy and use workflow file targeting to allow pull_request_target only for those files. Treat every file on that allowlist as high-risk: run it through the audit above before adding it, and re-audit whenever it changes.

Title: UK Biobank back online soon, months after someone tried to sell 500k people's data on Alibaba
Context: The charity, which runs the eponymous research project and describes itself as the custodian of the world's most comprehensive biomedical dataset, said it is waiting for...
Full Text: UK Biobank (UKB) says its platform is now "secure" and that academics will soon regain access, months after a major data leak of volunteer health data. The charity, which runs the eponymous research project and describes itself as the custodian of the world's most comprehensive biomedical dataset, said it is waiting for approval from health data controllers and central government before it relaunches the platform. UK Biobank's Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP) has locked out all medical researchers trying to access its dataset since the April attack, which led to all 500,000 volunteers’ data being listed for sale on Chinese ecommerce website Alibaba. More than 20,000 researchers use the dataset provided by the cloud-based platform. They upload research projects and run experiments informed by the genomic data UKB collected from 40-to-69-year-olds between 2006 and 2010. The org makes around 30 petabytes worth of the stuff available to researchers, who investigate conditions including cancer, dementia, Parkinson’s disease, and COVID-19 immunity. Professor Sir Rory Collins, CEO at UKB, said on Friday that the organization has "completed the work to ensure that the UKB-RAP is secure," and that the progress was checked by an independent cybersecurity company, whose report recommends reopening the platform. The charity will begin a phased re-introduction of researchers to its platform after it receives the necessary approvals, although boffins will not be able to download any results files at first. The platform will pilot a "manual output checking system," where human reviewers will inspect files researchers wish to download before allowing them to do so, ahead of an automated process expected to roll out next year. According to the guide UKB compiled for researchers outlining the changes to the platform, researchers will also be restricted from building public apps and sharing tools with external colleagues until that manual checking system is fully up and running. Researchers were also warned that they will not be able to refresh or dispense data, only work with pre-existing data. They were also told to expect automatic logout out after 15 minutes of inactivity, with 2FA required upon re-authentication. Other technical changes include no longer being able to SSH into jobs, interactive tools being run via "isolated browsing" which restricts data transfer between web apps and the user's local system, and some restrictions on CLI use. UKB is working toward a day when the researchers using its platform store no data on their own computers, working only with that which is uploaded to the repos it hosts. However, in uploading this data to online repos, de-identified data is accidentally included in the code. UKB says it runs daily automated scans of these repos to catch errors, and provides training to researchers to help prevent these occurrences. Collins said that since the attack, most researchers have confirmed the deletion of de-identified data from their projects, but others have not and won't be admitted back to the UKB-RAP until they do. "Despite our repeated reminders, we are still detecting a small number of code repositories that include de-identified participant data," he said. "As these constitute a serious breach of the Material Transfer Agreement, sanctions are being applied against the researchers who are responsible." The charity also said researchers caught exposing participant data in their code will be forced to move their analyses to UKB-RAP, delete any downloaded data, and undergo additional training before being allowed back on the platform. It had initially told researchers to expect a relaunch of the platform by September 2026, although an update penned last month confirmed that it needed to wait for an independent assessment to be completed, despite already making the required security improvements. ®

Title: Bias in Qwen3-Coder Model
Context: For the first time, we showed that this vulnerability lives in the model’s weights, and that removing the model’s CCP alignment removes it
Full Text:
Clive Robinson • October 26, 2026 2:51 PM

@ Bruce, ALL,

With regards,

“I would like more details on how the bias was removed.”

I can not give you specifics for this particular model and it’s token encoding, but I can give a more general explanation.

As I’ve noted previously on a numver of occasions the heart of these AI Large X Models is the so called “Digital Neural Network”(DNN).

That in reality is just a “Digital Signal Processing”(DSP) algorithm that implements an “Adaptive Filter Network”.

What this AFN does is at the basic level “Multiply and Add”(MAD) instructions that feed forward into a form of decision circuit (often a rectifier function). Often this decision circuit is at the output of the summer and is nonlinear in response to provide a normalised spectrum.

If you change the token weights that are in effect linear then you change the shape of the AFN spectrum.

Thus by increasing or reducing the weights for selected tokens, you change the spectrum in desirable ways.

Thus if you can identify the weights to change you change not just the specific part of the spectrum for the token you also change the general spectrum which it forms a part of.

In general LLMs fail after ML building of the DNN for various reasons. Where that behaviour around specific tokens or the broader themes they form part of is seen as undesirable “Reinforcement learning from human feedback”(RLHF) can be applied.

In essence all it does is adjust the specific token weights as well as to a lesser result adjust the more general weights for other tokens.

Thus if you know what token weights need adjusting you can do so.

The trick is making your RLHF the inverse of that used by the model originator.

There are other ways to achieve the same objective of weight adjustment, but this is generally the easiest way to see it as a distinct process.

Another way I’m not going to go into is by cloning the model. You can as part of the process add or subtract the measure you give for tokens or themes.

Look up “LLM logit leakage and distillation” techniques or have a browse through,

“Clone What You Can’t Steal: Black-Box LLM Replication via Logit Leakage and Distilation”

https://arxiv.org/html/2509.00973

Hopefully you will enjoy / have fun.

Title: Britain bets big on AI to defend against the threats AI is helping create
Context: The UK government is throwing £130 million at AI-powered cyber defenses, including plans to deploy autonomous AI agents across critical infrastructure to hunt down security...
Full Text: The UK government is throwing £130 million at AI-powered cyber defenses, including plans to deploy autonomous AI agents across critical infrastructure to hunt down security flaws before attackers get there first. The money is part of a wider £600 million-plus AI spending spree announced by the Treasury ahead of this week's Budget, with ministers also promising to tackle biological threats, bankroll British AI firms, and reduce the country's dependence on foreign technology. Of the cyber funding, £60 million will go towards a new National Cyber Shield that uses agentic AI to bolster Britain's defenses. That includes a £25 million challenge fund for UK cybersecurity firms and plans for a regulatory sandbox to test autonomous security tools across critical infrastructure, government and industry. Another £70 million will establish the National Exposure and Real-Time Vulnerability (NERV) Centre, using AI to sniff out vulnerabilities across Britain's infrastructure and wider economy. The announcement comes just days after the PHP2Shell security scare, which saw dozens of government websites taken offline after critical flaws were discovered in the widely used scripting language. Britain's National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) worked with OpenAI to coordinate disclosure of the PHP flaws and give affected vendors time to prepare fixes, after AI-assisted researchers uncovered the vulnerabilities. Whitehall has already been experimenting with AI-powered vulnerability hunting. AI minister Kanishka Narayan said last week that the technology had uncovered 500 previously unknown security flaws across significant parts of the public sector. It remains unclear how much freedom the new AI defenders will have to act without human intervention, or when they'll be deployed. Ciaran Martin, former head of the NCSC, welcomed the investment, pointing to the week's events as evidence that Britain needs to get its cyber defenses in order. "We need to padlock our systems, and harness AI for defense," he said. The Treasury is also handing another £120 million to the AI Security Institute (AISI), which tests advanced AI systems for dangerous capabilities and researches ways to keep them under control. Cybersecurity isn't the only threat keeping ministers busy. Another £165 million will fund a National AI Biosecurity Initiative, including £100 million for what the government claims will be the world's first dedicated AI Biosecurity Lab. The independent, non-profit lab will use frontier AI models to detect biological threats and accelerate the development of vaccines and treatments. OpenAI is contributing £100 million in compute and model credits, while Anthropic is offering up to £100 million in model credits, model access and technical support. Google DeepMind and British biotech firm Basecamp Research are also involved, while the remaining £65 million will go towards biosurveillance and medical countermeasures against dangerous pathogens. There's something for the homegrown AI industry, too. The government is adding £60 million to its Sovereign AI Fund to invest in British companies developing technologies including robotics and autonomous systems, plus another £60 million for AI research and development procurement. A further £18 million will fund an Advanced Chip Design Academy, intended to help Britain develop more of its own semiconductor expertise rather than relying quite so heavily on technology designed overseas. The package also includes £30 million for local AI partnerships, £15 million for an AI challenge prize initially focused on healthcare, and £23 million for research into AI's impact on jobs and the economy. Manchester will get a new NCSC AI Cyber Security Centre of Excellence to train government specialists. Additionally, ministers are setting aside £10 million a year to study how AI will reshape employment and industry, including the jobs it might make redundant. The government clearly has high hopes for AI. Whether the technology can live up to them without creating a fresh set of problems is another matter.®

Title: PHP2Shell: No login, no app code, no warning. What next?
Context: Two critical flaws disclosed last week, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed "PHP2Shell"), let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server with nothing more than...
Full Text: If you run PHP anywhere in your environment, patch to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 now. Two critical flaws disclosed last week, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 (nicknamed "PHP2Shell"), let an unauthenticated attacker run code on a server with nothing more than a crafted web request. Both carry a CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, every earlier release is affected, and exploitation in the wild has been reported. The patch is the easy part. The hard part is finding every copy of PHP you own, because PHP rarely shows up where you expect it. This post covers what the flaws are, how far exploitation has gone, and how to get to full coverage fast. What happened Details leaked before the planned embargo, so the PHP security team moved fast and shipped fixes within about a day of announcing them. The two vulnerabilities Both bugs live in PHP core, not in any framework or plugin, so they reach anything that runs PHP to serve web requests. Affected server setups include PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed. PHP rates mod_php as the highest risk. No login is needed: the attacker only has to reach a PHP endpoint over HTTP. Fixed versions: 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Every earlier release is affected. PHP has also published minimal source backports for 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1, but there are no official releases for those branches. Treat a backport as a stopgap and plan the upgrade. Is it being exploited? Yes, though reliable public exploits are still scarce. watchTowr reports exploitation in its honeypot network as of October 21, and Tenable relays Cloudflare's CTO saying Cloudflare is seeing early attacks. Other telemetry, such as Patchstack's, shows mostly probing so far. Neither CVE is in CISA's KEV catalog yet, and no public indicators of compromise have been released. How hard the bug is to weaponize depends on the platform. VulnCheck reproduced both flaws and found: Code execution works on ARM64, and on x86 systems where address space layout randomization (ASLR) is turned off. Dozens of public proof-of-concepts exist, but very few work and none bypass ASLR on x86-64. Red Hat likewise rates RCE as hard in practice on default PHP-FPM deployments. Don't read that as permission to wait. Exploits mature quickly once a patch diff is public, and fake PoC repositories for headline CVEs often carry malware, so treat any you find with caution. Tanium's research on exploitability is in Why PHP2Shell is real(opens in a new tab). Most at risk: internet-facing PHP applications, especially those running mod_php or on ARM64 hosts. It's also worth retro-hunting recent web server and PHP-FPM logs for unexplained worker crashes and unusual multipart requests. Why finding PHP is harder than it looks No one has a complete list of PHP-based applications, and anything custom-built won't be on any list. PHP hides in several places at once: OS packages on Linux (php, php-fpm, php8.x), which package managers and most inventory tools see. Homebrew and similar on macOS, outside the system's own package list. Bundled copies on Windows. PHP on Windows usually arrives as a zip extracted to a folder or inside a stack like XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon or a vendor product. It often never registers as an installed application at all. Applications that ship their own PHP, where the fix depends on the application vendor rather than the OS. Containers, where the version is baked into the image tag. PHP is often more widespread than teams expect, and it doesn’t only run on servers. Developer tools, local web stacks and bundled applications put it on workstations too, often without registering as an installed application. The reliable answer is to look at the binaries themselves. In testing, PHP builds from version 5 through 8 all embed their version string (X-Powered-By: PHP/x.y.z), so you can read the exact version straight from the file without running it. How Tanium helps Tanium itself is not affected. Tanium does not use PHP, so there is no impact to Tanium software or Tanium Cloud services. Tanium Guardian content for PHP2Shell is available now in Tanium Cloud. The dashboard shows where PHP is installed and running so you can prioritize patching, with a single fleet-wide count of endpoints with vulnerable PHP across Linux, Windows and macOS. It combines: The existing Installed Applications and Homebrew Applications sensors, which find PHP installed through package managers on macOS and Linux. A Windows PHP Installations sensor that finds PHP where Installed Applications can't see it, including IIS, XAMPP, WampServer, Laragon, package managers and manually extracted copies, and reports version, install type, install path and owning user. The version is read from the binary's file metadata without executing it. A pre-built Saved Question that lists running PHP processes so you can prioritize systems that may be serving traffic. A pre-built Saved Question that identifies PHP containers, matching running containers against php, FrankenPHP and about 25 common PHP-based images such as WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, Nextcloud and Magento. Requires Tanium Cloud Workloads. Tanium Comply finds PHP on disk. For customers licensed for Comply, the dashboard includes PHP2Shell findings by endpoint, full finding details and a 7-day trend, with a pivot to the Comply findings page filtered to the two CVEs. The finding details report shows the specific on-disk locations where PHP was found, which catches copies that package and registry inventories miss. Vulnerability Library definitions for Windows, Linux and macOS are live now — sync the TVL and run an assessment to pick them up. On-premises customers can import the Guardian content manually today. Steps and downloads are in Guardian content for on-premises customers(opens in a new tab) on the Tanium Help Center. Know what's exposed to the internet. More than 13 million internet-facing assets run PHP versions that may be affected, according to Censys Internet Intelligence. Tanium External Attack Surface Management (EASM) discovers the internet-facing assets tied to your organization and identifies the PHP services, versions and web properties among them, with these CVEs surfaced through its coverage of exploitable and weaponized vulnerabilities. Tanium Attack Path Mapping then shows which of those exposed assets share an exposure point with a cloud instance, role or privileged identity: the places where one exploited PHP server becomes a route deeper into your environment. Already using Tanium SBOM? Inventorying PHP versions there is a sound early step. It shows which applications carry a vulnerable PHP and need a vendor update. What to do now Work through these in order; the first three matter most today. Find every PHP install, including Windows copies that never registered as applications. Record the exact version of each. Rank by exposure. Internet-facing servers, mod_php setups and ARM64 hosts come first. Patch to 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35 through your OS vendor, a php.net build or your application vendor. Restart PHP-FPM and web server workers so the new binary is loaded. If you can't patch yet, isolate internet-facing PHP apps where you can, as CERT-EU advises, and put WAF or IDS rules in front of them (Cloudflare and VulnCheck have both shipped rules for the known vectors). Apply the partial setting with care. session.upload_progress.enabled=0 blocks one demonstrated path for CVE-2026-109619 only and does nothing for CVE-2026-109618. It must be set in php.ini, an FPM pool or server config, followed by a worker restart; ini_set() and .user.ini won't apply it. Hunt. Review recent web server and PHP-FPM logs for worker crashes and malformed multipart uploads. Plan off end-of-life PHP. Anything on 8.1 or older has no official fixed release. Where fixed packages stand (as of Oct 21, 16:30 UTC) Distro packages are still rolling out, so check your vendor before assuming a fix is available. The Remi repository won't ship updates today, so PHP advises switching to distro packages or building from source if you depend on it. Read more here. Supplied by Tanium
