Title: The apps are only the beginning.
Context: Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.
Full Text:
Attackers target critical PHP flaws, and former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI’s role in the vulnerability surge. Railway confirms a cyberattack. HPE patches critical ArubaOS flaws. Quest Diagnostics investigates a disruptive intrusion. Capcom reports a data breach. China-linked hackers put AI-powered attacks on autopilot. And researchers uncover a Microsoft 365 campaign that hijacks authentication tokens to bypass MFA. Our guest is Anudeep Parhar, COO at Entrust, sharing his thoughts on AI kill switches. eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

Today is Friday, October 23rd 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

Attackers ramp up attempts to exploit critical PHP vulnerabilities.

Attackers are ramping up attempts to exploit two critical PHP vulnerabilities known as PHP2Shell, but researchers have yet to confirm a successful compromise in the wild.

The flaws allow unauthenticated remote code execution and prompted emergency patches on October 21. Sophos identified attempts to deploy Potassium, a Mirai botnet variant, although the attack it examined was unsuccessful.

Researchers say exploitation is proving more difficult than initially feared, largely because successful attacks require specific server configurations or ways around memory protections.

VulnCheck has developed an exploit that bypasses one such protection, while an exposed attacker server revealed custom exploitation tools and unsuccessful attempts against dozens of targets.

Meanwhile, patching remains a challenge. Qualys estimates roughly 110 million PHP instances run unsupported versions that won’t receive fixes.

Security researchers have identified 426 mobile apps connecting to servers running PHP versions potentially affected by the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities.

NowSecure analyzed more than 15,000 Android and iOS apps, finding that 170 connected to servers running outdated PHP versions that no longer receive official security updates.

The vulnerabilities affect backend servers, not the mobile apps themselves, and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication.

Importantly, researchers caution that identifying a potentially vulnerable PHP version doesn’t establish whether a server remains unpatched or exploitable.

The findings also highlight the risks of third-party dependencies. One advertising provider’s server was contacted by 151 different apps.

NowSecure recommends developers work with their infrastructure providers to verify patching, upgrade unsupported PHP installations, and investigate potential exploitation.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs weighs in on AI and PHP.

Former CISA director Chris Krebs says artificial intelligence is fueling an unprecedented surge in software vulnerability discoveries, creating what some are calling “Black October” for cybersecurity.

Appearing on CNBC, Krebs said AI-powered tools are uncovering security flaws at a pace that threatens to overwhelm organizations’ ability to patch them.

He pointed to the recently disclosed PHP2Shell vulnerabilities as an example. While attackers have attempted exploitation, Krebs said no successful compromises have been confirmed.

His biggest concern isn’t necessarily large enterprises, which generally have the resources to respond quickly. It’s smaller businesses, rural hospitals, utilities, and managed service providers that lack dedicated security teams.

Krebs warned that vulnerabilities in third-party services could expose entire networks, while legacy systems can complicate patching.

He expects the situation to get worse before it improves, as AI continues uncovering vulnerabilities faster than organizations can address them.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack.

Cloud development platform Railway has confirmed a cyberattack that may have exposed customer passwords, API keys, and other secrets stored in encrypted environment variables. The company believes the breach affected a subset of customers but is urging all users to revoke and rotate their credentials as a precaution. Railway temporarily suspended new builds and deployments while investigating. The number of affected customers, the attack’s root cause, and the systems compromised remain unknown.

Railway suspects the incident is part of a broader campaign targeting AI inference providers. Earlier this week, AI coding tool OpenCode reported a similar attack that exposed credentials belonging to more than one percent of its customers. Railway says it plans to publish a detailed post-mortem.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise patches critical vulnerabilities in ArubaOS.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise has released security updates addressing 72 vulnerabilities in ArubaOS, including eight maximum-severity flaws that could allow attackers to bypass authentication or remotely execute malicious code.

The vulnerabilities affect multiple versions of ArubaOS 8 and 10, which power enterprise wireless networking equipment, including access points, controllers, and gateways. All eight maximum-severity flaws can be exploited remotely without authentication, using relatively simple attacks that require no user interaction.

HPE is strongly urging customers to install the patches, citing the number and potential impact of the vulnerabilities. The company also recommends restricting access to management interfaces through network segmentation and firewall controls.

So far, HPE says it has found no publicly available exploit code or evidence that attackers are exploiting these vulnerabilities in the wild.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a disruptive cyberattack.

Quest Diagnostics is investigating a cyberattack that may have exposed patient information and disrupted access to medical test results.

The company discovered unauthorized access to its Quanum Lab Services Manager platform, which healthcare providers use to order tests and retrieve results. Quest took the system offline Thursday and temporarily paused several other systems as a precaution.

The company believes some patient data was accessed but hasn’t determined what information was compromised. Quest says its other operations weren’t affected and is working with law enforcement.

Healthcare providers can use paper requisitions while the system is unavailable. Quest expects to restore service Friday.

The company says the attack is unrelated to recently disclosed PHP vulnerabilities. No threat actor has claimed responsibility.

Capcom discloses a data breach.

Japanese gaming giant Capcom has disclosed a data breach affecting nearly 11.8 million records associated with its CAPCOM ID service.

The compromised information includes email addresses, account identifiers, and login activity. Attackers also changed passwords on 196 accounts, which Capcom has since reset.

The company says it has no evidence that customers’ original passwords were compromised, and credit card information remains unaffected.

Capcom has contained the unauthorized access and notified Japanese authorities. Customers are being warned to watch for phishing attempts impersonating the company.

A China-linked threat actor is using Artex to automate cyberattacks.

Microsoft says a China-linked threat actor is using an open-source AI penetration testing framework called Artex to automate cyberattacks against hundreds of organizations.

The group, tracked as Storm-0940, used the tool in an October campaign targeting ConnectWise customers, accelerating reconnaissance, password spraying, and abuse of OAuth applications.

Microsoft observed more than 151,000 failed login attempts, along with successful authentication using compromised ConnectWise application identities.

The attackers attempted to access more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, sometimes progressing beyond authentication to modify credentials, manipulate directory settings, and establish persistent access.

In one burst of activity, the group targeted more than 300 accounts across eight organizations at over 2,900 attempts per minute.

Microsoft says the campaign illustrates how AI-assisted automation can dramatically accelerate established attack techniques, giving defenders less time to respond.

Researchers uncover a campaign that compromises Microsoft 365 accounts by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Security researchers at Huntress have uncovered a ten-week campaign that compromised Microsoft 365 accounts at 79 organizations by stealing and replaying authentication tokens.

Attackers used adversary-in-the-middle phishing and other techniques to capture legitimate login sessions, allowing them to bypass multifactor authentication without needing victims’ passwords.

Huntress observed at least 497 successful sign-ins alongside more than 200,000 failed attempts. Once inside, attackers registered 48 rogue devices, replaced victims’ authentication methods, and created hidden inbox rules to conceal suspicious communications.

In one case, a compromised account was used to send a payroll-related email to an outside contact.

The attacks relied partly on infrastructure belonging to a German hosting provider.

Huntress recommends properly configured Conditional Access policies and warns that password resets alone won’t eliminate persistent access. Organizations must also revoke sessions and remove unauthorized devices and authentication methods.

eMudra throws in the certificate towel.

From our “you can’t fire me, I quit!” desk, Indian digital trust company eMudhra is getting out of the global SSL/TLS certificate business following a security incident that attracted considerable scrutiny.

The company says it revoked the affected certificate authorities within 14 hours, with no infrastructure compromise, data breach, or affected customer certificates issued.

But eMudhra’s chairman says the resulting social media attention was disproportionate, particularly for a business representing just one percent of company revenue.

Add rising compliance costs and competition from free certificates, and the board decided it was time to pursue other opportunities.

eMudhra promises a smooth transition, including free replacement certificates for affected customers.

Its other digital trust services remain unaffected.

And so, after careful consideration, eMudhra has decided that SSL certificates just aren’t its thing anymore.

Title: PHP2Shell: What This Week Tells Us About the Web We Built
Context: com/blogs/security/amazon-threat-intelligence-identifies-php2shell-exploitation-prior-to-public-disclosure-in-madpot/ SecurityWeek: PHP2Shell patches land as first exploitation...
Full Text:
The week the web’s plumbing failed

On Wednesday afternoon, most of the world’s websites became exploitable at the same moment. The reason was PHP, the thirty-year-old language that still serves roughly seven out of ten sites you visit, including nearly every WordPress, Drupal, Magento and Joomla deployment on earth.

Two bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, now known collectively as PHP2Shell, let an unauthenticated attacker run code on any server that handles PHP web requests. They are present in every PHP version back to 5.4, released in 2012. The coordinated disclosure broke down a day early, after leaks on 20 October. Exploit attempts hit honeypots before a patch existed. Government sites in Europe chose to go dark on patch day rather than stay online and exposed.

I have watched a great many “critical” bulletins come and go. Most of them deserve a calm Tuesday and a ticket in the queue. This one does not, and I want to explain why in business terms rather than technical ones. The technical story will be told well by the researchers who found it, and our own research team at Orca has published its analysis. The business story is the one your board, your CFO and your customers are going to ask you about.

What happened

The two flaws sit in the parts of PHP that every request touches: memory management and error handling. CVE-2026-109618 abuses how PHP bails out of an out-of-memory condition while request data is only half initialised. CVE-2026-109619 abuses global state that keeps pointing at request memory after that memory has been freed. Both are rated 9.2 on CVSS v4 and work without credentials, and both can also be used to read process memory, which is where your database passwords, API keys and session secrets happen to live.

What makes this different from the usual PHP advisory is the discovery story. The out-of-memory weakness was first noticed in 2020 and rediscovered during an audit in 2024. Nobody could prove it was exploitable, so it was never fixed. In August 2026, a small group of researchers, among them Calif and OpenAI, used frontier AI models to build the exploit chain that human researchers had judged impractical. The flaw did not change. The cost of proving it had.

Then the disclosure process came apart. A video with a working proof of concept was published by mistake. A container vendor shipped fixed images six hours before the coordinated release, giving anyone who cared to look a binary diff of the patch. The PHP Foundation pulled its release forward by a day. By the time the fixes landed, proof-of-concept exploits were already circulating and several vendors were watching attempts against their sensors.

When (UTC)

What happened

11 Aug 2026

The OOM-to-RCE chain is reported to the PHP security team by two independent parties; further attack vectors follow over the next weeks

17 Oct 2026

Amazon’s MadPot honeypots record an exploitation attempt, four days before public disclosure

20 Oct 2026

CVE IDs leak online; PHP issues a pre-announcement and moves the release up a day; a research team’s exploit video follows that evening

21 Oct, 02:00

First public proof-of-concept exploits appear; multiple actors begin probing honeypots

21 Oct, 03:02

Cloudflare deploys WAF rules for the known vectors, about eleven hours ahead of the patch

21 Oct, 07:41

Chainguard publishes patched container images, more than six hours before the embargo lifts

21 Oct, 14:00

PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 released; minimal source backports for 7.4 through 8.1; nothing for 5.4 through 7.3

21 Oct, afternoon

Government websites in Europe taken offline; exploitation reported “at scale” against the session upload-progress path

22 Oct 2026

Open-source scanners released; mass exploitation under way

The PHP team’s own position is blunt: there are no complete mitigations and updating is the only safe choice. Configuration tweaks can narrow specific attack paths. They do not close the hole.

Censys counts roughly 2.58 million internet-facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP. Every one of them that serves web requests, whether through PHP-FPM, mod_php, php-cgi, FrankenPHP or LiteSpeed, is in scope.

Why this one hurts

The first thing to understand is that this is an engine bug, so every WordPress site, Drupal install and plugin inherits it. “Our application code is secure” is a true statement that does not matter. If your code runs on PHP, your code is the delivery vehicle for someone else’s payload.

The second thing is that almost nobody knows how much PHP they run. The flagship e-commerce platform, yes. The marketing microsite the agency built in 2019, the acquired brand’s storefront that was never migrated, the internal wiki, the staging box someone exposed to test a webhook, the customer portal your SaaS vendor runs on a hosting provider you have never heard of: these are the servers that will be compromised. Most of them are not in a CMDB. Many of them are not in anyone’s memory.

The third thing is what the attacker gets. The natural outcome of PHP2Shell is a web shell: a persistent backdoor living inside a legitimate, trusted, SSL-certified site that carries your brand. From there an attacker phishes your customers from your own domain, serves malware from a URL that every security product trusts, and reads credentials out of process memory to pivot into the cloud accounts behind the site. The breach does not look like a breach. It looks like your website.

The fourth thing is the patch itself. For PHP 8.2 and above there is a clean update. For 7.4 through 8.1 there are source backports, which means someone has to compile them. For anything older there is nothing at all. A great many enterprises are running end-of-life PHP underneath applications nobody wants to touch, because the last time someone touched them the site broke. Those organisations are now choosing between a planned outage and an unplanned compromise. That is where the stress in the market comes from this week: a bill for technical debt that was supposed to be deferred indefinitely has arrived all at once.

And the fifth thing is that the regulators are watching. Under NIS2, DORA and the SEC’s four-day disclosure rule, “we did not know we were running PHP” will be read as an admission.

Who

Exposure

What it costs

Companies with modern PHP (8.2+) and a known inventory

Patched within hours

A busy day and a hunt for anything that got in between 17 Oct and the patch

Companies with modern PHP and an unknown inventory

Patched the sites they know about

Weeks of discovery; the forgotten sites are the ones that get shelled

Companies on PHP 7.x or 8.0/8.1

Source backports only

Build and test effort, or an emergency upgrade with regression risk

Companies on PHP 5.x or 7.0 to 7.3

No fix exists

Take it offline, put it behind a WAF and hope, or rebuild

Everyone

Vendors and suppliers running PHP

Due diligence you cannot do yourself; you are only as patched as your weakest agency

The uncomfortable lessons

This embargo was handled by serious people with months of preparation, and it still leaked through a mistaken video upload and a vendor publishing early. Amazon saw exploitation attempts four days before anyone outside the circle was supposed to know. I would now treat any embargo as a courtesy. Plan on 24 to 48 hours of warning for the next one, and expect that warning to come from a honeypot rather than a mailing list.

The OOM flaw sat unfixed for six years because turning it into code execution looked impractical. Frontier models made it practical, so “not proven exploitable” should no longer be enough to close a ticket. The PHP Foundation has published 15 CVEs since July and says AI-assisted research is sending it far more reports than before. Every mature codebase written in C has a drawer full of bugs that were triaged as theoretical. That drawer is now being emptied, and not only by the people who will tell you about it.

Inventory was the control that mattered on Wednesday. Everyone was vulnerable, so the useful question was where PHP was running. The organisations that could answer that in minutes were patched within hours. The ones that could not are still discovering what they own, and they are discovering it in the same order the attackers are.

The sites that cannot be patched today were kept on old PHP because upgrading looked expensive and the risk looked abstract. For years that was a defensible trade-off. This week the risk became concrete, and the upgrade belongs on this quarter’s plan for anyone still running end-of-life runtimes on internet-facing systems.

The maintainers are carrying us. A handful of people at a foundation spent ten weeks fixing the engine that runs seventy percent of the web, under embargo, while watching that embargo fail around them. That arrangement held while bugs surfaced slowly. It will not hold once AI finds them faster than volunteers can fix them. Every enterprise that depends on PHP and does not fund the PHP Foundation is taking a free ride on infrastructure it would never accept for its own data centre.

What to do now

The next 72 hours are about containment. The next quarter is about never being in this position again.

In the next 72 hours

Find every PHP runtime you own, not every application you remember. Scan from the outside in. Include container images, serverless functions, appliances with embedded web interfaces, the marketing stack, acquired brands and anything an agency ever built for you. If you run Orca, the PHP2Shell news item in the platform includes a query that lists every asset with a PHP package installed across your connected cloud accounts.

Patch everything on 8.2 or later today, without waiting for a change window.

For 7.4 through 8.1, compile the backports or upgrade. For anything older, take it off the internet or put it behind a WAF with the PHP2Shell rules enabled, and accept that this is a bandage.

Assume compromise for any internet-facing PHP host that was unpatched after 17 October. In Orca, the PHP2Shell alerts flag which vulnerable hosts are reachable from the internet, so start there. Hunt for web shells, new admin users, modified core files and outbound connections you did not expect.

Rotate every secret that lived in PHP process memory on an exposed host: database credentials, API keys, cloud access keys, signing secrets.

Ask every vendor, agency and SaaS provider that touches your data the same question: which PHP version, patched when, and what did you find.

In the next quarter

Retire end-of-life PHP from anything internet-facing, with a budget line and an owner. If the application cannot move, treat the application itself as the risk.

Get secrets out of process memory. Short-lived credentials, workload identity and a secrets manager mean that the next memory-read bug leaks tokens that expire in an hour instead of keys that last for years.

Put an edge in front of everything. A CDN or WAF that can take a virtual patch in minutes bought the well-prepared organisations about eleven hours this week, which is often the difference between a hunt and a breach.

Create a pre-authorised emergency change path. The companies that patched within hours had already agreed, in calm times, who can push a change to production without a meeting.

Prioritise by exposure, not by CVSS. Two 9.2s on an internal admin tool behind a VPN are a Thursday. The same two on a public storefront holding card data are a board call. Your tooling should already know the difference.

How Orca can help

Most of the first 72 hours goes on finding out what you own, and that is where Orca starts. Orca’s agentless SideScanning reads installed packages directly from cloud workloads, so PHP is found on virtual machines, containers and container images without anything to deploy first. Detection for both CVEs went live in the platform on 21 October.

Finding PHP answers half of the question. The other half is deciding what to patch first and what an attacker could reach from each host. Each PHP2Shell alert shows whether the asset is reachable from the internet, whether the vulnerable component is loaded at runtime, and how critical it is to the business.

For the hunt and the clean-up, Orca’s lightweight eBPF Sensor adds runtime visibility on the hosts where it is deployed, and the asset graph shows which keys and cloud roles each exposed host holds, and that is where secret rotation should start.

Several customers told us the Early Intel query in the platform’s From the News item gave them a head start, letting them find their PHP hosts and begin mitigating before the official advisory went out.

None of this replaces patching. It shortens the time between the advisory and knowing where to patch first.

What this means for the next two years

PHP2Shell is the first widely visible instance of a pattern that will define vulnerability management for the rest of this decade.

AI has collapsed the cost of turning a theoretical bug into a working exploit. The backlog of “unproven” memory-safety issues in the foundational C codebases of the internet, the interpreters, the TLS libraries, the image parsers, the web servers, is enormous, and it was accumulated in an era when proving exploitability took a specialist a month. That era ended this summer. Expect the same story, with different names, in Python, Ruby, Node, OpenSSL and the kernel. Expect it more than once a quarter. Every CISO should assume their foundational dependencies have critical bugs. What they can still influence is whether they hear about them through a coordinated advisory or through an incident.

The window between disclosure and mass exploitation is now measured in hours, and sometimes it is negative. Monthly patch cycles were designed for a world where attackers needed weeks to weaponise a bug. For anything that faces the internet, that cadence is obsolete. The operating model that survives this decade treats patching exposed systems as a continuous process with a pre-approved fast lane, and treats a virtual patch at the edge as the normal first response rather than an exotic one. It also depends on an inventory that can answer “where do we run X” in a minute, across cloud, on-premises, containers, vendors and the long tail of forgotten sites.

If there is a single takeaway, it is about time. The weakness had been in PHP since 2012, the working exploit was about two months old, and the response had to happen within hours. The organisations under the most stress this week are the ones whose decision-making was built for a slower world, whatever the quality of their security teams. Most of what fixes that is deciding things in advance, so that the answers already exist before the next disclosure.

Context: Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026
Full Text:
What you will learn

Why PHP2Shell runs before your app code does, why a clean investigation proves nothing, which secrets to rotate first and how vaulting and just-in-time access limit what a stolen credential can reach.

Roughly seven in ten websites run on PHP. An unpatched PHP server can be broken into with one web request and no password. That hole has been there for 14 years, and attackers reached it before the patch did.

The flaw is PHP2Shell: two critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime itself, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. The fix shipped on October 21, 2026, four days after the first exploitation attempts were seen. PHP sits behind 69% of websites whose server-side language is known.

Upgrading PHP is the easy part. The hard part is what attackers already took: database credentials, API keys, session tokens and personal data, each still valid until someone rotates it. Treat every secret the server could read as stolen, including any it fetched from a vault.

A vault with automated rotation makes the cleanup fast. Without one, it is slow, manual work. Either way, rotation fixes the stolen credentials and does nothing about the other two problems. The leaked personal data will fuel targeted phishing and identity attacks for months, and breaches will spread from organizations that patched late to those that depend on them.

This is the first week of a long event.

Four reasons PHP2Shell is more dangerous than a typical critical flaw

Critical web vulnerabilities surface most weeks, and most of them don't deserve the label "dangerous". PHP2Shell does, for four reasons.

1. PHP2Shell runs before your application code does

With Apache mod_php, PHP is embedded in the web server itself. On those servers the exploit fires while PHP is still parsing the request, before any application code runs. PHP-FPM and other setups are affected too, under extra conditions.

The danger: the attack is over before your login page, your multi-factor check or your application's logging is reached. It can succeed and leave no trace where you would normally look.

2. PHP2Shell can leak server memory without leaving a web shell

PHP's advisory for CVE-2026-109619 lists memory disclosure as a confirmed impact. The process that handles requests keeps credentials, tokens and session data from earlier requests in memory, and an attacker can read it without dropping a file or running a command.

The danger: There may be no web shell to find. An investigation that finds nothing has not shown that nothing was taken. Rotate the server's credentials anyway.

3. Attackers were exploiting PHP2Shell before the patch existed

Amazon's threat intelligence team saw the first exploitation attempt on October 17, 2026. The CVE identifiers leaked on October 20, 2026, so PHP released the fix a day early. Proof-of-concept exploits were circulating hours before the planned release, and Amazon now describes PHP2Shell as broadly exploited in the wild.

The danger: A server patched the day the fix shipped may already have been compromised, and the gap between disclosure and mass exploitation was hours, not days.

4. PHP2Shell has been in PHP since 2012

Calif Research, the firm that found the bugs, traces the earliest affected code path to PHP 5.4.0, released in 2012. A related flaw surfaced in a 2024 audit, but nobody proved it exploitable, so nobody fixed it.

The danger: 14 years of PHP releases are exposed, and more than a third of PHP-powered sites run PHP 7 or older, branches that will never get an official fix. Those servers stay exploitable for months.

A web server is a credential store

Next to the PHP code on a typical server: a config.php with the database password. A .env file with API keys, cloud access keys, mail credentials and OAuth client secrets. Process memory holding the tokens and personal details of whoever was signed in. The PHP process reads all of it, so an attacker whose code runs inside that process can too.

With those secrets, the attacker no longer needs the vulnerability. Every login looks like legitimate traffic, and none of it trips a detection written for the PHP flaw. The vulnerability was the entry. The identities are the payload. A PHP vulnerability becomes an identity problem.

PHP2Shell's aftershocks will come in three waves

This is a forecast, based on how credential theft has played out before.

Wave 1 is now and runs for weeks. Automated exploitation of anything unpatched. Web shells and cryptominers installed. Config files and environment variables harvested at scale. Active sessions hijacked.

Wave 2 starts within a week and continues for months. The harvested credentials are used: database logins from new places, cloud keys to pull data and OAuth secrets to mint tokens for SaaS applications. None of it requires an exploit, and all of it appears to be authorized access.

Wave 3 runs for months or more. Leaked personal data and session details fuel targeted phishing and account takeover against your customers and employees. Some organizations will be breached through a vendor, partner or SaaS provider that ran PHP, patched late and rotated nothing. Their incident becomes yours.

What to do about PHP2Shell, in order

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged immediate patching but, at the time of writing, hasn't listed either CVE as known to be exploited. That is not a reason to wait; the first attempts came before any detection signature existed.

In the next hours. Find every place PHP runs, including appliances that bundle it. Upgrade to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 or 8.2.35, or to your vendor's backported package; there is no complete workaround. Isolate anything you can't patch. Investigate from October 17, not the disclosure date.

In the next days. Assume any secret the server could read is in someone else's hands. Inventory them, rotate them starting with the ones that reach the most systems, and invalidate active sessions. Then audit the systems those credentials open for use you didn't authorize.

In the next months. Change what a web server is allowed to hold. Static secrets in files on an internet-facing host are standing privilege. Move them into a vault that rotates them automatically. Give applications and services just-in-time access scoped to the task, so a stolen credential stops working quickly and reaches only what the task needs. Put phishing-resistant authentication in front of the people who will be targeted. Ask your vendors which of these they've done.

Where identity security does its work

If a credential is stolen, the damage should stop at that credential. The Delinea Platform is built for that outcome; it limits how far an attacker can move and what they can reach if they get in.

Credentials are vaulted and rotated automatically, and in brokered sessions they are injected at the proxy at the moment of use, so database passwords and API keys no longer live in config.php or .env. Access is granted just-in-time, scoped to the task and revoked when it's done. Each privileged action is authorized as it happens and tied to a named identity, so when the board, auditors or regulators ask what happened and why it was allowed, you have an answer.

Patch today, then treat the patch as the beginning. Exploitation started before disclosure, so patching does not mean the attacker is gone, nor does it restore a single credential that was stolen. This is week one. Plan for the year.

This release adds multiple new modules, and 6 of those modules point at a single target: Langflow, the open-source LLM workflow builder. Thanks to the work of rmhowe425, with research credit to Peter Girnus and n0k0. Beyond Langflow, open source contributor kmkz contributed a pre-auth RCE chain against OpenCTI. Why Caribbean Threats Cascade Into Global Cyber-Risk

The region is demonstrating what happens when exploits accelerate but assurance does not.

Marlon Cooper,CEO,Symptai Consulting Limited

October 23, 2026

4 Min Read

Source: FrankRamspott via Getty Images

COMMENTARY

On July 24, 2025, Curaçao's Tax and Customs Administration found ransomware on its network. Counter services, the call center, and internal processes went dark for more than a week, and the island's recovery depended on specialists flown in from the Netherlands.

A day earlier, the Joint Court of Justice had gone down as well. Because that court serves Curaçao, Aruba, Sint Maarten, Bonaire, Saba, and Sint Eustatius, a single intrusion degraded the judicial system of six jurisdictions at once.

One platform, six governments.

That is the Caribbean's defining security characteristic, and it is why the interval between an exposure appearing and an exposure closing matters more here than almost anywhere else.

The Speed Gap

Consider what that interval currently is.

Fortinet's "Global Threat Intelligence Report: 2026 Midyear Edition" recorded roughly 325 million attack attempts across the English-speaking Caribbean in 2025, an extraordinary volume against a small economic base, with critical vulnerabilities now targeted within 24 to 48 hours of disclosure, down from an average of nearly five days.

Related:Nigeria Deepens Cybersecurity Efforts as Cybercriminals See More Profits

IBM's 2026 "Cost of a Data Breach Report" puts the mean time to identify and contain a breach at 247 days, up 2.5% and reversing five consecutive years of improvement.

Both of those numbers moved this year, and they moved in opposite directions. Exploitation got faster. Finding and containing it got slower, for the first time in five years.

When Assurance Falls Behind

Here is the part that the security industry has not absorbed: third-party assurance still runs on an annual cycle. A global insurer assesses its Caribbean claims processor once a year.

A hotel chain reviews its regional franchisee's controls at renewal. A correspondent bank collects an attestation and files it. Every one of those instruments is calibrated to a threat landscape that stopped existing several years ago.

The questionnaire signed in March describes a network that was materially different by April and unrecognizable by October. Twelve months of assurance against 48 hours of exposure, and nobody has repriced the difference.

Global Issue

That mismatch is not a Caribbean failing. It is a global control design failing, and the Caribbean is simply where it shows up first because of what sits inside the interval.

The plumbing is ordinary. A business process outsourcer holds live credentials into a North American insurer's claims platform. A hotel group's property management system federates to a global loyalty program. A regional bank sits inside correspondent rails that clear in New York. An attacker who compromises the small end inherits trust at the large end, and does it inside a window where the large end's assurance process has no way to notice.

Related:Mexico's New Cyber Plan Faces Its First Real Test

The obvious response is that Caribbean organizations should simply patch faster.

Having spent two decades running security operations across these markets, I can tell you why that answer keeps failing. Security teams here are frequently two or three people covering an entire institution.

Critical systems often cannot be taken offline because there is no redundant capacity to fail over to. Vendor support is remote and time-zoned away. And where six jurisdictions share one platform, no single institution can authorize a maintenance window on it.

These are structural constraints, not attitudes, and telling the region to try harder has not moved the number in years.

Measure remediation against exploit velocity, not the audit calendar. Report critical MTTR as a distribution against a 48-hour benchmark. An average conceals the tail, and the tail is where the exposure lives.

Replace annual attestations with continuous evidence. If your assurance over a supplier is a document signed in March, you are not managing that risk; you're recording that you once looked at it.

Related:UK Social Media Ban for Minors Has Privacy Experts Worried

Assume some things can't be patched in time, and design for that. Segmentation, compensating controls, and explicit, owned, time-boxed decisions about what stays exposed. An undocumented exception is the same as no control.

Instrument the federated paths, not just the perimeter. Stolen credentials remain the primary route into cloud environments, and federated access is where a stolen credential stops being your incident and becomes your partner's.

Assess the shared provider, not just the institution. Where multiple entities run on one platform, assessing each separately measures the same risk repeatedly and reduces it once, at best.

The Caribbean isn't asking for allowances. It is showing the rest of the industry, early and in public, what happens when exploitation accelerates and assurance does not.

Anyone whose supply chain touches this region is measuring a snapshot of a system that has already changed.

Cyber Insurance's New Reality: Underwriting Isn't Enough

Rising AI, social engineering, and cloud risks are pushing carriers beyond risk transfer and deeper into cybersecurity itself.

Alexander Culafi,Senior News Writer,Dark Reading

October 23, 2026

6 Min Read

Source: Mohamad Faizal Bin Ramli via Getty Images

The relentless evolution of the threat landscape has pushed cyber insurance companies to follow suit with a continuous expansion of cybersecurity posture requirements as well as taking an active hand in the defense process.

While cyber insurance has existed for years, the ransomware boom of the late 2010s and early 2020s transformed it from a niche risk transfer product into a central component of many organizations' security strategies. Today, policies cover everything from incident response and business interruption to legal costs and, in some cases, ransomware payments. Some of the names you'll see pop up around this space include Coalition, Chubb, AXA XL, Cowbell, and Resilience.

The threat landscape, especially when discussing enterprises, was never moving at a slow pace. But compared to the business email compromise and conventional ransomware attacks of five or 10 years ago, techniques are now evolving faster than ever, meaning insurance agencies must work harder to keep up.

Related:Rethinking Cybersecurity Awareness in the AI Era

Large language models (LLMs) have enabled threat actors to orchestrate complex attacks, streamline malware and exploit development, design phishing lures without typos, and operate at a scale never before possible. AI introduces uncertainty into threat models built largely around ransomware and data extortion attacks, which insurers have accumulated years of claims data around. Social engineering advancements could alter both attack frequency and severity faster than historical loss data can account for.

While outside of AI, attackers are also coming up with new social engineering tactics all the time, and cloud resource consolidation means compromised credentials or a single stolen API key can lead to devastating consequences.

Thomas Pytel, vice president at Cowbell, tells Dark Reading his firm believes in underwriting that continuously adapts to risk. "AI is changing the speed, scale, and credibility of phishing and impersonation, so historical loss experience alone is insufficient. Underwriting must assess how a business verifies identities, authorizes payments, and controls its own use of AI," he says.

According to a 2025 report from the National Association of Insurance Commissioners (NAIC), cyber insurance premiums reached nearly $15 billion in 2024, up 7% year over year. Additionally, direct written premium (DWP) for the US market reached roughly $9.14 billion in 2024, compared with a market that was only a fraction of that size several years earlier. This underscores how cyber insurance has evolved to become a highly significant segment of the cyber-risk ecosystem.

Related:Threat Modeling With 4 Simple Questions on a White Board

On the other hand, that same NAIC report cited nearly 50,000 claims across the US in 2024, the highest on record and a nearly 40% increase year over year. This could speak to the increasing number of customers choosing insurance, the aggressiveness of attackers, or both.

What remains to be seen is whether the industry's growth has outpaced its ability to accurately model the threat landscape.

Broader Threat Landscape Means Stricter Underwriting Requirements

Increasing insurance popularity also gave way to the rise of certain requirements for coverage, primarily demanding insurance customers uphold a certain quality of cybersecurity posture.

George Gerchow, IANS faculty and chief security officer at Bedrock Data, tells Dark Reading that a few years ago, these requirements were contained on a short form that "no one checked," but insurers now expect multifactor authentication (MFA), endpoint detection and response (EDR), immutable backups, and privileged access controls, while "some are moving to continuous telemetry instead of a once-a-year attestation."

Daniel Woods, head of emerging risks at Coalition, agrees. He says legacy underwriting models based on point-in-time questionnaires cannot keep pace, and this has been true since the ransomware epidemic took hold around 2020.

Related:Attacker Relentlessly Scans for Credentials by Impersonating AI Bots

This occurred amid concerns that organizations would use cyber insurance as a replacement for patching, practicing defense in depth, or using strong data and authentication controls.

Better posture may be an objective net good no matter where it comes from, though it also risks turning security into a compliance exercise. Gerchow says these requirements can feel like that depending on who you ask.

"Insurance did more to get MFA and EDR deployed in the mid-market than any of us standing on a stage, and that part worked," he says. "But the application is a snapshot, and too many teams treat passing it as the goal. The carrier finds the gap for you at claim time. Lapsed MFA or an untested backup you attested to is now one of the fastest ways to get a claim denied."

Jeremiah Grossman, CEO of cyber loss prevention vendor Root Evidence, says insurance carriers are requiring more to be implemented, steadily, year over year, and "it seems to be working well for many." However, he says, "The issue is that organizations tend to not have the data to properly measure and model their risk, and their carriers are often in a better position to do so."

Cyber Insurers Become Active Players

One relatively recent development in this space has been the rise of insurance organizations as active participants in the security process. While insurers these days broadly require MFA, security products like EDR, managed detection and response (MDR), and validated backups, insurance firms will also offer security products and services directly to their customers.

Coalition's offering includes access to an automated detection and response product, for example, while Resilience offers risk management tooling and Cowbell offers services including risk assessment, penetration testing, and training. All of these firms also work with other security vendors to recommend preapproved products and incident response services. While on the other end, traditional security vendors like Arctic Wolf offer products specifically for insurability.

Coalition argues its "Active Insurance" model has resulted in 73% fewer claims than the industry average and is why 56% of claims reported in 2024 were resolved with no out-of-pocket expense to those insured. Woods says that as the threat landscape intensifies, insurers that passively issue policies and hope claims do not exceed premiums will face increasingly worse results.

"The solution is for insurers to bring threat researchers and security experts in-house to monitor the threat landscape and actively support customers in improving protections during the life cycle of their policies," he says. "Risk transfer is still a fundamental component of cyber insurance, but so is ongoing protection and prevention."

Some risk remains difficult to model. Gerchow argues that if a crisis were to occur tomorrow where a major cloud or identity provider was taken down or compromised, the market would struggle to absorb it, and, he says, "the carriers know it."

"Look at where policy language is moving: war exclusions applied to nation-state activity with no declared conflict, widespread-event carve-outs, and small sublimits for dependent business interruption. CrowdStrike in 2024 was a bad update with no attacker anywhere in it, and it still grounded flights and stalled hospitals in a single morning," he says. "A real compromise of a major identity provider means every downstream customer needs forensics, counsel, and notification at the same time. If I'm a CISO this week, I'm reading the systemic-event exclusions in my policy first and assuming a big piece of that loss stays with me."

Title: UK threatens subsea cable saboteurs with 14 years behind bars
Context: Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of...
Full Text: Britain is threatening subsea cable saboteurs with up to 14 years in prison and unlimited fines, having apparently decided that Victorian-era laws aren't quite up to the job of keeping Russian submarines away from critical infrastructure. The government on Thursday set out plans to overhaul legislation dating back to 1885 and introduce tougher penalties for damaging the underwater cables and pipelines that keep Britain's internet and energy supplies running. According to Whitehall, subsea cables carry around 99 percent of the UK's international data traffic, while underwater pipelines account for 74 percent of its gas supply. Yet much of this infrastructure is protected by laws written when the telegraph was cutting-edge technology. The Submarine Telegraph Act 1885 originally imposed a £100 maximum fine for damaging a cable through culpable negligence. That might have been a reasonable deterrent back then, but it's unlikely to give today's would-be saboteurs much pause. Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical subsea energy or telecoms infrastructure could face up to 14 years behind bars. The proposals also set tougher penalties, including unlimited fines, for reckless or negligent damage. Subsea telecoms operators would face new legal duties to identify and manage security risks, while ministers would gain powers to direct companies and cable repair providers to take action where necessary and proportionate to protect national security. The government also wants to regulate fiber-optic sensing technology, which uses subsea cables to detect activity at sea but could pose a security risk if sensitive data falls into hostile hands. Unsurprisingly, Russia features prominently in Whitehall's thinking. In April, British forces exposed a covert Russian submarine operation near critical undersea infrastructure. The operation reportedly involved an attack submarine acting as a decoy while two specialist vessels surveyed Britain's cable routes. "The threats we face have changed dramatically, with suspicious Russian activity around critical undersea infrastructure, yet some of the laws protecting these vital connections date back more than a century," said telecoms minister Ian Murray. The plans aren't entirely new. In May, the government announced its intention to toughen penalties and introduce security obligations for cable operators. Thursday's White Paper spells out the proposed penalties and how far ministers could go in directing operators to act. It also follows warnings from Parliament's Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, which concluded last year that Britain was insufficiently prepared for a coordinated attack on its subsea infrastructure. MPs and peers warned that government assessments focused too heavily on individual cable failures, rather than what might happen if attackers simultaneously targeted connections to Europe and across the Atlantic. Russian submarines aren't responsible for every severed cable. Fishing boats and ships dragging their anchors do most of the damage, accounting for up to 97 percent of faults, according to previous government estimates. And even when sabotage is suspected, catching those responsible is another matter. Britain already has laws allowing life sentences for serious acts of state-backed sabotage, but they're not much use if nobody can prove who did it. That's rather difficult when the crime scene is at the bottom of the sea. And it might prove equally difficult to extradite suspects from enemy nation states. None of this is law yet. The government has opened a 12-week consultation on the plans, after which ministers will decide how to proceed. Whether the threat of a lengthy prison sentence will trouble Russian submariners is debatable. Even so, after 140 years, Britain's subsea cable laws are finally getting dragged out of the Victorian era. ®

Title: Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3
Context: On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be...
Full Text:
What happened?

On October 17, 2026, a researcher reported that the private keys of eight intermediate eMudhra certificate authorities were generated with insufficient entropy and could be derived from their public certificates. The derived private keys can be used to issue certificates for any domain, and software that trusts the eMudhra root will accept them.

Mozilla, Google, Apple, and Cloudflare have blocked the affected intermediates. Mozilla has removed the emSign ECC Root CA – G3 from its trust store, and Chrome will remove it on October 27, 2026. eMudhra has revoked the intermediates.

Okta’s response

Okta and Auth0 are removing trust in emSign ECC Root CA – G3 and the eight affected intermediates across our services.

Security Patching Services: The change has been deployed across Okta’s production environment. The change is continuing to roll out across Auth0 production.

No Evidence of Exploitation: To date, Okta and Auth0 have observed no evidence of exploitation.

Do I need to do anything?

Only if Okta or Auth0 connects to a server you control and that server's certificate chain includes the eMudhra emSign ECC Root CA – G3. Inbound access to Okta and Auth0, including sign-in, is not affected.

The case to check is a non-browser connection or webhook that calls your own API, such as an Okta Inline Hook or Event Hook, or Auth0 Action, Custom Database connection, or Auth0 Federated Connection.

These connections may not have shown you any error before now. Run

openssl s_client -showcerts -connect <your-host>:443

and look for "emSign" in the chain. If you find it, replace the certificate with one from another trusted CA. Connections to that endpoint will fail once our change is applied to your tenant.

References

eMudhra Statement on distrust of select Global TLS Intermediate and one Root CA

Google - Protecting Chrome and Android Users from Compromised eMudhra Intermediate CA Certificates

Mozilla - Protecting Firefox users following the compromise of eMudhra intermediate certificates

DR's Alex Culafi: We have an interesting story. Russian authorities arrested three suspected members of the hacking group Data Suckers, including a 19-year-old member. And this is following the breach of Russian pizza chain Dodo Pizza —

DR's Alex Culafi: Stinks, obviously. I hope that —

DR's Alex Culafi: No, I mean, it's a tough one, right? Because you hope that they can track these gift card serial numbers and invalidate them.

They have great copy printing services and they seem like a company that should have shuttered a long time ago but is finding new ways to become relevant in the 21st century, the 2020s. So I hope they figure this out. Other than that, for the purposes of a cybersecurity audience, I don't know what else to say other than it stinks. I don't know.

DR's Rob Wright: I know, I know. I mean, there's a lot of details here that have not been cleared up about how the hackers got into — I think it was called Nexus — the internal sort of support system, how they were able to get into applications or processes or systems to issue these gift cards. But 15,000 gift cards?

And you know what they use them for — scams and whatnot. And they use it to launder money. And I just think it's one of these cases where I'm sure Staples ... their cybersecurity posture is probably pretty good, but this is one area that maybe they didn't shore up because they didn't think it was going to be targeted. And it's like, every part of your infrastructure and your network and your environment is going to be targeted these days if you're a big company. So, you know, it's a painful lesson.

DR's Alex Culafi: You know, that's true. And especially as these AI-orchestrated attacks get more powerful, the idea that having one blind spot will hurt you. But I don't know. This is tough, and it kind of stinks that maybe their posture is good elsewhere, but it just takes one weakness, one blind spot for something like this to happen.

DR's Rob Wright: Exactly.

DR's Alex Culafi: So I don't know if there's a lesson learned, but it is a bummer.

DR's Rob Wright: Yeah. All right, well, that's it for this week, Alex. Thank you so much for joining me. I appreciate it.

Title: PHP2Shell: One Upload, Full Server
Context: PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws that let unauthenticated attackers run code remotely on PHP installations serving web requests
Full Text:
How many servers are one malformed upload away from leaking your secrets?

PHP2Shell is a pair of critical flaws that let unauthenticated attackers run code remotely on PHP installations serving web requests. Because PHP runs roughly 70% of the world’s websites and the bugs fire before any application code executes, even a fully patched WordPress, Drupal, or Joomla site is exposed until the PHP underneath is updated, and attackers are probing for it.

Calif, a security research firm working under OpenAI’s Patch the Planet initiative, found the bugs first on August 1 and reported them to PHP on August 11. Wiz Research found them separately.

What we know so far

Two critical flaws in PHP itself. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 sit in the core engine, so even secure application code can’t protect a vulnerable server. An unauthenticated remote attacker can read a PHP worker’s memory (passwords, tokens, API keys) and, in some cases, run code on the server.

Wide reach. Every PHP version back to 5.4 is affected, across PHP-FPM, Apache modphp, php-cgi, FrankenPHP and LiteSpeed, with modphp carrying the greatest risk.

Proven on real platforms. Remote code execution was demonstrated against the latest WordPress, Drupal and Joomla container images. Even a "Hello World" PHP app can be vulnerable.

A fix is out, but the leak came first. Patched releases shipped on October 21: PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. PHP 8.1 and older have no official release.

Why this matters

Most teams will log this as two PHP bugs, now patched. The exposure behind it is bigger than that.

The flaws sit beneath the application. CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 live in the PHP runtime, so the framework, CMS, or custom code on top is irrelevant. Exploitation can occur before any application code executes, which means app-level logging may capture little or nothing.

No application mistake is required. The attack doesn’t depend on a vulnerable plugin, a weak login flow, or sloppy session handling. A site with clean code can still be exposed if the PHP underneath is not updated.

It can be abused unauthenticated. An attacker needs no account, no password and no foothold, just the ability to send a request to your server.

The cost of building an exploit has dropped. The researchers report that AI models compressed what used to take months of specialist work into days. Decade-old bug classes once considered impractical to weaponize are now within reach, and attackers have access to the same tooling.

With PHP running a vast portion of the web, from WordPress and Drupal to the internal tool nobody has touched in years, the question isn’t whether you run it. It’s where, and whether, you can find every instance.

Actions to take this week

Detection

Look for the setup phase. Malformed or unusual multipart upload requests, followed by memory-limit errors or bursts of HTTP 500 responses, are the pattern to hunt for.

Inspect outbound cookies. An oversized or malformed PHPSESSID in a response can indicate that process memory is leaking back to the client.

Flag process creation during upload handling. A PHP worker should never spawn a child process while it is still parsing an upload, before application code has run. Treat it as a high-confidence signal.

These signals guide an investigation. They do not replace patching.

Remediation

Inventory every PHP install. Go beyond the obvious web apps. Bundled software, appliances, and forgotten internal tools all count.

Patch internet-facing systems first. Move to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, depending on your branch.

Rotate secrets on exposed servers. If an attacker could have read worker memory before you patched, assume the credentials, tokens, and API keys resident in that memory are compromised.

Want to know how a single out-of-memory crash turns into code execution? Keep reading.

A deep dive on what we know about PHP2Shell

The PHP disclosure describes four bugs, classified as two CVEs. Together, they are the PHP2Shell. The first three share a common "pre-phase" that sets them up for success and essentially allows the final target of the desired RCE (remote code execution). The fourth is a more internal process, and how it was abused was not disclosed.

To see how they affect the server, we first need a few concepts.

PHP who? A short glossary

PHP web server worker. A process that handles an HTTP request and is reused for later requests rather than restarted each time.

Multipart request parsing. PHP reading an incoming multipart/form-data request (a file upload) and breaking it into labeled parts. This starts very early in the request.

Session upload-progress handling. A PHP feature that tracks a file upload's progress so a page can show a progress bar. It runs while the server is parsing the multipart request.

Session. PHP's way to remember a user across requests (the PHPSESSID cookie).

Memory limit. The maximum memory a single request may use.

Engine-global pointers. Internal bookkeeping variables the PHP engine uses to track global execution state. Three matter here:

PS(id): the session ID.

BG(unserialize): the unserializer state (the state of rebuilding the original array or object from a serialized string).

EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace): stores information about the last error.

Worker cleanup. A normal teardown process in PHP is supposed to run between requests on a reused worker, resetting the engine-global pointers so the next request starts clean. The bug chain exists because out-of-memory fatal errors abort the request before this cleanup runs, leaving those pointers stale.

OPcache. Shared memory holding precompiled script bytecode that all workers can read, which removes the need to re-read and recompile the same PHP file.

Now that we have the vocabulary, let's move to the part that makes it all possible.

The pre-phase

The core concept being abused is a use-after-free (UAF): memory is freed, but a pointer to it is still kept and later used. If an attacker gets new data placed into that freed memory, PHP treats the attacker's bytes as its own trusted structure.

The attacker sends a crafted multipart upload that causes PHP to run out of memory during session upload-progress handling early in the request. The request ends unexpectedly, worker cleanup is skipped, and stale pointers remain. That can lead to memory disclosure or corruption.

Attacker flow:

Craft an arming request. The attacker sends a multipart/form-data upload with session upload-progress data sized to run out of memory while still parsing.

Early, pre-app parsing. Upload-progress handling runs before normal PHP startup finishes, so the engine-global pointers are set up early.

Out-of-memory fatal error. The request exceeds memory_limit; PHP aborts and frees the request heap.

Cleanup is skipped. The pointers are never reset.

The worker survives and is reused. The same worker handles the next request, still holding the stale pointers.

Memory usage. The attacker's data reclaims one of the freed allocations (each pointer has its own separate allocation).

This is the setup the first three bugs depend on.

Bug 1: Remote process-memory disclosure

After the pre-phase, another multipart request on the same worker still trusts the freed allocation of PS(id). PHP reads the reclaimed bytes as a live session ID and URL-encodes them into the PHPSESSID response cookie. An attacker can simply read the cookie to get leaked worker's memory. That lets them defeat address uncertainty, which is what makes the next step toward RCE practical.

Bug 2: Unserializer use-after-free

Here, the freed allocation of BG (unserialize) is trusted to trigger memory corruption. PHP keeps "unserializing" using attacker-reclaimed memory as if it were still valid, becoming a memory-corruption primitive. Combined with Bug 1's leak, this bug exploited address uncertainty to achieve an unauthenticated RCE and was demonstrated on WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla.

Bug 3: Fatal-error backtrace use-after-free

Another pointer abuse of the EG(last_fatal_error_backtrace). If the same worker sends out a diagnostic event (any subsequent error or warning) after the failed cleanup it can access the freed pointer before the reinitialization of the state. PHP will update or destroy pointer backtrace and will follow the attacker-reclaimed memory. This use-after-free could be developed into memory corruption that can lead to RCE.

Bug 4: OPcache type confusion (a separate flow, across workers)

The Wiz disclosure does not describe specific requests or steps for this bug, only an internal mechanism flaw. So, in short:

Shared compiled-code cache. OPcache stores precompiled bytecode in shared memory so every worker can reuse it instead of recompiling (php.net: "removes the need for PHP to load and parse scripts on each request").

Two trackers. A process-local tracker (CG(map_ptr_last)) and a shared tracker (ZCSG(map_ptr_last)) both track how far the shared memory has been filled.

Allocation failure mid-update. In the window between the two trackers being updated, an allocation failure can leave the shared tracker out of sync with what was written.

Cross-worker reuse. Wiz says this can allow a different worker to reuse that memory slot, it will resolve to a pointer of the wrong type. This causes a type confusion and corrupts the shared OPcache state, which was later leveraged to an RCE. Exactly how and when this happens is not spelled out, so treat this as the general shape of the bug rather than a precise sequence.

Varonis product impact

Varonis proactively assessed the potential impact of PHP2Shell across its product portfolio and completed the necessary remediation measures. We have found no evidence of compromise related to these vulnerabilities. Customers do not need to take any additional action specific to Varonis products.

References

PHP Official Security Advisory

CVE-2026-109618

CVE-2026-109619

How Varonis can help

Varonis helps customers address PHP2Shell and other threats by detecting suspicious lateral movement and abnormal data access, then automatically contains compromised accounts to protect sensitive data.

Managed Data Detection and Response (MDDR) provides an added layer of protection alongside patching, with Varonis experts monitoring data activity 24x7x365, investigating threats such as stolen credentials accessing sensitive data, and taking action to contain them. Customers gain around-the-clock expert coverage without having to staff their own 24x7 team.

Summary

PHP2Shell is a chain born from one unglamorous event: a request that runs out of memory and skips its cleanup. From that single stale pointer, researchers got memory disclosure, two flavors of use-after-free, and a separate OPcache type confusion, all below the application layer and present since PHP 5.4.

Title: Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour
Context: ICS/OT Security Cyberattacks & Data Breaches Cyber Risk Vulnerabilities & Threats Research Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around...
Full Text:
Read in English: Click Here

This translation is provided by our internal AI translation tool.

Des centaines de supermarchés français ont subi cette semaine des pertes s'élevant à plusieurs dizaines, voire plusieurs centaines de millions d'euros, à la suite de cyberattaques qui ont perturbé leurs systèmes de réfrigération.

Dans la nuit de lundi, des pirates informatiques ont piraté les contrôleurs des systèmes de réfrigération commerciaux de grandes chaînes de supermarchés françaises. Ils ont transformé les réfrigérateurs, les congélateurs et les chambres froides en appareils de chauffage, faisant grimper leur température jusqu’à 50 degrés Celsius (plus de 120 degrés Fahrenheit), ce qui a complètement abîmé tous les aliments qu’ils contenaient et aurait même provoqué quelques petits incendies. L’identité et les motivations de l’auteur de cette attaque restent inconnues.

Les contrôleurs de réfrigération permettent aux commerçants de régler et de surveiller à distance la température de leurs réfrigérateurs, 24 heures sur 24 et 7 jours sur 7. Il s’ensuit donc que les gérants de magasin auraient pu être alertés ou se rendre compte manuellement que quelque chose n’allait pas. Pour empêcher cela, des sources françaises indiquent que les attaquants ont prolongé les cycles de dégivrage des systèmes ciblés — processus au cours duquel les congélateurs font fondre intentionnellement le givre et la glace accumulés — afin que le réchauffement passe pour un entretien de routine.

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

Selon les propres rapports des entreprises, les attaques ont touché un peu plus de 700 magasins d’alimentation et commerces de détail, tous au cours de la même nuit. Un analyste de la société française de cybersécurité Sekoia a déclaré à Reuters que l’Espagne, le Portugal, la Pologne, l’Allemagne et la Belgique avaient également été touchés, et qu’une grande chaîne de supermarchés aux Pays-Bas avait mis ses systèmes hors service par mesure de précaution, selon l’AP. Une seule chaîne française, Intermarché, a fait état de pertes s’élevant à plusieurs dizaines de millions d’euros.

Pire encore, les experts soulignent que ces attaques auraient très certainement pu être évitéesgrâce à des mesures élémentaires de cybersécurité.

Qu'est-ce qui a provoqué l'incendie des congélateurs ?

Les premiers rapports suggéraient que les attaques de lundi étaient liées aux contrôleurs de réfrigération du fabricant danois Danfoss. Danfoss occupe une place importante dans le domaine des solutions de contrôle pour les supermarchés et la grande distribution alimentaire, avec plus de 50 000 installations de sa technologie à travers le monde, selon son site web.

Related:Taiwan Bullet Train Hack Highlights Cybersecurity Gaps in Rail Systems

Le 9 août, des chercheurs en cybersécurité de l’équipe Team82 de Claroty ont révélé trois vulnérabilités dans la plateforme AK-SM 800A de Danfoss. Ces failles — référencées sous les numéros CVE-2025-41450, CVE-2025-41451 et CVE-2025-41452 — permettaient aux attaquants de procéder à l’exécution de code à distance (RCE) ou à un déni de service (DoS) contre les parcs de réfrigération des entreprises. Danfoss a corrigé ces failles mais comptait sur ses clients pour mettre à jour eux-mêmes leurs systèmes.

Dans une déclaration à Reuters, Danfoss a rejeté la responsabilité sur les clients utilisant un micrologiciel obsolète, indiquant qu’elle « conseillait depuis longtemps à ses clients de maintenir les systèmes pris en charge à jour avec le dernier micrologiciel et de migrer les systèmes hérités vers des solutions de dernière génération ».Le fabricant d'équipement d'origine (OEM) a fourni davantage d'informations à une publication spécialisée dans la réfrigération, Cooling Post. Selon lui, la « majorité » des unités concernées fonctionnaient sous AK-SM 800 ou son prédécesseur, l'AK-SC355. Ces deux systèmes ont depuis longtemps atteint leur fin de vie : le premier en 2021, le second en 2016.

Related:AI-Driven Cyberattack on Mexico Couldn't Breach OT Systems

Mardi, le CERT national français (CERT-FR) avait identifié qu’une autre plateforme de contrôleurs de réfrigération — « XWEB », des fournisseurs Dixell et de sa société mère Copeland — avait également été impliquée dans les attaques. Il n’a pas précisé quelles vulnérabilités ou versions de micrologiciel pouvaient être en cause, bien que les indices circonstanciels indiquent désormais clairement que les auteurs de ces menaces s’appuient sur les recherches de Team82. Le jour même où ils ont révélé ces vulnérabilités affectant Danfoss, ces mêmes chercheurs ont divulgué 23 autres touchant XWEB Pro, dont 21 de gravité élevée.

Les commerçants ont été avertis de possibles attaques contre leurs réfrigérateurs

Le 26 août, une série étrange de rapports similaires a commencé à filtrer depuis des installations militaires américaines.Les groupes frigorifiques tombaient en panne. Dans chaque base où cela se produisait, les gens ont probablement pensé qu’il s’agissait d’un problème électrique inhabituel. Mais peu à peu, de plus en plus de sites ont signalé le même phénomène.

Après être tombée sur ces rapports étranges sur les réseaux sociaux, une journaliste indépendante a émis une hypothèse hasardeuse. « Je suis suffisamment lucide pour savoir que cela semble insensé, mais je vous demande de me suivre », a écrit M. Elizabeth sur Substack. « Je pense qu’il y a une probabilité non nulle que quelqu’un ait piraté les congélateurs des commissariats. »

À ce jour, l’armée américaine n’a pas confirmé qui ou quoi était à l’origine des pannes survenues dans les cantines réparties sur au moins 14 bases de l’armée de l’air, installations de la marine et postes de l’armée de terre distincts. Il se pourrait que ce soit une coïncidence que ces attaques aient eu lieu seulement deux semaines après la divulgation des vulnérabilités par Danfoss.

Ce serait d’autant plus une coïncidence que la Defense Commissary Agency (DeCA) — l’agence centrale du ministère de la Défense (DoD) chargée de superviser les magasins militaires — a explicitement mentionné avoir utilisé les technologies de Danfoss par le passé. Par exemple, dans un modèle de cahier des charges techniquedestiné aux prestataires des magasins militaires datant de juin 2022, la DeCA citait le Danfoss AK-SM 800A comme « base de conception » pour les différentes unités de contrôle.

Attention, commerçants du monde entier

Fort de son expérience, Bill Moore, PDG de Xona Systems, se souvient : « Dans bon nombre de ces magasins physiques — mais aussi dans les usines de fabrication, les centrales électriques, les sites pétroliers et gaziers, c’est le cas partout —, le plus gros problème est que les organisations parviennent plutôt bien à segmenter leurs propres réseaux. Mais en matière de technologies opérationnelles (OT), il y a tous ces équipementiers et tiers qui ont besoin d’un accès. Et les entreprises n’y ont pas vraiment prêté attention. »

En accordant à de nombreux fournisseurs et équipementiers l’accès à leurs systèmes, les entreprises finissent par s’exposer à des attaques à distance. « Et il n’y a littéralement aucune visibilité ni gouvernance sur bon nombre de ces connexions. Je dirais que c’est vrai dans un pourcentage élevé de cas — la moitié, peut-être plus, dans l’ensemble. Elles laissent en quelque sorte tous leurs équipementiers agir à leur guise, mais nous avons constaté que de nombreux pirates compromettent ces connexions tierces », déplore-t-il.

Dans un e-mail adressé à CNBC, Les Mousquetaires — société mère d’Intermarché et de Netto — a expliqué que l’attaque avait eu lieu via un prestataire de services chargé des systèmes de réfrigération dans certains de ses magasins.

« En résumé : déconnectez vos équipements d’Internet », déclare Andrew Ginter, vice-président chargé de la sécurité industrielle chez Waterfall Security Solutions. Les recherches effectuées cette semaine sur Shodan ont par exemple révélé des milliers de systèmes Danfoss exposés sur Internet, dont environ 1 500 rien qu’en France.

« Dans un monde idéal, les entreprises protégeraient leurs systèmes de contrôle derrière un accès à distance contrôlé par du matériel », explique M. Ginter, « mais même un simple pare-feu entre ces appareils et Internet serait déjà utile. »

Pour les pare-feu de base, il conseille aux entreprises :

De mettre en place une règle « tout refuser »

De n’autoriser les connexions qu’à partir d’adresses IP spécifiques

D’appliquer un mot de passe et une authentification à deux facteurs à ces connexion

De mettre à jour automatiquement le pare-feu, pour éviter de l’oublier

Utilisent des appareils de qualité commerciale ou industrielle, et non grand public ; de nombreux appareils grand public ne proposent pas de mises à jour, ou ne se mettent pas à jour rapidement

Enfin, ajoute-t-il, « Remplacez le pare-feu strictement tous les quatre ans. Pourquoi ? Parce que si nous avons des appareils exposés à Internet, neuf fois sur dix, nous n’avons pas d’équipe de sécurité, et nous ne remarquerons pas quand nos pare-feu ne seront plus pris en charge et que les mises à jour automatiques cesseront. »

« Les mesures de base ne suffisent pas pour les infrastructures critiques de grande envergure ou l’industrie lourde, mais elles contribueront grandement à empêcher les hacktivistes de s’introduire dans vos congélateurs », conclut Ginter. « Retirez vos équipements d’Internet. Faites-le de toute urgence. »
