Title: Managing identity source transition for AWS IAM Identity Center
Context: October 20, 2026: This post was republished to reflect the new migration capability from Active Directory to an external identity provider (IdP) or the Identity Center...
Full Text:
October 20, 2026: This post was republished to reflect the new migration capability from Active Directory to an external identity provider (IdP) or the Identity Center directory, now available in IAM Identity Center.

September 2, 2026: This post was republished to include Active Directory migration strategies and automation for permission sets.

AWS IAM Identity Center manages user access to Amazon Web Services (AWS) resources, including both AWS accounts and applications. You can use IAM Identity Center to create and manage user identities within the Identity Center identity store or to connect to other identity sources.

Organizations that are switching identity providers (IdPs), consolidating identity infrastructure, adopting new single sign-on capabilities, or migrating off legacy on-premises systems may need to change the identity source in IAM Identity Center. Previously, migrations from Active Directory to another identity source deleted users, groups, memberships, and assignments at the moment of cutover. Now, migrations away from Active Directory preserve your users, groups, memberships, and assignments, just as transitions between an external IdP and the Identity Center directory already do. Only switching to Active Directory still removes users, groups, and assignments. Because the change applies to the entire Identity Center instance at once, test validation and a dress rehearsal are strongly recommended.

This post walks you through the migration process and provides sample code to assist the transition. It includes architectural guidance and a step-by-step runbook for switching from Active Directory to Okta. This guide helps AWS administrators, identity engineers, and project teams switch identity sources safely.

Note: This walkthrough uses Okta as a representative example of a SAML 2.0 identity provider. The inclusion of Okta in this example does not constitute an endorsement of any specific identity provider.

Identity source options in IAM Identity Center

The identity source is the definitive system of record: it determines which directory holds the primary copy of user identities and group memberships used for AWS access.

Each IAM Identity Center instance connects to one identity source at a time. IAM Identity Center supports three main identity sources:

Identity Center directory – The default identity store. Users and groups are created and managed directly within IAM Identity Center, with no dependency on an external provider. Suitable for organizations without an existing enterprise directory or those wanting a setup that uses only AWS services.

Active Directory – Integration with an on-premises Microsoft Active Directory or AWS Managed Microsoft AD through AWS Directory Service for Microsoft Active Directory. This lets organizations reuse their existing AD identities, group memberships, and access policies.

External IdP – Integration with third-party providers that support SAML 2.0, including Okta Universal Directory, Microsoft Entra ID (formerly Azure AD), Ping Identity, and others. This is the approach covered in the migration runbook that follows.

For example, migrating from Active Directory to an external IdP carries your existing users and groups over to the new identity source. IAM Identity Center keeps the same identity store, user IDs, and group IDs, and SCIM updates only the external identifier (externalId) to reflect the new source.

How access flows to AWS resources

IAM Identity Center grants access to AWS resources in two ways, as shown in Figure 1:

Permission set assignments – Users or groups are assigned permission sets within specific AWS accounts. This enables assume-role access, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles (named AWSReservedSSO_...) are automatically created in each account to back these assignments.

Application assignments – Users or groups are granted access to AWS-managed applications (such as Amazon SageMaker Studio, Amazon OpenSearch Service and so on) and customer-managed applications integrated with IAM Identity Center.

Figure 1: Granting access to AWS resources for users and groups managed by an identity source in IAM Identity Center

When you change the identity source, the downstream impact on these assignments depends heavily on which sources you’re switching from and to. In some transitions, assignments remain intact.

When you switch the identity source from Active Directory to an external IdP or to the Identity Center directory, users, groups, user and group IDs, group memberships, and their associated assignments are preserved. Users keep their access to AWS accounts and applications after the new identity source takes over. Switching to Active Directory from any source removes users, groups, and assignments at the moment of cutover, so pre-migration backup and post-migration restoration are still essential in that scenario.

What changes when switching identity source in IAM Identity Center

Migrations away from Active Directory, and transitions between an external IdP and the Identity Center directory, now preserve users, groups, memberships, and assignments. Transitions to Active Directory removes users, groups, and assignments permanently from IAM Identity Center at the moment of cutover, as shown in the following table. For more information, see Considerations for changing your identity source.

IAM Identity Center item

Status upon switch from AD to external IdP or Identity Center directory

Status upon switch from external IdP or Identity Center directory to AD

Users and groups in Identity Center

Preserved (same user and group IDs; the externalId changes as the new source takes over)

Deleted (must be re-provisioned from AD)

Account assignments

Preserved

Deleted (must be recreated)

Application assignments

Preserved*

Deleted (must be recreated)

Note: *Test each application in a non-production environment before you migrate. Also inventory any assignments that live inside an application itself, because those sit outside IAM Identity Center.

Before you start: common blockers

Matching attribute – Confirm which attribute your target IdP uses to find an existing user (sometimes called matching precedence or existing resource lookup). The IdP must take over each existing Identity Center user and group rather than create a duplicate. Test this in a non-production environment.

Required attributes – Every user must have a username, first name, last name, and display name. If any required attribute is missing, that user silently fails to provision. If you send email, it must be unique and single-valued.

Username and NameID – Each user’s IdP userName must exactly match the existing Identity Center username, and the SAML NameID must map to the same value. Decide your sign-in identifier (for example, a legacy sAMAccountName or a UPN) before cutover.

Groups – Confirm that your IdP supports group provisioning through SCIM (for example, Google Workspace provisions users only). Group names must be unique, and renaming a group can cause it to be treated as new, which strands its assignments. Depending on the external Identity provider, users who belong to a group only through a nested group are not provisioned and lose group-based access. Inventory nested groups and directly assign the child groups that contain those users before cutover.

Emergency access – Set up a break-glass administrative access path that does not depend on AWS Identity Center.

Sample deployment

The following five-step summary (expanded into seven phases in the runbook that follows) applies to an identity source transition in IAM Identity Center from Active Directory to Okta, focusing on permission set assignments. The AD-to-Okta runbook in the next section expands each of these steps with specific instructions and commands. To assist users, you can also use the Identity Center migration tool script, which provides a structured workflow for Identity Center migrations with commands for precheck, cutover, validation, and cleanup. Because assignments are now preserved, the restore command is used only for manual rollback. The sample scripts and detailed steps are available on GitHub.

Note: This solution is available in the GitHub aws-samples repository. You can report bugs or make feature requests through GitHub Issues. The builders of this solution can help with GitHub issues. Enterprise Support customers can reach out to their Technical Account Manager (TAM) for further questions or feature requests.

Prerequisites

Before you start this walkthrough, make sure you have the following prerequisites in place:

Python 3.10 or later

AWS credentials configured using environment variables, an AWS configuration file, or a named AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) profile (specified with --profile)

An active IAM Identity Center instance in the target account

Okta Global Admin access

Install the migration tool as described in the README file

Basic solution walkthrough

The following steps summarize the migration process. The next section expands each step with detailed Okta-specific instructions and commands.

Step 1: Back up users, groups, and assignments – Before making any changes, export your current identity data such as users, groups, and all assignments. This backup protects you if something goes wrong during migration. Store them in a secure, access-controlled location. The runbook includes a script that exports all current IAM Identity Center assignments and principals to a CSV file, then validates referential integrity.

Step 2: Prepare and validate users and groups in the target identity source – Before switching the IAM Identity Center identity source, confirm that your users and groups exist in the new authoritative source. Verify usernames, display names, email addresses, group names, group memberships and other required attributes. Each user’s userName in the new source must exactly match the existing Identity Center username, because this is how the new source usually takes over the user. In a test environment, confirm that an existing user is matched, not duplicated.

Step 3: Switch IAM Identity Center to the new identity source, and configure sign-in – Update IAM Identity Center to point to the new identity source. For external IdPs, upload the SAML metadata and configure the Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) and issuer URLs in your IdP. Before enabling SCIM (System for Cross-domain Identity Management), confirm that a pilot user can sign in.

WARNING: The identity source change applies to the entire Identity Center instance. After you confirm it, Active Directory sync and authentication stop, and users can’t sign in until SAML sign-in works with the new IdP. Users, groups, memberships, and assignments are preserved.

Step 4: Enable SCIM provisioning and verify takeover – Enable automatic provisioning and assign users and groups to the IAM Identity Center application in your IdP. The IdP takes over each existing user and group. Then run the validate command to compare the live assignments against your backup and find any missing or extra assignments.

If drift is found, the script writes a drift_report.csv file with MISSING and EXTRA entries.

Step 5: Validate access – Test access for a sample of users across different roles and permission levels before declaring the migration complete. Confirm that users can authenticate through the new identity source, access their expected AWS accounts, and assume the correct IAM roles. Confirm that the identity source shows your external IdP, that users and groups keep the same IDs, and that no duplicates were created.

Detailed runbook for Okta migration

This runbook covers one of the most common identity source transitions: migrating from an Active Directory to Okta as a SAML 2.0 identity provider.

The sample deployment describes what happens during a transition. It walks through seven phases: stakeholder alignment and pre-migration inventory, pre-cutover validation, the identity source switch itself, takeover verification, post-migration testing, ongoing cleanup and monitoring, and a documented manual rollback procedure for when things don’t go to plan.

If you’re migrating to Active Directory, which still removes users, groups, memberships and assignments, you can adapt the backup and restore scripts from this guide.

Phase 1: Plan your pre-migration activities

Pre-migration planning has four components: stakeholder engagement, inventory, scheduling, and access verification. Complete all four before you schedule the cutover.

1.1 – Document relevant stakeholders:

Fill out this table with actual contact information. You’ll need to reach these people during the cutover window.

1.2 – Inventory current state:

Before any changes are made, document the complete current state of your IAM Identity Center configuration. Capture a baseline of all three assignment layers: the users and groups assigned to the IAM Identity Center application in your IdP, the account and application assignments in IAM Identity Center, and any assignments inside the applications themselves:

Run the precheck script to export all current Identity Center assignments and principals to CSV.

```bash python -m idc_migration_tool precheck --output-dir ./export ```

This will produce the following artifacts:

assignments.csv – One row per account, permission-set, and principal assignment

principals.csv – All users and groups from the identity store

1.3 – Define the cutover window:

Schedule the migration during a low-usage period to minimize user impact. Size the maintenance window using timings from a full-dress rehearsal in a test environment. SCIM provisioning is rate-limited, so for large directories, sync users in batches. Identify a maintenance window of sufficient length to complete all phases, including time for validation and potential manual rollback (described in Phase 7) if needed. Notify all affected users in advance of the potential temporary disruption to single-sign-on access.

1.4 – Confirm access requirements:

Verify that the following access is confirmed and tested before the cutover window:

AWS Administrator access to IAM Identity Center and AWS Organizations.

Identity provider (IdP) administrator access (for example, Okta) to configure the IAM Identity Center application, create the SCIM integration, and assign users to the AWS app.

A break-glass or emergency administrative access path that does not depend on the identity source you are migrating.

Phase 2: Complete final pre-cutover steps

Before starting the cutover, complete the final validation, access, and communication checks described in this phase.

2.1 – Export IAM Identity Center configuration:

Validate that the backup files generated in Step 1.2 are present and non-empty before proceeding.

2.2 – Communicate impact to users:

Send advance notice to all affected users covering:

The migration timeline and expected impact window.

That users can’t sign in between the identity source change and the new IdP’s sign-in going live, but that their access and assignments are unchanged.

The new sign-in process. After migration, users sign in through your IdP (for example, the Okta My Apps dashboard) or the AWS access portal, depending on the sign-in flow you choose.

Whether the new sign-in flow is IdP-initiated (through Okta) or SP-initiated (through the AWS access portal), and any differences in the user experience.

After migration, the d-xxxxxxxxxx.awsapps.com/start access portal URL is no longer supported, and the console shows the supported dual-stack regional URL (https://ssoins-<instance-id>.portal.<region>.app.aws) instead, so you must communicate the new URL and update bookmarks/allow-lists.

That the custom access portal alias (friendly URL) isn’t supported after migrating away from Active Directory. If a proxy or bookmark relies on redirect flows, plan to update it.

Prepare a user guide for the new sign-in process and an FAQ for common issues. Schedule a training session to demonstrate how to access AWS through Okta. Ensure your support team is briefed and ready to handle an influx of access issues during and immediately after the cutover.

2.3 – Validate Okta-to-IAM Identity Center sync (pre-cutover testing):

Using a sandbox or test environment if available, perform the following validation steps before executing against production:

Run the full migration in a test instance that mirrors your production AD configuration and applications and confirm that existing test users are matched by Okta and not duplicated.

Use the AWS Management Console for IAM Identity Center to verify that groups and users appear in Users & Groups with the correct attributes.

Test the complete end-to-end sign-in flow for a test user. Authenticate through Okta, access the AWS portal, and assume a role in a test account. Confirm that the user keeps access to their assigned accounts, permission sets, and applications.

Phase 3: Complete the cutover

You’re ready to configure Okta, switch the IAM Identity Center identity source, and complete the production cutover.

Important: Downtime begins when you confirm the identity source change in Step 3.2 and ends when SAML sign-in works through Okta. Have the Okta application, SAML metadata, and signing certificate ready before you start. Users, groups, memberships, and assignments are preserved.

3.1 – Configure the Okta application:

Sign in to Okta as an administrator.

Navigate to Applications and then to Browse App Catalog.

Search for AWS IAM Identity Center and choose Add Integration. Choose Done.

Choose the newly created app and select the Sign On tab.

Locate the Metadata URL (it will look like: https://<your-okta-domain>/app/<app-id>/sso/saml/metadata). Open this URL in a new browser tab.

An XML file will render in the browser. Save this file. This is your SAML metadata file, which will be uploaded to IAM Identity Center.

Download and save the SAML signing certificate from the Sign On tab.

3.2 – Switch the identity source in IAM Identity Center:

In the IAM Identity Center console navigation pane, choose Settings.

Choose Actions and select Change Identity Source.

Important: This change applies to the entire Identity Center instance. On the confirmation screen, you must enter ACCEPT to confirm. During this step and before SCIM provisioning is enabled, if the change could not be completed by Identity Center you will see a clear error message in the console to retry changing identity providers. It is safe to retry.

Select External Identity Provider.

Upload the XML metadata file and the SAML signing certificate downloaded from Okta.

Confirm the change. IAM Identity Center will display progress updates as it migrates to the new identity provider.

Don’t enable automatic provisioning yet. Complete Step 3.3 and confirm pilot sign-in in Step 3.4 first.

3.3 – Configure the ACS and issuer URLs in Okta:

In the IAM Identity Center console, choose Settings and then Actions. Select Manage Authentication.

Copy the IAM Identity Center Assertion Consumer Service (ACS) URL and the IAM Identity Center Issuer URL.

Return to Okta and choose Applications and select IAM Identity Center app. Select the Sign On tab and choose Edit.

Under Advanced Sign On Settings, paste the ACS URL and Issuer URL into the corresponding fields.

Choose Save.

3.4 – Confirm pilot sign-in:

Before you enable SCIM provisioning, assign an existing pilot user to the IAM Identity Center application in Okta and confirm they can sign in through the AWS access portal. The SAML NameID that Okta sends must exactly match the user’s existing Identity Center username. If sign-in fails, fix the mapping now before proceeding to the next step.

3.5 – Enable automatic provisioning (console) and connect SCIM in Okta:

In the IAM Identity Center console, choose Settings, then choose Enable Automatic Provisioning. Copy and securely record the SCIM endpoint URL and access token.

Return to the IAM Identity Center app in Okta. Choose the Provisioning tab.

Choose Configure API Integration.

Paste the SCIM Endpoint URL into the Base URL field.

Paste the Access Token into the API Token field.

Choose Test API Credentials. You should receive confirmation that the credentials are valid.

Choose Save.

On the Provisioning page, choose Edit and under To App enable all three provisioning options (Create Users, Update User Attributes, and Deactivate Users). Choose Save. (The To App settings control how Okta provisions users to IAM Identity Center. All three options are required for the migration to work correctly.)

On the Push Groups tab, push the groups that are assigned to the AWS application. Group names must exactly match the existing group names in IAM Identity Center.

In the attribute mappings, confirm that userName maps to the existing Identity Center username and that first name, last name, display name, and a single email address are populated.

3.6 – Test SCIM takeover:

Before you assign all users, verify that Okta takes over existing users correctly:

In Okta, select an existing pilot user who already exists in IAM Identity Center (People).

Open the user and navigate to the Applications tab.

Assign the AWS IAM Identity Center app to this test user.

Wait 5–10 minutes for SCIM sync to run.

In the IAM Identity Center console, select Users and confirm that the pilot user still has the same user ID, that no duplicate user was created, and that the user’s assignments still work.

Note: If the user is duplicated or doesn’t update after 10 minutes, check the Okta System Log for SCIM provisioning errors and verify the SCIM endpoint URL and token are correctly configured.

After the pilot user is taken over successfully, assign the remaining users and groups to the application in Okta. For large directories, assign them in batches.

Phase 4: Verify takeover

Now that you’ve completed cutover, verify that Okta has taken over all users and groups and that the preserved assignments match your pre-migration baseline.

4.1 – Verify SCIM takeover:

Confirm that all production users and groups are provisioned from Okta, that they keep the same user and group IDs, and that no duplicates were created. Check the Okta provisioning logs for errors such as “Refused to create a new, duplicate resource.”

4.2 – Check for assignment drift: Compare the live assignments against the pre-migration CSV

```bash python -m idc_migration_tool validate --csv ./export/assignments.csv --output-dir ./export ```

If drift is found, the script writes a drift_report.csv file with MISSING and EXTRA entries. Because assignments are preserved, investigate any entries before you continue.

Phase 5: Post-migration validation

After the cutover, validate end-to-end access for representative user roles and confirm that assignments were preserved.

5.1 – Test end-to-end access:

Using a test Okta user account, complete the following validation steps:

Sign in to the Okta Dashboard.

Choose the AWS IAM Identity Center tile under My Apps.

Select an assigned AWS account from the portal.

Confirm that you can assume a role and access the AWS console.

Test role switching within the console to validate permission boundaries.

5.2 – Spot-check multiple user types:

Validate access for a representative sample of users across different access levels, including Administrator, Developer, Read-Only or Audit, and any other standard roles defined in your environment. Confirm that permission sets are correctly mapped and that no unintended access has been granted or denied.

For each application, confirm that user-specific data and settings are intact and that any assignments inside the application still work.

Phase 6: Post-migration cleanup and monitoring

After confirming the migration is stable, shift focus to ongoing monitoring of provisioning and authentication, and update your operational documentation.

6.1 – Decommission AD only when stable:

Don’t decommission the Active Directory domain controllers until you’re confident the migration is stable and rollback is no longer needed. Keep AD online as a fallback. Deleting the AD directory removes the manual rollback option and the AD-based access portal endpoint.

The following command will identify disabled users, empty groups, and unassigned permission sets.

```bash # Report only python -m idc_migration_tool cleanup # Report and prompt for deletion python -m idc_migration_tool cleanup --delete ```

6.2 – Monitor SCIM sync:

Confirm that SCIM provisioning continues to run without errors in the days following migration.

Monitor new user onboarding from Okta to verify that newly created Okta users are automatically provisioned into IAM Identity Center.

Review IAM Identity Center and AWS CloudTrail logs for failed sign-in attempts or unexpected authentication errors.

6.3 – Update documentation:

Update all internal documentation to reflect the new identity architecture:

Record the SCIM integration details, SAML metadata links, and new group-to-permission-set mappings.

Update internal SOPs and onboarding guides to reflect the new Okta-based login process.

Document troubleshooting procedures for the most common failure modes.

6.4 – Post-migration checklist:

Before closing the migration project, confirm all of the following:

Users can authenticate successfully through Okta.

Permission sets are correctly assigned to the correct users and groups.

Account assignments are working correctly across accounts.

Monitoring and logging are configured and alerting on anomalies.

Internal documentation and SOPs are updated.

Support team is trained on the new login process.

Rollback procedures have been reviewed and are ready if needed.

Active Directory integration cleanup is scheduled (do not rush decommission).

Phase 7: Rollback (if needed)

Rollback requires manually switching the identity source back to Active Directory, which deletes users, groups, memberships and assignments, and then rebuilding assignments from the pre-migration backup files, as described in the following steps.

Note: Define in advance what counts as a failure, who makes the rollback decision, and the acceptable discrepancy threshold. Only initiate rollback if the Okta migration has failed and cannot be recovered within the migration window. Rollback is a manual, time-consuming process. There is no single-button undo for an identity source switch.

7.1 – Switch identity source back to Active Directory:

Navigate to IAM Identity Center and choose Settings, then Actions, and then Change Identity Source.

Select Active Directory as the identity source.

Select your existing AD domain. Ensure AD is still running and reachable before confirming.

Accept the conditions and confirm the switch. Identity Center will display progress updates.

When complete, choose Resume Sync, then choose Start Guided Setup.

Confirm the attribute mappings and select the users and groups to sync.

Review and save the configuration.

7.2 – Wait for AD users and groups to repopulate:

After completing the guided setup, AD users and groups will begin to reappear in IAM Identity Center through the directory sync. This might take several minutes depending on the size of your directory.

7.3 – Recreate account assignments:

Recreate the assignments from the pre-migration CSV file. This will resolve each principal name in identity store, create the assignment, and poll until completion, and produce a summary of succeeded, failed, and skipped counts.

```bash python -m idc_migration_tool cutover --csv ./export/assignments.csv ```

7.4 – Validate access:

Confirm users can authenticate using the original AD-based AWS access portal URL and can access their expected AWS accounts and roles. Test key role types (such as Admin, Developer, and Audit) before declaring rollback complete.

Troubleshooting the cutover

The identity source change in Step 3.2 runs as a sequence of steps: stopping Active Directory sync, disconnecting the directory, and deleting the AD sync profile. If a step after “Stopping Active Directory sync” fails, the Confirm change screen reports which steps failed and offers a Retry failed steps button. You will see one of two error messages, both safe to retry:

“The identity source change could not be completed. Please try again.” — AD sync was stopped but the directory wasn’t disconnected, so new users and changes are not currently syncing from Active Directory. Choose Retry failed steps to complete the transition. If instead you want to stay on Active Directory, choose Start guided setup in the Settings page to reconfigure the sync.

“The identity source change could not be completed. Your identity source has been reverted to Active Directory. Please try again.” — IAM Identity Center automatically rolled back to a healthy AD-connected state, and a banner confirms that AD sync resumed. You don’t need to reconfigure the sync; choose Retry failed steps when you’re ready to try again.

Important: In both cases, choose Retry failed steps on the Confirm change screen. If you navigate away from this screen, you can no longer retry the failed steps and will need to restart the identity source change.

For troubleshooting tips, see Troubleshooting IAM Identity Center issues.

If you have feedback about this post, submit comments in the Comments section below.

Conclusion

This post covered how to migrate your IAM Identity Center identity source from Active Directory to an external identity provider (Okta), including backing up existing assignments, validating your target identity source, performing the cutover, verifying that the new identity source took over your users and groups with their assignments intact, validating access, and rolling back if needed.

For the backup and restore scripts referenced in this guide, see the aws-samples GitHub repository. For more information about IAM Identity Center configuration and permission set management, visit the AWS Security Blog and the AWS IAM Identity Center documentation.

Title: Close Identity Gaps in Software Development Before Unleashing AI
Context: Artificial intelligence is complicating security in the software development life cycle, but a Dark Reading roundtable found collaboration, better identity visibility, and...
Full Text:
When Renee Guttmann ran her first Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) meeting in New York City in the early 2000s, the general sentiment among the industry (and attendees) was one of skepticism. Why on earth would anyone care about scanning Web applications for vulnerabilities?

Flash forward 20-plus years, and Guttmann, founder of security consultancy Cisohive, no longer has to beat down doors to get people to listen. Initiatives like OWASP, which aims to improve software security, are now regularly invited into software development life cycle (SDLC) conversations to help developers and teams embed secure software practices throughout planning, testing, deployment, and maintenance.

However, the ever-expanding attack surface and the increasing amounts of code written by non-developers or artificial intelligence (AI) has made that goal more challenging. Yet experts also see opportunity, as increased collaboration among teams, better visibility into identities to pinpoint the most vulnerable attack vector, and technologies that decrease patching costs offer teams a blueprint for keeping pace.

Related:When AppSec Scanners Become a Supply Chain Attack Vector

The sheer volume of vulnerabilities being uncovered by AI and rapidly evolving AI security needs mean the ways security has been integrated into the SDLC needs to be updated to fit the current threat landscape.

It's a Great Time for Collaboration

During an exclusive Dark Reading roundtable discussion in early October about shifting the SDLC security focus, Guttmann stressed that it is far easier to bring security and development teams together than it used to be. Security teams and CISOs have moved from being outsiders to sought-after collaborators as organizations recognize the importance of integrating security earlier and more frequently in software development. Security teams can do more from the onset in what Guttmann called "radical collaboration."

Leadership, including boards and shareholders, is looking for more guardrails — not just policy, but the ability to implement solutions for writing clean code, she explained. Now is the time to go back to developers, including user developers outside of IT, and establish partnerships to embed security scanning more deeply into the development environment, she said.

"It's a great time for us to exercise the momentum that's been built for us, to really be partners and active in the space," Guttmann said.

Fellow roundtable panelist Bobby Bauer, CISO of BlueFlag Security, said communication between the security team and the rest of the company is a big opportunity.

Related:Robinhood Cuts Access Approval Time to Support High-Velocity Development

"[There are] lots of things that people don't know [that] security does for them," he said, pointing to legacy software, which is often secured quietly in the background so updates don't slow down business processes, as one primary example of work that goes unnoticed by the rest of the company.

"As we start to get included at the beginning of the process, then we're also allowed to have a voice in that whole process as well," Bauer said, calling it a "big improvement."

Fix First, Go Fast Later

Organizations content with many risks as they juggle long lists of vulnerabilities they need to patch, not to mention all of the possible issues hiding in open source components and AI-generated code. But Bauer warned that the identity space is the most wide-open attack vector right now.

The current development life cycle is flooded with non-human identities. A recent Entro report found that the average enterprise environment has 144 non-human identities for every single human identity. Applications, bots, AI agents, and devices can communicate with systems without human oversight, which challenges visibility. If guardrails are not established, it could lead to shared, weak, or long-lived credentials that an attacker will find and abuse to breach an organization.

Related:For Enterprises, Security Remains Agentic AI's Biggest Challenge

Recent studies have shown that there isn't a single source of truth for these identities, especially non-human ones, Guttmann said, and organizations may not know what they can access or their level of authorization they have. She cited a Cloud Security Alliance study that found 68% of organizations can't distinguish between actions performed by AI agents and those performed by humans.

Therefore, it's important for organizations to provide short-lived credentials for these identities and establish a process to log the agent's activity and the whole life cycle, she recommended.

Security teams are using AI to develop code faster; that speed is not going away, and agents will make up a big part of it, said Rusty Perry, former VP of cybersecurity strategy at Western Union, during the roundtable discussion. In order for teams to move fast safely, they need to ditch the assumption that they always know who or what is acting within their systems, he said.

"For me, it's fix that first and then you can really kind of go as fast as you want," Perry said.

The boom in AI-generated code has upended the long-standing assumption that every line of code in an application was written by a human — one with clear intentions and accountability. Source code and the broader SDLC environment is a huge attack surface that has been traditionally underserved, said Aftab Banth, former global enterprise head of security for TikTok, during the roundtable discussion. He noted that BlueFlag gave organizations visibility into where gaps exist and the ability to quickly remediate those gaps.

BlueFlag also gives security teams direct visibility into which development tools have administrative rights to pipelines or repositories and breaks down barriers between security and engineering teams. Guttman said she didn't realize how much risk she had in that area, particularly when it came to acquisitions.

"I always joke that it's not the doors in your house; it's a small one that you forgot about that ends up being your biggest risk," Guttman said.

Does AI Actually Benefit SDLC?

However, even as AI has complicated the SDLC, AI models and tools also help organizations reduce costs, Banth said. Securing code can now be as cheap as creating it, which opens new creative avenues for security teams. While attackers are using AI to find vulnerabilities or develop exploits more quickly, Banth said remediation is the greatest benefit he has observed from AI in software security.

"We talk a lot about [vulnerability] velocity and, sure, that has increased. But for the first time, the ability to fix, or at least find a patch, has become close to zero," he added.

Guttmann agreed, noting that AI helps identify vulnerabilities at machine speed. The first time she conducted a system test in the early 2000s, a vendor charged her company $75,000 to test if the code was vulnerable. Now she can't imagine telling an organization it will cost that much to test one unit.

"I think the next shoe that's dropping, if it hasn't already, is the ability for AI to predict the impact of automating the patch or the fix," she said. "I think AI is giving us that ability to actually apply patches and fix things more quickly, with greater confidence."

Title: Head of AI Security Roles Surge in Large Organizations
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
A head of AI security role has been established in 65% of large organizations with an annual revenue of $10bn plus, according to new data.

The research, conducted by IANS and Artico Search, found that large businesses are taking steps to update their security organizational structure to enhance accountability and board level oversight for enterprise AI governance.

Around a fifth (18%) of all $10bn+ firms have made the head of AI security a dedicated position, while 47% combined it with another leadership role, making it “one of the fastest emerging functional roles,” according to the researchers.

Head of AI security was observed to be less common in medium and small companies, with the position established in 9% of organizations with a revenue of $1-$10bn, and 6% in firms with under $1bn in revenue.

Steve Martano, IANS Faculty and partner at Artico Search’s cyber practice, commented: “The growth of AI is creating a premium for leaders who can bridge technical security, risk and compliance while still understanding how the business wants to use the technology.”

AI Governance Rarely Falls Under the CISO Remit

The IANS report, published on October 20, found that despite the growth of dedicated head of AI security roles in large organizations, overall accountability for enterprise AI governance remains unsettled.

CISOs hold primary accountability in 26% of small businesses, in 11% of medium firms and just 7% of large organizations. The position that most often is held accountable for AI governance in large businesses are chief AI officers, at 22%.

Read now: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds

Across all three tiers, 14-19% of organizations reported that no single executive is accountable.

In addition, most organizations have not yet fully implemented a board committee dedicated to AI ethics or responsible AI, with 43-48% across all three tiers stating that they have no such committee planned.

Martano said organizations must restructure security teams to ensure that their governance strategies keep pace with rapid AI adoption.

“Companies need to strategically think about what they need from the function and whether they can develop that expertise internally before going to an increasingly competitive external market,” he noted.

Experience the Biggest Dictator of Security Pros’ Pay

The report assessed experience level as the single biggest driver of compensation differences in the same role – more significant than factors such as company size and geographic location.

In $10bn+ businesses, security professionals with eight to 15 years’ experience earn about $35,000 more than those with fewer than eight years’ experience.

The gap grows to around $50,000 between early-career staff and professionals with more than 16 years’ experience.

In large businesses, the average salary for Deputy CISOs was $350,000 per annum.

BISOs earnt a similar amount on average, at $342,000.

Data around average compensation levels for CISOs was not included in the report.

Title: How Do Financial Institutions Measure and Control Cyber Risk?
Context: Identify available policies that are not enforced, test relevant attack paths and document coverage and exceptions
Full Text:
What do financial regulations require institutions to demonstrate about cybersecurity controls?

Across five major regulatory regimes, financial institutions are expected to demonstrate effective management of technology risk and operational resilience. The requirements differ by jurisdiction, but they share an emphasis on accountable management, appropriate controls and evidence that those controls work.

United States: NYDFS Part 500 NYDFS Part 500 connects cybersecurity safeguards with executive accountability. For covered entities subject to the relevant provisions, annual submissions must be supported by evidence of material compliance or an acknowledgment identifying noncompliance and remediation. The regulation also addresses vulnerability management, access controls and tested incident response and recovery.

Runtime evidence can contribute to that record when it shows how an applicable control operated.

Canada: OSFI OSFI B-13 sets expectations for technology and cyber risk management, including control testing, asset inventories, preventive defenses and recovery.

E-21 connects that work to critical operations, dependencies, disruption tolerances and scenario testing. Full adherence was expected by September 1, 2026, with scenario testing for all critical operations to be completed by September 1, 2027. B-10 retains the institution’s accountability for third party arrangements.

A blocked container action becomes more useful when the institution can connect it to the critical operation it protects.

European Union: DORA DORA places ultimate responsibility for ICT risk with the management body. Its requirements cover ICT risk management, incident reporting, resilience testing and third party risk.

For financial entities subject to Article 24, appropriate tests must cover ICT systems and applications supporting critical or important functions at least annually. Control results should therefore inform remediation and the wider assessment of operational resilience.

Singapore: MAS MAS combines binding technology risk and cyber hygiene notices with supervisory guidance on technology risk, outsourcing and business continuity. For banks, the relevant notices are FSM-N05 and FSM-N06.

MAS emphasizes recoverable critical IT systems, customer information protection and critical business services with external dependencies.

A consultation on further technology risk management notice amendments ran from June 10 to July 31, 2026. Those proposals should be distinguished from requirements already in force.

Australia: APRA The Australian Prudential Regulation Authority places control effectiveness and operational resilience under board oversight.

CPS 234 requires information security controls proportionate to the information assets they protect, with systematic testing of effectiveness. CPS 230 connects operational risk to critical operations, disruption tolerances, tested continuity plans and oversight of material service providers.

For a payment service, runtime test results can help demonstrate which supporting workloads are protected, alongside evidence that the service can continue or recover within its tolerances.

Context: These insights can support security, governance, exposure analysis, threat detection, and automated remediation across the Varonis platform

Title: AI Agent Adoption Creates Risk as Oversight Struggles to Keep Pace, Splunk Finds
Context: Attackers Hide Malware Behind Signed ChatGPT and Claude Binaries Attackers Exploit Teams External Chat to Breach Organizations in Under 15 Minutes Online Scam Volumes Double to...
Full Text:
Businesses are rolling out AI agents across their networks much faster than they can implement monitoring procedures and security controls, leaving organizations exposed to security threats, hallucinations and other common issues associated with the technology.

Published by Cisco on October 20, the2026 Splunk State of Observability warned that while many businesses are keen to explore the potential benefits of using AI in their ecosystem, many do so without a strategy in place to ensure it is being used safely.

According to the 2050 ITOps and engineering respondents, 38% said their organization does not yet have clearly defined ownership and accountability for monitoring AI.

Much of this confusion stems from how responsibility for deployment and monitoring of AI agents cuts across traditional boundaries within the IT department such as software engineering, infrastructure management, web development and information security.

Read more: Agentic AI will Supercharge Cyber Threats. But Not the Way You Think

This fragmentation has made it difficult to monitor the use of AI within the organization and 42% of those surveyed said that their main challenge in observing AI is that a different team is responsible for it.

“When agent observability is everyone’s job, it becomes nobody’s job,” said Mark Woods, field CTO and chief technical advisor for EMEA at Splunk.

Organizations Struggle to Manage AI Agents at Scale

Many IT and security teams are also struggling to keep up the potentially unintended consequences of swift rollout of AI tools within the enterprise. For example, while 85% of respondents said that having visibility into AI hallucinations is important, only 58% said that their organization can effectively monitor for potential AI hallucinations.

For many organizations, identifying when an AI agent is making or acting upon an error is difficult and they might not have a means of preventing the action from happening.

This could lead to negative consequences for the business. For example, a malicious attacker could take advantage of an AI agent to trick it into exposing sensitive information. If an organization had appropriate monitoring tools in place, this kind of activity could be prevented.

"Managing agents at scale requires reimagining both security and observability. Have our agents been compromised? Are they doing their job well? In the world of agentic AI, these questions are inseparable, and they're moving at machine speed,” said Jeetu Patel, president and CPO at Cisco.

“This report shows that observability and security data are converging, and that teams need to collaborate more than ever. Common data platforms that help us detect and respond to issues in real-time are the key to deploying agents we can trust at scale,” he added.

The report also noted that when AI agents are deployed correctly, they can provide a significant boost to IT and security teams.

Of those surveyed, 86% said that the deployment of AI had improved the speed at which they are able to detect IT or security issues and 36% classed that improvement as “significant”.

However, while the majority of those surveyed said that agentic AI had made them more efficient at work, some disagreed: 14% suggested that the deployment of AI agents had made issues harder to detect and resolve. One of the main issues cited was the extra time it took to double check if what the agent was saying was correct.

Title: The New Release Metric: Less Cleanup Per Release
Context: A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project,...
Full Text:
AI makes it easier to create code. That does not automatically make software easier to ship.

A team can move from an idea to a pull request in minutes, then lose those gains to a failed build, a dependency conflict, a late finding, or an upgrade that was not worth making. The code arrived faster. But the release did not.

That gap matters when engineering leaders evaluate the effectiveness of AI-assisted development. Code output shows how much activity a tool generates. It does not show how much production-ready software reaches users, or how much unplanned work teams take on along the way.

A more useful question is: How much avoidable cleanup does each release require? The answer reveals how much of AI's speed advantage survives the trip from pull request to production.

Code Volume Is the Wrong Scoreboard

Code volume is the wrong scoreboard because it measures how much code a team produces, not how much production-ready software it ships. In AI-assisted development, that matters even more.

More generated code means more tests to review, more dependencies to validate, more pull requests to untangle, and more changes that may need to be rolled back. Agents can add, replace, and update components quickly, but each dependency decision can affect compatibility, maintainability, licensing, and security.

The result can look like progress: more code, more pull requests, more activity. Yet releases may still take longer because teams have to resolve the downstream work those changes create.

If AI-assisted delivery is improving, teams should see less avoidable cleanup, such as:

Dependency-related build failures and rework.

Late findings that require teams to replace components and retest.

Rollbacks and emergency fixes tied to dependency changes.

Unnecessary upgrades and version changes.

Time spent investigating components that entered the workflow.

Planned engineering work displaced by urgent remediation.

These signals matter alongside delivery speed and reliability. Fewer cleanup tasks do not represent progress if teams are shipping less or accepting more production risk.

Cleanup Is Where AI Gains Disappear

AI-assisted development delivers less value when teams spend the time saved during coding to resolve issues that surface later.

A dependency problem discovered after development has started can interrupt feature work while an engineer investigates the component, finds an alternative, updates the project, reruns tests, and determines whether a release is affected.

If the issue reaches a build or release, the work can extend to:

Identifying where the component was used and what it could access.

Replacing the dependency and validating affected builds.

Assessing whether credentials, systems, or releases may have been exposed.

That work appears as release churn, missed delivery dates, and engineers pulled away from planned work. It is easy to miss in an AI adoption dashboard, especially if the dashboard focuses on code generated or pull requests completed.

Not every build failure or dependency issue can be prevented at the point of intake. But known malicious packages are one avoidable source of downstream work. Blocking them before they are served through the repository path can keep them out of developer and build workflows in the first place.

Measure the Work Behind Each Release

Measure cleanup per release by tracking the dependency issues that trigger unplanned work and the time teams spend resolving them.

Start with a baseline and follow the trend across comparable releases.

Useful signals include:

Dependency-related build failures: How often do dependency issues cause failed builds, retries, or rework?

Late-stage findings: How many component issues surface after development has started or a release is in motion?

Dependency-related rollbacks and emergency fixes: How often do component changes contribute to release instability?

Remediation time: How long does it take to investigate a dependency issue and land a validated fix?

Engineering time redirected: How much planned work is displaced by dependency cleanup and release interruptions?

While tracking cleanup work is critical to understand the effort involved to ship production-ready code, tracking preventative measures like blocked malicious packages is equally as important. A blocked request is not a cleanup task, but it shows that a known malicious component was stopped before it could become one.

The point is not to create another vanity metric. It's to give engineering leaders a clearer view of where release effort goes, what causes avoidable rework, and whether teams are getting more useful work through to production.

Make the Trusted Path Easy to Use

Developers and agents should be able to request components through the repository they already use, with security checks applied in that path. Developers should not have to recognize every suspicious package name or track every attack campaign, and teams need a way to evaluate agent requests even when people are not reviewing each choice in real time.

Adding a ticket or manual approval to every dependency choice would move the bottleneck, not eliminate it. Consistent controls belong in the path developers, pipelines, and agents already use.

Sonatype Nexus Repository provides a one trusted place to proxy, store, and distribute the components and build inputs teams rely on. Sonatype introduced Pro+ and Enterprise editions to help address a growing source of release cleanup: dependency decisions that outpace manual review. Both editions add malicious package protection and configurable policies to Nexus Repository, so teams can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds.

This does not prevent every dependency conflict, late vulnerability finding, or release issue. Teams still need testing and other controls throughout development. Repository protection addresses one specific problem earlier: known malicious packages entering through the managed repository path.

Sonatype Guide extends that trusted path into dependency selection and remediation. It helps developers and AI agents evaluate components in context, choose safer versions, and address risk in the codebase with guided fixes. Together, Nexus Repository and Guide help teams make better dependency choices up front and spend less time correcting them later.

Measure the Release, Not the Output

AI increases activity across the software development life cycle: more code, more pull requests, and more dependency changes. The better test is if teams can turn that activity into reliable releases with less unplanned work.

Track dependency-related build failures, late fixes, and remediation time across comparable releases. If those costs fall while delivery remains reliable, teams are getting more from faster code generation.

This is why Nexus Repository now offers Pro+ and Enterprise to help teams keep the speed of AI assisted development from becoming more dependency cleanup and release time. Both editions can block known malicious packages before they reach developers and builds, giving developers and agents a trusted route to software inputs while teams focus on getting releases out the door.

Title: The ballot box meets the bot.
Context: Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections.
Full Text:
State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security. Stolen credentials force ConnectWise to suspend cloud services. Fake calendar invites steal Microsoft logins. Temu settles Texas privacy allegations. Toronto police arrest seven in a cryptocurrency kidnapping case. The G7 sounds the alarm on quantum threats. Monday business briefing. Ben Yelin, sits down with Kevin Tian, CEO and Co-Founder of Doppel, to share how AI is changing the threat landscape for sports organizations. MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

Today is Monday October 19th 2026. I’m Dave Bittner. And this is your CyberWire Intel Briefing.

State election officials question CISA’s commitment to election security.

According to ProPublica, political appointees at the Department of Homeland Security asked CISA to secretly acquire and hack a voting machine, then report its findings to the White House. Career employees resisted, concerned the results could be used to challenge election outcomes. The request was eventually dropped.

The revelation comes amid a dramatic retreat from CISA’s election security mission. Since President Trump returned to office, the agency has lost more than a thousand employees, roughly a third of its workforce, while cutting critical monitoring and support services.

State election officials say CISA was largely absent during preparations for November’s midterms. Meanwhile, the administration’s release of previously confidential election security information has damaged relationships built over years of cooperation.

CISA finally released an election security plan in late September, but state officials say it arrived too late to make much difference. Several now question whether they can trust the agency with sensitive information.

Meanwhile, the FBI and CISA released a joint warning that AI-generated phishing attacks could threaten November’s midterm elections. Election officials, candidates, and political organizations are attractive targets because of their access to sensitive voter and campaign information.

Attackers are using AI to produce convincing emails, text messages, and deepfake audio and video, eliminating traditional warning signs like poor grammar.

The agencies recommend phishing-resistant multifactor authentication, stronger email filtering, and independent verification of suspicious requests.

The alert describes an emerging threat rather than a specific ongoing attack.

ConnectWise suspends its Cloud Backup service following stolen credentials.

ConnectWise has suspended its Cloud Backup service and taken two other cloud services offline after attackers stole credentials associated with seven application identities, potentially exposing customer Microsoft 365 environments.

The stolen credentials allowed attackers to impersonate trusted ConnectWise applications without needing customer passwords.

Security firm Huntress identified suspicious sign-ins across roughly a thousand Microsoft tenants, including approximately 300 successful authentications. Researchers also observed a targeted campaign against 16 organizations in sensitive sectors, though those attempts failed.

ConnectWise says it has disabled the compromised credentials and found no evidence that encrypted backup archives were accessed.

However, backups and restoration services remain unavailable. Huntress warns that attackers may have established persistent access inside affected tenants before the credentials were revoked, making additional investigation essential.

Calendar invites steal credentials.

Cybercriminals are turning ordinary calendar invitations into credential-stealing traps. Researchers at Check Point identified more than 300,000 unique phishing emails targeting over 40,000 organizations, disguised as Microsoft Teams meetings and other workplace appointments.

The invitations contain links to counterfeit Microsoft login pages designed to capture usernames and passwords. Some include legitimate calendar attachments, making the invitations appear more convincing.

The campaign has accelerated dramatically, with Check Point recording more than 740,000 messages during the first two weeks of October alone.

Researchers emphasize that attackers aren’t exploiting vulnerabilities in Microsoft products. Instead, they’re exploiting employees’ familiarity with routine meeting requests.

Check Point recommends checking unexpected invitations carefully and using phishing-resistant authentication, such as passkeys or hardware security keys, to protect accounts against credential theft.

Temu settles with Texas over privacy allegations.

Chinese online retailer Temu has agreed to pay Texas three million dollars to settle allegations that it improperly collected user data potentially accessible to the Chinese government.

The agreement requires Temu to store personal data on U.S. servers and restrict transfers to China. It also mandates independent product safety testing and stronger consumer protections.

Violations of certain data security provisions could trigger annual penalties of eight million dollars.

Temu denies wrongdoing. Several other states have filed similar lawsuits, making Texas the first to reach a settlement.

Toronto police make arrests in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner.

Toronto police have arrested seven men in connection with the alleged kidnapping of a cryptocurrency exchange owner, including three active members of the Canadian Armed Forces.

Investigators say the victim was abducted at gunpoint in July, handcuffed, and assaulted as his captors attempted to access cryptocurrency holdings and business security systems. He was eventually released after being threatened not to contact police.

The investigation uncovered an extensive collection of weapons, including firearms with 3D-printed receivers, silencers, and more than 2,700 rounds of ammunition. Approximately 2,500 rounds were allegedly stolen from the Canadian military.

Police also seized substantial quantities of illicit drugs, GPS tracking devices, and other equipment.

The seven suspects face a combined 82 charges. The investigation remains ongoing.

The G7 urges post-quantum readiness.

The G7 is urging governments and businesses to accelerate their transition to post-quantum cryptography, warning that quantum computing could eventually undermine widely used encryption systems.

In a call to action led by France’s national cybersecurity agency, the group argues that quantum threats should be treated as a near-term concern, even though the timeline for developing cryptographically capable quantum computers remains uncertain.

The recommendations include identifying critical systems, inventorying cryptographic assets, and developing phased migration plans. Organizations are encouraged to incorporate quantum-safe technologies into routine equipment upgrades to reduce costs.

The G7 also calls for national strategies, additional research, public-private partnerships, and updated cybersecurity requirements.

France plans to begin rejecting security products without quantum-safe encryption during certification reviews starting in 2027.

Monday business briefing.

Investment in AI-driven cybersecurity continues to attract substantial funding, with eight companies announcing rounds totaling nearly $143 million.

San Francisco-based Harmonic Security leads the pack with a $50 million Series B, followed by Israeli startups Pluto Security, raising $42 million, and Rein Security, securing $25 million.

Other recipients include France’s Netsec and Fleuret AI, Tennessee-based Hilt, London’s CodeWall, and Utah’s Guardrail Technologies. The funding will support product development, hiring, and international expansion.

On the acquisition front, quantum computing company IonQ has agreed to purchase zero-trust security firm Elisity in an all-stock deal valued at up to $1.3 billion.

CrowdStrike is reportedly negotiating a $500 million acquisition of Israeli data loss prevention startup Orion Security.

Meanwhile, government contractor SAIC has acquired cryptographic software provider Information Security Corporation, and Singapore-based V-Key has announced a majority investment in AI security firm CloudsineAI.

MapQuest puts surveillance on the map.

MapQuest, the venerable mapping service that once helped drivers navigate the world with printed directions and a healthy supply of printer ink, has found a new way to stay relevant.

Its latest mobile app update introduces a surveillance layer that shows users the locations and directions of known license plate readers and outdoor security cameras.

The feature covers equipment from Flock Safety, Motorola Solutions, Axon, Verkada, and several other surveillance vendors.

Flock alone reportedly operates at least 120,000 cameras across the United States, and independent projects have already been mapping their locations.

Now MapQuest is bringing that information directly into its navigation app, helping users identify surveillance infrastructure along their routes.

Apparently, the company that once helped you avoid getting lost can now help you see who’s watching you.

And that’s the CyberWire.

Title: OpenAI Engineer Accused of Spying on Executives Ordered to Remain in Custody
Context: “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said
Full Text:
The former OpenAI engineer accused of bugging a company conference room must stay in custody while he awaits trial, a federal judge ruled on Monday after expressing concerns about his ties to Saudi Arabia.

US prosecutors alleged Abdulrahman Alfozan is a flight risk because the Saudi Arabian government has offered to support him with no strings attached. They cited, for example, the Saudi consulate’s offer to work with a bail bonds firm to help fund Alfozan’s release.

Federal magistrate judge Alex Tse questioned whether Alfozan is an “asset” for the kingdom and how a bond backed by the government could keep him in the country. “I find that problematic,” Tse said. “It seems like a blank check. ‘We’re going to pay whatever the court wants to get him out.’ I’m more interested in people from his family wanting to put up assets.”

William Pernik, an attorney for Alfozan, dismissed the flight risk worries as baseless. But he failed to convince the judge that Alfozan was committed to his life in the US. “There is a real threat here that once he leaves the case is over,” Tse said.

Aflozan appeared in an orange prison uniform and a medical face mask pulled down over his neck on Monday in Tse’s San Francisco courtroom, which was filled to capacity with journalists, students on a field trip, and about 20 people supporting Alfozan.

Employee attempts to steal confidential company information are common in Silicon Valley. But Alfozan’s case has drawn international attention for the alleged amateur spycraft and geopolitical tensions at the center of it. Authorities haven’t offered a potential motive but have noted Alfozan has worked for a Saudi venture capital firm, offered consulting services to Saudi companies, and is supposedly friendly with people high up in the Saudi government.

Pernik said there is no evidence of Alfozan spying for Saudi Arabia or engaging in something covert. “It’s not as if he sneaked in under the covers of darkness,” he said of the OpenAI conference room. “This was an open room where anybody could work in.” The Saudi embassy didn’t respond to a request for comment.

After the hour-long hearing, Pernik told reporters he was disappointed with the custody ruling and would continue to try to fight it.

While Alfozan is a US permanent resident who had been on the path to obtaining citizenship, his ties to his native Saudi Arabia have come under scrutiny. Prosecutors allege that Alfozan was “in frequent communications via WhatsApp” with a member of the Saudi royal family throughout 2025 and 2026.

Context: Because AI agents are becoming a new class of identity with real permissions, you must understand how an attacker could compromise and abuse them
Full Text:
Discover how to secure AI agents in your cloud environment with Tenable One Cloud Exposure. We explore Microsoft Entra Agent ID and provide essential best practices for robust agentic AI identity security.

Key takeaways

Understand your current maturity level and then build an appropriate action plan to secure your agent identities.

As AI agents move from experimental toys to tools that make autonomous decisions, interact with databases, and call external APIs, organizations need to be clear on who — or what — is executing these actions in their cloud environments.

Why non-human identities (NHIs) aren’t secure enough for AI agents

Security teams categorize identities into two buckets: human identities and non-human identities (NHIs), such as service accounts, secrets, and automated scripts.

Treating AI agents as standard NHIs is a recipe for disaster. AI agents combine their non-deterministic nature with their ability to execute flexible, outcome-oriented actions, rather than following strict, prescribed instructions.

Unlike classic, predictable scripts that follow rigid code paths, AI agents:

Make creative, runtime decisions using LLMs.

Interact with dynamic external tools, memory caches, and knowledge bases.

Constantly adapt to solve problems, making it difficult for a security team to establish AI agents’ baseline behavior.

To address this challenge, major cloud providers have introduced dedicated, specialized agentic AI identity models. Let’s break down one major model: Microsoft Entra Agent ID.

Announcing Tenable One Cloud Exposure support for Microsoft Entra Agent ID

Identity and cloud providers' native identity management tools present only basic information about agentic identities, without providing context about their security flaws and how they extend your attack surface. Because AI agents are becoming a new class of identity with real permissions, you must understand how an attacker could compromise and abuse them. At Tenable, we believe visibility is the foundation of security. You can’t secure assets that you do not know exist.

As organization-wide adoption of agentic AI accelerates, the immediate challenge for security teams is first and foremost finding them. Because these identities are brand new, conventional identity and access management (IAM) systems may not recognize or monitor them, which creates security blind spots.

To help our customers address this issue, Tenable One Cloud Exposure now brings Microsoft Entra agentic AI identities directly into your unified asset and identity inventory.

Microsoft Entra Agent ID Model

The Microsoft Entra Agent ID framework functions through a four-tiered structural model:

Agent identity blueprints serve as the master templates for shared attributes. Residing exclusively within the agent provider’s home tenant, they establish cross-tenant links that heighten exposure to potential supply-chain attacks.

Agent identity blueprint principals are the localized instantiation of a blueprint within every specific tenant where the AI agent is deployed and active.

Agent identities represent the functional identities utilized for routine tasks. To maintain oversight of agent behavior, these are the primary entities your security team must monitor.

Agent users offer an optional layer for each agent identity requiring human-centric features — like Microsoft Teams access or a personal mailbox — to function effectively as integrated “digital colleagues.”
